Two and a half days, twelve weeks, one written paper

The exam is written, 2 hours, any calculator, printed notes only. The Week 13 revision lecture shows the style: derive, sketch, calculate. Work from the sample questions outward: see the target first, then fill in each week.

How to use each topic tab (about 60–90 min per week)
  1. Skim the intuition cards and play with the widget (5 min).
  2. Read each subtopic’s three layers: picture → derivation → recipe. Click a slide link (p. N) to see the lecturer’s page beside it.
  3. Do the guided problems on paper. Open hints one at a time, type your number into the checker, then read the full solution.
  4. Blank-page test: close everything and re-derive the week’s key result.
  5. Mini-quiz, and mark ✓/✗ honestly. Your ✗ counts appear in the table below.

Notation used everywhere on this site

SymbolMeaning
\({}^A\mathbf T_B\)pose of frame {B} expressed in frame {A} (4×4). Maps points from B to A: \({}^A\mathbf P={}^A\mathbf T_B\,{}^B\mathbf P\).
\({}^A\mathbf R_B\), \({}^A\mathbf t_B\)its rotation (columns = B’s axes in A) and translation (B’s origin in A)
\(R_x, R_y, R_z,\; t_x, t_y, t_z\)elementary rotations and translations (right-hand rule); a product of them is an ETS
\(a_{i-1}, \alpha_{i-1}, d_i, \theta_i\)proximal (Craig) DH parameters; link transform \(R_x(\alpha_{i-1})t_x(a_{i-1})R_z(\theta_i)t_z(d_i)\)
\(c_i, s_i, c_{ij}\)\(\cos\theta_i\), \(\sin\theta_i\), \(\cos(\theta_i+\theta_j)\)
\(\mathbf q,\dot{\mathbf q},\ddot{\mathbf q}\)joint positions (rad or m), velocities, accelerations
\(\mathbf J(\mathbf q)\)Jacobian: tool velocity = \(\mathbf J\dot{\mathbf q}\); joint torques for a tool force: \(\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf J^\top\mathbf F\)
\(\mathbf M,\mathbf V,\mathbf G\)mass matrix, Coriolis/centrifugal vector, gravity vector: \(\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf M\ddot{\mathbf q}+\mathbf V+\mathbf G\)
\(M, D, N, J, F_i, R_C, R_M\)mobility; 6 (3D) or 3 (2D); links incl. ground; joints; joint DoF; over-constraints; local mobilities

Exam technique (written, 2 hours, printed notes)
  • Calculator in radians unless a question is in degrees. Write the unit of every angle.
  • Draw frames first. Most FK, IK, Jacobian and dynamics errors are sign errors that a labelled sketch prevents.
  • State the general equation, then substitute (ETS, cosine rule, Euler–Lagrange, G–K, cubic boundary conditions). This is where method marks are.
  • Use atan2 and give every IK branch. Say how many solutions exist and when there are none.
  • Order matters: right-multiply for moves about the current frame. Check the product at θ = 0 against the drawing.
  • Units: mm vs m in link lengths; rad/s vs rpm in wheels; °/s in trajectories.
  • Say what you assume (“no joint limits”, “point masses”, “rest-to-rest”, “rollers ⊥ drive so γ = 0”).
  • Explain answers are 2–4 sentences: claim, reason, consequence (e.g. “det J = 0, so the arm loses a direction of motion; joint speeds blow up nearby”).
  • Stuck? Write the set-up and the equation you would solve. Partial credit is real. Move on, come back.
  • Booklet: start at its index (“if the question says … go to page …”). Don’t read; look up.

Week 1 · Mechanisms

How many ways can it move, and how many motors does it need?

A mechanism is a set of rigid links joined by joints. Its degrees of freedom (DoF, also called mobility) say how many numbers fix its configuration, and so the minimum number of actuators needed to control it. The Grübler–Kutzbach (G–K) equation counts the DoF from the number of links and joints alone. Master that count, and know when it lies.

Lecture: Introduction to mechanisms65 slides (content pp. 18–62) · Dr KM Digumarti · notebook “1 basics of mechanisms”
Open in new tab ↗
How this is examined

Sample questions 6 and 7 are both mobility counts. Q6 (W13 p.12): “Mobility of parallel manipulators”, a planar platform on three R–P–R legs, answered as \(3(8-9-1)+9 = 3\) (W13 p.13). Q7 (W13 pp.14–17): a delta mechanism. Plain G–K gives \(6(11-15-1)+(1+4\times3)\times3 = 9\) (p.15), but the extended equation \(M=D(N-J-1)+\sum F_i+R_C-R_M\) with \(R_C=0,\ R_M=6\) gives 3 (p.17). Week 4 owns the extended equation; this week gives you the count and the habit of checking it.

Where the marks are (indicative; marks not published): the right D (3 planar, 6 spatial); N counted with the ground; J and every Fi listed; the substitution shown; the answer; and, for a delta or a parallel robot, one sentence saying why plain G–K and the real mobility may differ.

Where marks are lost: forgetting the ground link (N one too small); counting the two halves of a prismatic joint as one link; using D = 6 on a planar drawing; treating a drawing’s “3D look” as planar (W13 p.14: the delta “is still 3D despite this depiction”); stopping at 9 for the delta; and writing “M = 0, so it cannot move” without the p.49 caveat.

Practical (optional, no coding in the exam)

The Week 1 practical folder holds test.py and a CoppeliaSim scene testScene.ttt (the scene file was not opened). test.py connects to a running CoppeliaSim through the ZeroMQ remote API, gets the joint /Joint1, turns on stepping mode, starts the simulation, then sets that joint’s target position to 60° (written as 60 * math.pi/180) on every step until 3 s of simulated time have passed, and stops. It exercises one revolute joint (1 DoF). No outputs are saved. The lecture notebook’s seven questions are solved below.

Intuition first

DoF = how many knobs

A coin slid on a table needs three knobs: left–right, forward–back, spin. Pin a stick on a nail and one knob is enough: its angle. DoF counts the independent knobs, nothing else.

Joints take freedom away

Two loose coins have 3 + 3 = 6 knobs. Push a drawing pin through both: the second coin can only spin about the pin, so 3 + 1 = 4 knobs remain. The pin removed 2.

G–K is an allowance sheet

Every moving link starts with D freedoms. Every joint confiscates D, then hands back the F it allows. Ground never spends. What is left is the mobility M.

The third rope that adds nothing

Hang a plank from two equal parallel ropes: it swings, one knob. A third identical rope between the same bars restricts nothing new, but the formula charges for it and says 0. The count assumes every constraint is a fresh one.

Reach vs dexterity

You can touch a spot on a wall (reachable). You can touch it with your palm facing up, down, left and right (dexterous). Everything dexterous is reachable; not the reverse.

1 · Kinematics, mechanisms and kinematic chains pp. 18–26

Picture

Kinematics is the geometry of motion with no forces (p.18). Dynamics is the forces and torques that cause motion, split into statics (no acceleration) and kinetics (acceleration) (p.19). The notebook warns that these words are used loosely in other languages and that the course sticks to this split.

A mechanism is “a mechanical system that transfers/modifies motion and/or forces from one or more sources to one or more outputs” (p.21). A kinematic chain is “a system of rigid bodies connected by joints” (p.22). Parts: links (rigid), joints (allow relative motion), an end effector (touches the world), a base (rigidly fixed to the ground) (p.23).

Classifying chains
WordMeaningExample on the slides
Closed chainforms a closed loop (p.25)gripper linkage, delta robot (p.24)
Open chainnot closedan industrial arm
Serial chainopen chain in which every link except the first and last connects to two other linksan industrial arm (p.24)
Parallel mechanism addedthe end effector is joined to the base through several chains at once, so there are closed loops. The slides show pictures only, no definitionABB FlexPicker delta; Stewart platform

Why use closed loops (p.26): the actuators can sit on the base, so the moving parts are lighter; the load capacity is larger (several legs share it); and loops give interesting motion paths (Strandbeest, Cyber Tiger).

Worked example

A 6-joint industrial arm: open and serial. A delta robot: closed loops, parallel. A four-bar linkage: closed, and no link is a “first” or “last”, so it is not serial. Motor placement is the usual exam justification: a delta’s three motors sit on the base, so the light rods are all that move quickly.

Definition questions here are easy marks lost by a swapped word: kinematics (no forces) against kinetics (forces with acceleration); statics against kinetics. A scenario question asking “why a parallel robot for a fast pick-and-place line” wants: base-mounted actuators, low moving mass, larger load.

2 · Degrees of freedom and joints pp. 27–36

Picture

DoF = “number of independent parameters that define the configuration of a mechanism” (p.27). Link lengths are taken as known; the DoF do not depend on the lengths (notebook). Examples (pp. 28–33): a point in 2D has 2 DoF; a pendulum in 2D has 1 (x and y are tied together by the fixed length, so one angle is enough); a rigid body in 3D has 6 (three translations, three rotations); a rigid body in 2D has 3 (two translations, one rotation; notebook Q1).

Joint types (p.34). The last two columns are added: the constraints a joint removes are \(D - F\).

JointSymbolDoF \(F\)Removes in 3D (\(6-F\))Removes in 2D (\(3-F\))
Revolute (hinge, pin)R152
Prismatic (slider)P152
Helical (screw)H15spatial only
CylindricalC24spatial only
UniversalU24spatial only
Spherical (ball)S33spatial only

The slides list no planar joint, so planar mechanisms in this unit use only R and P.

Derivation

A free rigid body has \(D\) DoF (\(D = 3\) planar, \(D = 6\) spatial). Two free bodies have \(2D\). A joint with \(F\) DoF between them leaves \(F\) relative freedoms, so it removes \(D - F\) of the \(D\) relative freedoms. For the planar revolute pair: \(6 - (3-1) = 4\) (p.36). checked

Typical short question: “how many DoF does a rigid body have in 2D?” (3, not 2: a point has 2, but a body also has orientation), “a rigid body in 3D?” (6), “the DoF of a spherical joint?” (3), “a helical joint?” (1: rotation and translation are locked together by the pitch). Do not confuse the DoF of a joint with the mobility of the mechanism.

3 · Controllable versus total DoF pp. 37–38

Picture

A DoF is controllable if an actuator drives it (a motor on a joint). Unactuated DoF are uncontrollable (p.37). Compare the number of actuators with the total DoF:

Controllable vs totalName on the slide
equalfully actuated
lessunder-actuated: fewer actuators than joints; low cost, simpler design, lower weight (p.38)
more“redundant”
The “redundant” wording

Slide 37 reads, word for word: “Controllable DOF > Total DOF, the robot is called redundant”. Notebook cell 8 adds “An example of this is a 7DOF robot arm in 3D space”. Taken literally these disagree. A serial arm with 7 revolute joints has mobility 7 by G–K, and with 7 motors its controllable DoF equal its total DoF, so by the wording it would be fully actuated.

The standard meaning added is kinematic redundancy: the arm has more joint DoF than the task needs. A 3D end-effector pose has 6 numbers, so a 7-joint arm is redundant (7 > 6), and so is a planar 3R arm used only to position a point (3 > 2). Redundancy gives a family of joint configurations for the same tool pose (the usual use: avoiding obstacles and joint limits).

What to write in the exam: for “fully / under / redundant” compare actuators with the DoF of the mechanism as the slide does; if the question names a 7-DoF arm as redundant, answer “redundant: more joint DoF than the 6-DoF task” and say that you are using this meaning. checked

Worked example

A 6R arm with 6 motors: fully actuated. The same arm with 4 motors: under-actuated (two joints free-swinging). A Stewart platform (M = 6, section 5) with 6 linear actuators: fully actuated. A delta robot with 3 motors and true M = 3: fully actuated, whereas the plain G–K value 9 would wrongly suggest under-actuated. checked

Slides vs notebook

The definition on p.37 and the “7DOF arm” example (notebook cell 8) do not match unless “total DOF” means the task’s pose DoF (6). Use the standard meaning above for redundancy; for under-actuated and fully actuated the slide’s comparison with the mechanism’s DoF is the one to quote.

A scenario question may ask “why build an under-actuated robot?” Answer from p.38: fewer actuators means lower cost, simpler design and lower weight, at the price that not every DoF can be commanded.

4 · Mobility and the Grübler–Kutzbach equation pp. 39–47

Picture

Mobility is the DoF that remain after all joints have applied their constraints. It is the commonly used word for a mechanism, and the “minimum number of actuators you need” (p.39). The equation does bookkeeping: start with every moving link free, subtract what each joint takes, add back what each joint allows. It uses only the topology (how many links, which joints), never the lengths.

Derivation

Form 2 (p.41), the one used in the W13 sample questions:

\[ M = D\,(N-1) - D\,J + \sum_{i=1}^{J}F_i \;=\; D\,(N-J-1)+\sum_{i=1}^{J}F_i \]

\(M\) mobility; \(D = 3\) (planar) or \(6\) (spatial); \(N\) number of links including the grounded link; \(J\) number of joints; \(F_i\) DoF of joint \(i\). The \(N-1\) moving links have \(D(N-1)\) DoF if free; each joint removes \(D\) and returns \(F_i\).

Form 1 (p.40) collects the joints by their DoF, \(P_i\) = number of joints with \(i\) DoF. A joint with \(i\) DoF removes \(D-i\) (section 2):

\[ M_{3D} = 6(N-1) - 5P_1 - 4P_2 - 3P_3 - 2P_4 - P_5, \qquad M_{2D} = 3(N-1) - 2P_1 - P_2 \]

The two forms are the same sum grouped differently: \(\sum_i (D-F_i) = \sum_i (D-i)\,P_i\). checked Both forms agree on every count on this page.

Counting links. Ground is link 0 and counts. A prismatic joint joins two parts that slide on each other (cylinder and rod); these are two links. Several ground pivots are still one link (the ground).

Exam recipe
  1. Decide D: planar drawing with joint axes all perpendicular to the page gives D = 3. Anything with S, U, C, or a note that it is “still 3D” gives D = 6.
  2. Number the links, ground = 0. Split every prismatic joint into its two links.
  3. List every joint with its F (R, P = 1; C, U = 2; S = 3). Count J and \(\sum F_i\).
  4. Substitute into \(M = D(N-J-1)+\sum F_i\) and show the line.
  5. Cross-check with form 1 if time allows.
  6. Sanity checks: a serial chain has \(N = J+1\), so \(M = \sum F_i\); M should be at least 1 for a moving machine; if M is 0 or negative, ask whether constraints are dependent (section 6).
Worked examples from the slides (all planar, D = 3)

Planar serial RPR (pp. 42–43): links 0–3, so \(N = 4\); three 1-DoF joints, \(P_1 = 3\), \(P_2 = 0\).
Form 1: \(M = 3(4-1) - 2\times3 - 1\times0 = 3\). Form 2: \(M = 3(4-3-1) + (1+1+1) = 3\). checked (A serial chain: M = sum of joint DoF.)

Planar four-bar (pp. 44–45, notebook Q2): ground plus three moving bars, \(N = 4\); four revolutes, \(P_1 = 4\).
Form 1: \(M = 3(4-1) - 2\times4 - 0 = 1\). Form 2: \(M = 3(4-4-1) + 4 = 1\). checked One motor on the crank drives the whole linkage.

Planar parallel manipulator (pp. 46–47, notebook Q3; the same figure is W13 Q6): a triangular platform on three R–P–R legs. Links: ground, platform, and \(3\times2\) leg parts (each prismatic joint has a cylinder and a rod), so \(N = 8\). Joints: \(3\times3 = 9\), all 1 DoF.
Form 1: \(M = 3(8-1) - 2\times9 - 0 = 3\). Form 2: \(M = 3(8-9-1) + 9 = 3\). checked Three actuators (one per leg) position the platform’s x, y and angle.

Two extra planar counts added that exam questions like: five-bar (N = 5, five R): \(3(5-5-1)+5 = 2\); slider-crank (N = 4, three R and one P): \(3(4-4-1)+4 = 1\). checked Both are presets in the widget above.

Slides vs notebook

Notebook cell 9 introduces the equation for “simple serial” kinematic chains, yet the slides and notebook then apply it to the closed four-bar and the parallel manipulator, and the answers (1 and 3) are the standard ones. Treat G–K as valid for any rigid-body mechanism whose constraints are independent (the real condition, section 6).

The classic traps are all in the bookkeeping: N without ground (3-RPR gives 0 instead of 3), \(D=6\) on a planar drawing (four-bar gives −2), swapping “constraints removed” with “DoF allowed” (four-bar gives 5), and counting each prismatic joint as one link. Writing the substitution line earns method marks even when the count is off. checked All four wrong answers are reproduced in the check script.

5 · Spatial mechanisms: Stewart platform and the delta p. 48 · W13 pp. 14–17

Picture

The Stewart platform (p.48) is a base and a platform joined by six identical legs. Each leg is ground–U–P–S–platform: a universal joint at the base, a prismatic actuator, a spherical joint at the platform. The slide shows one leg and asks “What is the mobility of this system?” as homework. It gives no answer, so the count below is added.

The delta (W13 Q7, p.14) has a base, a platform and three legs. Each leg is a revolute joint at the base driving an upper arm, then a parallelogram of two rods with a spherical joint at each of its four ends.

Derivation

Stewart platform, D = 6. Links: ground, platform, and \(6\times2\) leg parts (lower cylinder, upper rod), so \(N = 14\). Joints: six U (2 DoF), six P (1), six S (3), so \(J = 18\) and \(\sum F_i = 6(2+1+3) = 36\):

\[ M = 6\,(14-18-1) + 36 = -30 + 36 = 6 \]

Six DoF, driven by the six prismatic actuators: fully actuated, and the platform can take any 3D pose. checked The one leg drawn on p.48 has \(N=4\), \(J=3\): \(M = 6(4-3-1) + 6 = 6\), the same number because a serial chain has \(M=\sum F_i\) (here \(2+1+3\)). checked

Why the U matters added: with an S at both ends of each leg (six SPS), \(\sum F_i = 42\) and \(M = 12\). The extra 6 are the legs spinning about their own axes, which move nothing. The U at the base blocks that spin, so the UPS count of 6 is the real one. checked

Delta, D = 6 (W13 p.14: “still 3D despite this depiction”). Links: base, platform, and per leg one upper arm plus two rods: \(N = 2 + 3\times3 = 11\). Joints: per leg 1 R and 4 S, so \(J = 3\times5 = 15\), \(\sum F_i = (1 + 4\times3)\times3 = 39\) (W13 p.15):

\[ M = 6\,(11-15-1) + 39 = 9 \quad\text{(plain G–K)} \]

The delta’s platform really has 3 DoF (it translates in x, y, z and stays parallel to the base). The six rods each spin freely about their own axis, since a rod has a ball joint at both ends. These six spins are local mobility \(R_M = 6\) and have no effect on the platform. The extended equation (W13 p.16) subtracts them, with \(R_C = 0\) over-constraints (p.17):

\[ M = D(N-J-1) + \sum F_i + R_C - R_M = 6(11-15-1) + 39 + 0 - 6 = 3 \]

checked Week 4 derives \(R_C\) and \(R_M\) in full. For now: plain G–K is a first estimate; local spins add fake DoF (subtract \(R_M\)) and dependent constraints hide real ones (add \(R_C\)).

Exam recipe (W13 Q7 style)
  1. Write D = 6 (state why: spherical joints, “still 3D”).
  2. List the links by name (base, platform, each leg’s parts) and sum to N.
  3. List the joints by leg and sum J and \(\sum F_i\). Each S is 3.
  4. Give the plain answer (9). Then say: six rods spin about their own axes, so \(R_M=6\); with \(R_C = 0\) the extended equation gives 3.
  5. Final check: a delta robot has 3 motors and moves a point in x, y, z, consistent with 3.
A short-answer version expects you to say whether 9 or 3 is wanted. The trap is stopping at the plain-G–K value. If the question only quotes the plain equation, 9 is the answer it wants; if it quotes the extended equation or asks for the platform’s real DoF, it is 3. Read which equation is given.

6 · Where G–K fails pp. 49–51

Picture

Slide 49 shows a body hung from the ground by three legs, each with an R at the ground and an R at the body (the notebook’s Q4 uses the same figure). The count gives 0, “but the system can move: it has 1 degree of freedom!”. The slide’s reason: the equation “assumes that the constraints on motion are independent”; one of the middle links can be removed without changing what the mechanism does, so it is redundant “and should not be counted”.

Counting it, and why it miscounts

Links: ground, three legs, the body: \(N = 5\). Joints: six R, \(P_1 = 6\), \(P_2 = 0\) (p.49):

\[ M = 3(5-1) - 2\times6 - 1\times0 = 0, \qquad\text{form 2: } 3(5-6-1)+6 = 0 \]

Counted 0, real 1. Why, in terms of the geometry added: the unknowns are the three leg angles and the body’s \(x, y, \theta\) (6 numbers); each leg gives two closure equations (6 equations). G–K treats the 6 equations as independent, hence \(6-6 = 0\). But when the three legs are equal in length and parallel, and the body’s pivots are spaced exactly like the ground pivots, the third leg’s two equations are implied by the first two (they say the same thing again). Only 5 of the 6 are independent, leaving 1 free motion. The remedy on the slide, deleting one middle leg, gives \(N=4,\ J=4\): \(M = 3(4-1) - 2\times4 = 1\), the parallelogram four-bar, which is correct. checked The constraint Jacobian has rank 5 at the parallel geometry (so 1 DoF) and the whole family closes exactly; with unequal legs, 20 random assemblies all give rank 6 (0 DoF).

So the miscount is a property of the special geometry, not of the topology: change one leg length slightly and the structure locks, and then G–K’s 0 is right. G–K only sees N, J and F, never the lengths, so it cannot tell the two cases apart. W13 p.16 names the correction: over-constraints \(R_C\) are added back (Week 4).

Hoberman mechanism (p.51): the slide gives only “24 links and 36 revolute joints”, no calculation. Putting those into G–K (my arithmetic, taking one link as the frame, added) gives \(3(24-36-1)+36 = -3\) for D = 3 and \(6(24-36-1)+36 = -42\) for D = 6. Both are negative, yet the object expands and contracts: the same lesson, G–K is not a proof that nothing moves. checked

Exam recipe: “Did you notice anything odd?”
  1. Do the count and show it (M = 0).
  2. State the observation: the mechanism visibly moves (1 DoF).
  3. Give the reason in the slide’s words: G–K assumes the constraints are independent; here one leg is redundant.
  4. Show the fix: remove one leg, recount, N = 4, J = 4, M = 1.
  5. Add the geometry caveat: it works because the legs are equal and parallel.
Absolute-word traps live here: “M = 0 means the mechanism cannot move” (false, p.49) and “G–K always gives the true mobility” (false). The true statement: M from G–K is exact only if the constraints are independent; otherwise it can undercount (p.49) or, with local motions, overcount (the delta).

7 · Workspace: reachable and dexterous pp. 52–57

Picture

The workspace is the set of points the end effector can reach. Its size and shape come from (1) the geometry (link lengths) and (2) the constraints on the joints (limits on angles or strokes) (p.52).

Reachable workspace: points the end effector can reach in one orientation. Dexterous workspace: points it can reach in all possible orientations. So \(W_{Dexterous}\subseteq W_{Reachable}\) (p.57; notebook Q7 answer \(W_R \supseteq W_D\)). The inclusion is non-strict: the sets can be equal in a degenerate case, so “\(\subset\)” is a trap.

The four arm types on the slides, with the shapes shown in the pictures (pp. 53–56; figures by A. Becker et al., “Robot Manipulator Workspaces”). Joint-limit cut-outs are visible in the slide images; the shape descriptions are added from reading those images.

ArmJointsWorkspace shape (as drawn)
PUMA (p.53)RRRthick spherical shell around the shoulder, with a wedge cut out by joint limits
SCARA (p.54)RRPa flat ring (annulus) swept by the two vertical-axis revolutes, made thick by the vertical stroke; a gap where the limits stop it
Cylindrical, PlateCrane EX (p.55)RPPa thick-walled cylinder sector: angle from the R, height and radius ranges from the two P
Cartesian, Yamaha (p.56)PPPa rectangular box with edges equal to the three strokes
Derivation (planar examples) added

2R arm, links \(L_1, L_2\): the tip distance \(r\) from the base satisfies \(|L_1-L_2| \le r \le L_1+L_2\) (elbow fully folded to fully stretched). For \(L = 0.5, 0.3\) m this is \(0.2 \le r \le 0.8\) m. checked

3R arm, links \(L_1, L_2, L_3\), tool at \(\mathbf p\) with direction angle \(\phi\): the wrist is at \(\mathbf w = \mathbf p - L_3(\cos\phi, \sin\phi)\), and \(\mathbf p\) is reachable at that \(\phi\) iff \(|L_1-L_2| \le |\mathbf w| \le L_1+L_2\). Reachable: some \(\phi\) works. Dexterous: every \(\phi\) works, i.e. the whole circle of radius \(L_3\) about \(\mathbf p\) lies inside the 2R annulus. For equal links \(L\): the annulus is \(0 \le |\mathbf w| \le 2L\), so the circle fits iff \(r + L \le 2L\), that is \(r \le L\). With \(L = 0.3\) m: \(W_R\) is the disc \(r \le 0.9\) m and \(W_D\) the disc \(r \le 0.3\) m. checked by sampling points and tool angles.

A mechanism with fewer DoF than the pose has (3 planar, 6 spatial) cannot reach all orientations at any point, so its dexterous workspace is empty.

Expect: “which is true, \(W_R \subseteq W_D\), \(W_R \subset W_D\), \(W_R \supseteq W_D\), \(W_R \supset W_D\)?” Answer \(W_R \supseteq W_D\) (dexterous is the harder condition, so the smaller set). The strict options are traps. Also expect to name the arm from its joint string (RRR PUMA, RRP SCARA, RPP cylindrical, PPP Cartesian) and to say what limits a workspace (link geometry, joint limits).

8 · The manipulation problems this unit solves pp. 58–62

Picture

Slide 59 previews the unit. Forward kinematics: joint coordinates to end-effector pose (W2). Inverse kinematics: tip pose to joint coordinates (W3). Velocity kinematics: how fast the end effector moves for given joint rates, or the joint rates needed (W6). Dynamics: the torque to accelerate the tip, or the force it exerts (W7–W9). Trajectory generation: a path in joint or tool space (W5). A pose is position plus orientation (p.60). Relating two frames takes 6 numbers, 3 translation and 3 rotation, written as a 4×4 homogeneous matrix (p.62). Frames named: {B} base, {W} wrist, {T} tool, {S} station, {G} goal, {C} camera (p.61).

Low weight alone, but the 6-number pose is why a 6-DoF arm is the minimum for arbitrary tool poses, and why 7 joints are “redundant”.

Guided problems: solve on paper first

P1.1 · Planar serial RPR (slides pp. 42–43)calculate

A planar chain has a revolute, a prismatic and a revolute joint in series from the ground. Find M with both forms of the equation.

Hint 1: D and N

Planar, so D = 3. Links: ground (0) and three moving links.

Hint 2: the joints

All three joints have F = 1, so \(P_1 = 3\), \(P_2 = 0\).

Full solution

Form 1: \(M = 3(N-1) - 2P_1 - P_2 = 3(4-1) - 2\times3 - 0 = 9 - 6 = 3\).

Form 2: \(M = D(N-J-1) + \sum F_i = 3(4-3-1) + 3 = 0 + 3 = 3\). Both agree. For any serial chain \(N = J+1\), so \(M\) is simply the sum of the joint DoF: here 3. Three actuators (one per joint) are needed, and they are enough to set the tip’s x, y and angle. checked

Common wrong answer: N = 3 (forgetting ground) gives \(3(3-1)-6 = 0\).

P1.2 · Planar four-bar (notebook Q2)calculatederive

Determine the mobility of the planar four-bar mechanism (four revolute joints, ground link included). Then explain in one line why the answer is not 3 even though each moving bar is a planar body.

Hint 1

Three moving bars have \(3\times3 = 9\) DoF if free.

Hint 2

Each revolute removes 2, so 4 revolutes remove 8.

Full solution

\(N = 4\), \(P_1 = 4\), \(P_2 = 0\): \(M = 3(4-1) - 2\times4 - 0 = 1\). Form 2: \(3(4-4-1) + 4 = 1\).

Why not 3: the loop closes, so the joints impose 8 constraints on 9 DoF. One motor on the crank sets the whole linkage. checked

Common wrong answers: −2 (D = 6) and 5 (constraints counted as 1 each).

P1.3 · Planar parallel manipulator (notebook Q3, W13 Q6)calculatespot the error

A triangular platform is connected to the ground by three legs, each R–P–R (revolute at the ground, prismatic, revolute at the platform). Find M. A student gets 0 by taking N = 7: what did they miss?

Hint 1: count the links

Ground, platform, and each leg has two parts because a prismatic joint joins a cylinder to a rod.

Hint 2: count the joints

Three legs times three joints each, all 1 DoF.

Full solution

\(N = 1 + 1 + 3\times2 = 8\), \(J = 9\), \(\sum F_i = 9\), \(D = 3\): \(M = 3(8-9-1) + 9 = 3\). Form 1: \(3(8-1) - 2\times9 = 3\). Three actuators, one per leg, control the platform’s x, y and angle: fully actuated.

Spot the error: N = 7 omits the ground link. Then \(3(7-1) - 18 = 0\), which would call a working robot a rigid structure. checked

P1.4 · The odd mechanism (notebook Q4 and Q5, slide p.49)explaincalculate

Three equal, parallel legs connect a body to the ground, each with an R at both ends. (a) What does G–K give? (b) What is the true number of DoF? (c) Explain the difference in two sentences.

Hint 1

\(N = 5\) (ground, 3 legs, body), \(P_1 = 6\).

Hint 2

Delete one middle leg and recount: four-bar.

Full solution

(a) \(M = 3(5-1) - 2\times6 - 0 = 0\). (b) The body moves: 1 DoF (slide: “it has 1 degree of freedom”). Check: remove one leg, \(N=4\), \(J=4\), \(M = 1\).

(c) G–K assumes the constraints are independent. Because the legs are equal and parallel, the third leg repeats a restriction already imposed by the other two (a redundant link), so only 5 of the 6 closure equations are independent. With unequal legs the structure would lock and 0 would be right. checked (rank 5 versus rank 6)

P1.5 · Stewart platform (slide p.48 homework)calculate

Six identical legs, each ground–U–P–S–platform. Find the mobility of the whole platform.

Hint 1

D = 6. Links: ground, platform, and two parts per leg.

Hint 2

\(J = 18\); the sum of joint DoF is \(6(2+1+3)\).

Full solution

\(N = 14\), \(J = 18\), \(\sum F_i = 36\): \(M = 6(14-18-1) + 36 = 6\). Six DoF, six actuators: fully actuated. checked

Caution: counting only the single drawn leg also gives 6 (a serial chain’s M is the sum of its joint DoF), but that is the leg’s DoF, not the platform’s count. Common wrong answers: 0 (no ground), 21 (D = 3).

P1.6 · Delta mechanism (W13 Q7)calculateexplain

A delta has a base, a platform and three legs. Each leg is one R at the base driving an arm, then two rods, each rod with a spherical joint at both ends. Find M by plain G–K, then with the extended equation using \(R_C = 0\) and \(R_M = 6\).

Hint 1

\(N = 2 + 3\times3 = 11\); per leg 1 R and 4 S, so \(J = 15\).

Hint 2

\(\sum F_i = 3\times(1 + 4\times3)\). Then subtract \(R_M\).

Full solution

Plain: \(6(11-15-1) + 39 = -30 + 39 = 9\). Extended: \(9 + 0 - 6 = 3\). The six rods can each spin about their own axis (ball joints at both ends); these local spins do not move the platform, so they are subtracted. The delta moves its platform in 3 DoF (x, y, z) with 3 motors. checked

Explain in the exam: “plain G–K counts local rod spins as DoF; \(R_M\) removes them.” Week 4 shows how to find \(R_C\) and \(R_M\) yourself.

P1.7 · Reachable and dexterous workspace (notebook Q7)explainsketchcalculate

(a) Which relation is true for the reachable workspace \(W_R\) and dexterous workspace \(W_D\): \(W_R\subseteq W_D\), \(W_R\subset W_D\), \(W_R\supseteq W_D\), \(W_R\supset W_D\), or \(W_R=W_D\)? (b) A planar 2R arm has \(L_1 = 0.5\) m and \(L_2 = 0.3\) m and no joint limits. Sketch its reachable workspace and give the inner and outer radii.

Hint

Fold the elbow fully and stretch it fully: the tip distance from the base runs between \(|L_1-L_2|\) and \(L_1+L_2\).

Full solution

(a) \(W_R\supseteq W_D\): every point reachable in all orientations is certainly reachable in one. \(W_R\subseteq W_D\) and \(W_R\subset W_D\) are backwards. The strict \(W_R\supset W_D\) is not guaranteed, because the sets can be equal (for example both empty), and \(W_R=W_D\) is not true in general.

(b) An annulus (a flat ring) centred on the base: \(r_{min} = |0.5-0.3| = 0.2\) m, \(r_{max} = 0.5 + 0.3 = 0.8\) m. Sketch two concentric circles and shade between them. The 2R arm has 2 DoF, fewer than the 3 of a planar pose, so it has no dexterous workspace. checked

Close everything and draw the WR and WD of a planar 3R arm with equal links L, with the radii in terms of L (3 minutes).

P1.8 · Classify the actuationexplain

Name each as fully actuated, under-actuated or redundant, and say which meaning you use: (a) a 6R arm with 6 motors; (b) the same arm with 4 motors; (c) a 7R arm with 7 motors used to place a tool in a 3D pose; (d) a Stewart platform with 6 actuators.

Model answer

(a) Fully actuated: controllable = total = 6. (b) Under-actuated: 4 < 6, lighter and cheaper but two joints cannot be commanded. (c) Redundant in the standard sense: 7 joint DoF for a 6-DoF task. By the slide’s literal wording (controllable 7 = total 7) it would be called fully actuated, so state which meaning you use. (d) Fully actuated: M = 6 (section 5), 6 actuators. checked

P1.9 · Workspace shapes of four arms (notebook Q6)explainsketch

Describe and sketch the workspace of a PUMA 560 (RRR), a SCARA (RRP), a cylindrical (RPP) and a Cartesian (PPP) arm, and say what limits each.

Model answer

PUMA (RRR): a thick spherical shell about the shoulder, the outer radius set by the sum of the upper-arm and forearm lengths, with a cut-out wedge where the waist angle is limited. SCARA (RRP): a flat ring (annulus) from the two vertical-axis revolutes, extruded by the vertical prismatic stroke, with a gap from joint limits. Cylindrical (RPP): a thick-walled cylinder sector: the R gives the angular span, one P the height, the other P the radial range (the inner hole is the minimum radial extension). Cartesian (PPP): a box whose edges are the three strokes. Every shape is limited by the link geometry and the joint limits (p.52). The shapes are read from the slide figures (pp. 53–56).

P1.10 · Spot the errorsspot the error

A student writes: “Four-bar: D = 6, N = 4, J = 4, so \(M = 6(4-4-1)+4 = -2\); a negative mobility means the mechanism cannot be built.” And: “Delta with three motors: M = 9, so it is under-actuated.” Find all the errors.

Model answer

1) A planar four-bar needs D = 3: \(3(4-4-1)+4 = 1\). 2) A negative or zero G–K value does not prove a mechanism cannot be built or cannot move (p.49, Hoberman p.51); it signals dependent constraints to look for. 3) 9 is the plain-G–K value; the delta’s real mobility is 3 (\(R_M = 6\)), so three motors make it fully actuated. checked

Mini-quiz

Q1trap

Which is true? (a) \(W_R\subset W_D\) (b) \(W_R\supseteq W_D\) (c) \(W_R=W_D\) always (d) \(W_R\subseteq W_D\)

Answer

(b). Dexterous (all orientations) is the stronger condition. (a) and (d) are backwards; (c) is “always”.

Q2calculate

A serial 6R arm in 3D: N = ?, J = ?, M = ? With 4 motors, what is it called?

Answer

N = 7 (ground plus 6 links), J = 6, \(M = 6(7-6-1)+6 = 6\). With 4 motors it is under-actuated.

Q3concept

G–K gives M = 0 for a mechanism you can see moving. Give the reason and the usual fix.

Answer

G–K assumes the constraints are independent; here some are redundant (an extra link repeating a constraint, as in the three equal parallel legs). Remove the redundant link (or add the over-constraint term \(R_C\), Week 4) and recount.

Week 2 · Forward kinematics

Where is the tool, given the joints?

Forward kinematics (FK) turns joint coordinates \(\mathbf q\) into the pose of the end effector. Every method in this week builds one 4×4 matrix by multiplying small, simple matrices in the right order. Get the order and the signs right and the rest is arithmetic.

Lecture: Forward Kinematics50 slides · Dr KM Digumarti · notebook “2 forward kinematics”
Open in new tab ↗
How this is examined

Sample question 1 (W13 p.4): “Write down the transformation matrix relating the tool frame {T} to the station frame {S} for the following RRR manipulator. Indicate intermediate frames.” The lecturer answers it with an elementary transform sequence (W13 p.4). Expect the same: a drawn arm, write the chain, multiply.

Where the marks are (indicative; marks not published): frames drawn on the figure with correct axes; the ETS in the right order with the right signs; each intermediate transform written; the product (at least the position column) simplified; a sanity check at θ = 0.

Where marks are lost: multiplying in the wrong order; a rotation sign flipped because the drawn joint arrow points the other way (the lecturer writes \(R_y(-\theta_2)\)); forgetting the constant tool rotation at the end (\(R_x(90^\circ)\)); mixing proximal and distal DH in one table; leaving a calculator in degrees for a radian answer.

Practical (optional, no coding in the exam)

puma560_fk_proximal_dh.py builds a PUMA 560 from a proximal DH table, one row at a time as \(R_x(\alpha_{i-1})\,t_x(a_{i-1})\,R_z(\theta_i)\,t_z(d_i)\), and prints the robot. plot_workspace.py in this folder is empty. The lecture notebook’s exercises are solved below.

Intuition first

A transform is a set of directions

\({}^A\mathbf T_B\) says “stand at A’s origin, walk along vector \(\mathbf t\), then turn so you face like B”. Like telling a friend: “from the station, go 200 m north, then face the café door”.

Walk along the arm

An ETS is a walk from the base to the tool, writing down every step (translation) and every twist (rotation) in the order you meet them. The product of that list is FK.

Each step is relative to where you now face

“Turn left, then go two blocks” only makes sense from where you stand after turning. Multiplying on the right means: the next move is measured in the frame you just arrived in.

DH is an ETS with a dress code

Denavit–Hartenberg allows only four moves per link, in a fixed order: twist, slide, rotate, slide. That strict code puts every frame in a standard place, so any arm fits in one table.In the practical: the PUMA 560 script is exactly this four-move pattern, repeated six times.

1 · FK by trigonometry: the planar RRR arm pp. 6–9

Picture

In a planar arm every link lies in the same plane and every joint axis points out of it. Each link is a vector of fixed length whose direction is the sum of all joint angles before it. The tip is just the sum of those vectors.

Derivation

Link \(k\) points at the absolute angle \(\phi_k = q_1+\dots+q_k\). Adding the three link vectors (p.7):

\[ x = L_1\cos q_1 + L_2\cos(q_1+q_2) + L_3\cos(q_1+q_2+q_3) \] \[ y = L_1\sin q_1 + L_2\sin(q_1+q_2) + L_3\sin(q_1+q_2+q_3) \]

Orientation in the plane is one angle, the sum of all joint angles (p.9): \( q_E = q_1+q_2+q_3 \).

The same answer as a chain of transforms: \( {}^0\mathbf T_E = R_z(q_1)\,t_x(L_1)\,R_z(q_2)\,t_x(L_2)\,R_z(q_3)\,t_x(L_3) \). Its position column is the pair above, and \(\operatorname{atan2}(T_{21},T_{11}) = q_E\). checked in checks/w02.py

Exam recipe
  1. Write each link’s absolute angle as a running sum.
  2. Sum \(L_k\cos\phi_k\) for x and \(L_k\sin\phi_k\) for y.
  3. Orientation = sum of revolute angles.
  4. Check at q = 0: the tip must be at \((L_1+L_2+L_3, 0)\).
Worked example

L = (0.5, 0.4, 0.2) m, q = (30°, 45°, −60°). Absolute angles: 30°, 75°, 15°.

\(x = 0.5\cos30^\circ + 0.4\cos75^\circ + 0.2\cos15^\circ = 0.4330 + 0.1035 + 0.1932 = 0.7297\) m
\(y = 0.5\sin30^\circ + 0.4\sin75^\circ + 0.2\sin15^\circ = 0.2500 + 0.3864 + 0.0518 = 0.6881\) m,   \(q_E = 15^\circ\). checked

A trap answer uses the joint angles directly (cos 45°, cos −60°) instead of the running sums. At q = 0 every method gives the same answer, so test your formula at a non-zero pose too.

2 · The homogeneous transformation matrix p. 12

Picture

\({}^A\mathbf T_B\) is the pose of frame {B} as seen from frame {A}. The top-left 3×3 block is a rotation whose columns are B’s axes written in A’s coordinates. The last column is where B’s origin sits in A. The bottom row \([0\;0\;0\;1]\) only makes the 4×4 maths work.

Derivation \[ {}^A\mathbf T_B = \begin{bmatrix} {}^A\mathbf R_B & {}^A\mathbf t_{B} \\ \mathbf 0^{\top} & 1\end{bmatrix} \in SE(3),\qquad {}^A\mathbf R_B\in SO(3),\qquad {}^A\mathbf t_B\in\mathbb R^3 \]

A point known in B maps to A by one multiplication, using homogeneous coordinates \([x\;y\;z\;1]^\top\): \( {}^A\mathbf P = {}^A\mathbf T_B\,{}^B\mathbf P \) (p.12). This is just \( {}^A\mathbf P = {}^A\mathbf R_B\,{}^B\mathbf P + {}^A\mathbf t_B \) written as one matrix.

The elementary rotations (right-hand rule about each axis) are the building blocks for everything else:

\[ R_x(\theta)=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&c\theta&-s\theta\\0&s\theta&c\theta\end{bmatrix},\; R_y(\theta)=\begin{bmatrix}c\theta&0&s\theta\\0&1&0\\-s\theta&0&c\theta\end{bmatrix},\; R_z(\theta)=\begin{bmatrix}c\theta&-s\theta&0\\s\theta&c\theta&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix} \]

Note where the minus sign sits in \(R_y\): bottom-left, the opposite place from \(R_x\) and \(R_z\). It follows from the cyclic order z→x (positive rotation about y turns z towards x). added

The inverse is cheap because \(\mathbf R^{-1}=\mathbf R^\top\): \( {}^B\mathbf T_A = ({}^A\mathbf T_B)^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf R^\top & -\mathbf R^\top\mathbf t\\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1\end{bmatrix} \). added checked

Worked example

\( {}^A\mathbf T_B = R_z(30^\circ)\,t(1,2,0) \). B’s origin in A is \(R_z(30^\circ)[1,2,0]^\top = (0.8660-1.0000,\;0.5000+1.7321,\;0) = (-0.1340,\;2.2321,\;0)\). The point \({}^B\mathbf P=(1,0,0)\) lands at \((0.7321,\;2.7321,\;0)\) in A, which is the origin plus B’s x-axis \((0.8660, 0.5, 0)\). checked

“Find \({}^B\mathbf T_A\)” is a favourite one-liner. The rotation transposes, and the translation becomes \(-\mathbf R^\top\mathbf t\), not \(-\mathbf t\). Also expect “what does column 2 of R mean?”: it is B’s y-axis expressed in A.

3 · Compound transformations and the order of multiplication p. 13

Picture

Chaining frames chains matrices in the same order: \( {}^A\mathbf T_C = {}^A\mathbf T_B\,{}^B\mathbf T_C \). The inner subscripts cancel like fractions. Each new factor on the right moves along the axes of the frame you have just reached (the moving frame).

Derivation

Slide 13: {B} is {A} rotated by θ about xA, then {C} is {B} translated by d along zB. So \( {}^A\mathbf T_C = R_x(\theta)\,t_z(d) \). The translation is along the rotated z-axis, so C’s origin in A is \( R_x(\theta)[0,0,d]^\top = (0,\,-d\sin\theta,\,d\cos\theta) \).

Swap the order and you get \( t_z(d)\,R_x(\theta) \): slide along the old z first, then rotate in place. The origin is at \((0,0,d)\). Different matrix, different pose.

Rule added: right-multiplication = “then move in the current frame”; left-multiplication = “then move in the fixed/original frame”.

Worked example

θ = 30°, d = 2: \(R_x(30^\circ)t_z(2)\) puts C at \((0, -1.000, 1.732)\); \(t_z(2)R_x(30^\circ)\) puts it at \((0,0,2)\). checked

If the question says “rotated about its own / the new axis”, multiply on the right. If it says “about the fixed / original axis”, multiply on the left. Write a one-line sentence saying which you used; it earns method marks even if the arithmetic slips.

4 · Elementary Transform Sequence (ETS) pp. 15–19

Picture

Only six moves exist: \(t_x, t_y, t_z, R_x, R_y, R_z\) (p.16). Each takes a parameter η that is either a constant (a link length, a fixed twist) or a joint variable \(q_j(t)\). Walk from the base to the tool and write each move as you meet it. A joint becomes one move about (or along) its own axis.

The lecturer’s tip (p.18): redraw the arm with every joint displaced from rest. Then you can see which way each angle is measured, and therefore its sign.

Derivation: Furuta pendulum

Base {B} at the floor, z up. Up the post by L0, rotate by θ1 about the vertical, along the arm by L1, rotate by θ2 about the arm’s axis (x), down the pendulum by L2, then flip so that zE points down the link (p.19):

\[ {}^B\mathbf T_E = t_z(L_0)\,R_z(\theta_1)\,t_x(L_1)\,R_x(\theta_2)\,t_z(-L_2)\,R_y(\pi) \]

Multiplying out, the position column is checked symbolically:

\[ x = L_1\cos\theta_1 - L_2\sin\theta_1\sin\theta_2,\quad y = L_1\sin\theta_1 + L_2\cos\theta_1\sin\theta_2,\quad z = L_0 - L_2\cos\theta_2 \]

Sanity check: at θ2 = 0 the pendulum hangs straight down, so \(z = L_0-L_2\) and the tip sits at the end of the arm. ✓

Intermediate (link) frames are just partial products (notebook): \({}^B\mathbf T_1 = t_z(L_0)R_z(\theta_1)\), \({}^1\mathbf T_2 = t_x(L_1)R_x(\theta_2)\), \({}^2\mathbf T_E = t_z(-L_2)R_y(\pi)\).

Exam recipe (W13 Q1 style)
  1. Draw {S} on the figure. Mark each joint axis and the positive sense of each angle (from the drawn arrow).
  2. Walk to the first joint: write the translations (\(t_z(\cdot)\) etc.).
  3. At each joint write \(R_{axis}(\pm\theta_i)\). Use the minus sign if the drawn positive rotation is opposite to the right-hand rule about your chosen axis.
  4. Continue to the tool. Finish with any constant rotation that makes your last frame match the drawn {T}.
  5. Draw and label an intermediate frame after each joint. Write \({}^{i-1}\mathbf T_i\) for each group.
  6. Multiply, or at least give the position column. Check at all joints = 0 against the picture.
Worked example

L = (0.5, 0.4, 0.3) m, θ = (60°, 45°). Then \(x = 0.4(0.5) - 0.3(0.8660)(0.7071) = 0.0163\), \(y = 0.4(0.8660) + 0.3(0.5)(0.7071) = 0.4525\), \(z = 0.5 - 0.3(0.7071) = 0.2879\) m.

\[ {}^B\mathbf T_E=\begin{bmatrix}-0.5000&-0.6124&-0.6124&0.0163\\-0.8660&0.3536&0.3536&0.4525\\0&0.7071&-0.7071&0.2879\\0&0&0&1\end{bmatrix} \]

checked with sympy and roboticstoolbox

5 · Proximal (modified, Craig) Denavit–Hartenberg pp. 20–36

Picture

Links are numbered 0 (fixed base) to n. Joint i joins link i−1 to link i (p.23). In the proximal convention, frame {i} sits on joint axis i, at the near end of link i, with zi along that axis. Between two neighbouring axes there is exactly one shortest line, the common normal. The four parameters describe how to get from one axis to the next along it.

Definitions and the link transform
ParameterMeasuredSlide
\(a_{i-1}\) link lengthdistance from \(z_{i-1}\) to \(z_i\) along \(x_{i-1}\) (common normal); never negativep.24, p.30
\(\alpha_{i-1}\) link twistangle from \(z_{i-1}\) to \(z_i\) about \(x_{i-1}\) (right-hand sense)p.25
\(d_i\) link offsetsigned distance from \(x_{i-1}\) to \(x_i\) along \(z_i\)p.26
\(\theta_i\) joint angleangle from \(x_{i-1}\) to \(x_i\) about \(z_i\)p.27

A revolute joint’s variable is \(\theta_i\); a prismatic joint’s variable is \(d_i\). The link transform is the ETS twist → slide → rotate → slide (p.28):

\[ {}^{i-1}\mathbf T_i = R_x(\alpha_{i-1})\,t_x(a_{i-1})\,R_z(\theta_i)\,t_z(d_i) = \begin{bmatrix} c\theta_i & -s\theta_i & 0 & a_{i-1}\\ s\theta_i c\alpha_{i-1} & c\theta_i c\alpha_{i-1} & -s\alpha_{i-1} & -s\alpha_{i-1} d_i\\ s\theta_i s\alpha_{i-1} & c\theta_i s\alpha_{i-1} & c\alpha_{i-1} & c\alpha_{i-1} d_i\\ 0&0&0&1\end{bmatrix} \]

Then \({}^0\mathbf T_n = {}^0\mathbf T_1\,{}^1\mathbf T_2\cdots{}^{n-1}\mathbf T_n\) (p.35).

Frame-assignment recipe (slide 29)
  1. Identify all joint axes. Work on axes i and i+1.
  2. Find their common normal, or their intersection point. The origin of {i} is where the common normal meets axis i (or the intersection point).
  3. zi along joint axis i.
  4. xi along the common normal, pointing towards axis i+1. If the axes intersect, xi is normal to the plane containing both.
  5. yi completes a right-handed frame.
  6. Choose {0} to coincide with {1} when q1 = 0. Choose {N}’s origin and xN freely, making as many parameters zero as possible.
  7. Fill the table row by row: \(a_{i-1}, \alpha_{i-1}\) look backwards (from axis i−1 to axis i); \(d_i, \theta_i\) look along axis i.
Worked example: Furuta pendulum DH table (slide 34)
i\(a_{i-1}\)\(\alpha_{i-1}\)\(d_i\)\(\theta_i\)
100L0q1 + 90°
2090°L1q2
3090°L20°

The slide warns that {3} is not {E}. Multiplying the three rows and comparing with the ETS of section 4 shows the missing piece is a constant \({}^3\mathbf T_E = R_z(-90^\circ)\):

\[ {}^0\mathbf T_1\,{}^1\mathbf T_2\,{}^2\mathbf T_3\;R_z(-90^\circ) \;=\; t_z(L_0)R_z(\theta_1)t_x(L_1)R_x(\theta_2)t_z(-L_2)R_y(\pi) \quad\text{for all }\theta_1,\theta_2 \]

This is the slide 36 homework (“verify that it is the same as the ETS”). checked symbolically Why +90° in row 1: with q1 = 0, x1 must point along y0 so that z2 (the arm axis, reached by twisting 90° about x1) points along +x0, as in the ETS.

6 · Distal (standard) DH, and how to tell them apart pp. 37–41

Comparison (slide 40)
Proximal / modified (Craig, this unit)Distal / standard (DH 1955, Corke’s default)
Frame {i} sits onaxis i (near end of link i)axis i+1 (far end of link i)
Link transform\(R_x(\alpha_{i-1})\,t_x(a_{i-1})\,R_z(\theta_i)\,t_z(d_i)\)\(R_z(\theta_i)\,t_z(d_i)\,t_x(a_i)\,R_x(\alpha_i)\)
Row i uses\(a_{i-1},\alpha_{i-1},d_i,\theta_i\)\(a_i,\alpha_i,d_i,\theta_i\)
Joint i moves about\(z_i\)\(z_{i-1}\)
Constraint that makes 4 enough (p.43)\(x_i \perp z_{i+1}\) and \(x_i\) intersects \(z_{i+1}\)\(x_i \perp z_{i-1}\) and \(x_i\) intersects \(z_{i-1}\)
\[ \text{distal: } {}^{i-1}\mathbf T_i = \begin{bmatrix} c\theta_i & -s\theta_i c\alpha_i & s\theta_i s\alpha_i & a_i c\theta_i\\ s\theta_i & c\theta_i c\alpha_i & -c\theta_i s\alpha_i & a_i s\theta_i\\ 0 & s\alpha_i & c\alpha_i & d_i\\ 0&0&0&1\end{bmatrix} \]
Slides vs textbook

Craig (your book) uses proximal. Corke’s book and Robot Academy videos mostly use distal, and roboticstoolbox.DHRobot is distal unless you use RevoluteMDH. A table copied from one into the other’s matrix gives a wrong robot. In the exam, state “proximal (Craig) DH” at the top of your answer.

7 · Why four parameters are enough, and what a good model needs pp. 42–44

Argument

A general rigid-body pose needs 6 numbers (3 rotation, 3 translation). DH spends 2 of them on rules about where frames go: in proximal DH, xi must be perpendicular to zi+1 and must intersect it. Each rule removes one freedom, so 6 − 2 = 4 (p.43). The price: a link frame need not lie on the physical link.

A kinematic model should be (p.44): complete (it can describe any geometry of successive joints), continuous (small geometry change gives a small parameter change; DH fails this when two axes become nearly parallel, because the common normal jumps), and minimal (no redundant parameters).

A 2–4 mark “explain” question: state 6 − 2 = 4 and name the two constraints. Then add one limitation: DH is not continuous for nearly parallel axes, and frames may sit off the link.

8 · URDF pp. 45–47

Picture

URDF (Unified Robot Description Format) is XML that lists <link>s and <joint>s. Each joint names a parent and child link, an origin (a fixed transform, i.e. constant ETS steps) and an axis (the joint variable’s axis). It can also carry visual geometry. The slide’s planar robot (p.46) is the ETS \(R_z(q_1)\,t_x(1)\,R_z(q_2)\,t_x(1)\): joint q2’s origin is xyz = “1 0 0” and the fixed joint to “end” adds another \(t_x(1)\).

Low exam weight. Be able to read a URDF snippet as an ETS: origin → constant translations and rotations, axis → which \(R\) the joint is.

Guided problems: solve on paper first

P2.1 · Furuta pendulum positioncalculatederive

For the Furuta pendulum with L0 = 0.5 m, L1 = 0.4 m, L2 = 0.3 m, θ1 = 60°, θ2 = 45°, find the tip position in {B}.

Hint 1: what to write

The ETS from base to tip: \(t_z(L_0)R_z(\theta_1)t_x(L_1)R_x(\theta_2)t_z(-L_2)\). The final \(R_y(\pi)\) does not move the origin.

Hint 2: the governing equation

Position = \(t_z(L_0)\) + \(R_z(\theta_1)\big([L_1,0,0]^\top + R_x(\theta_2)[0,0,-L_2]^\top\big)\).

Hint 3: first substitution

\(R_x(45^\circ)[0,0,-0.3]^\top = [0,\;0.2121,\;-0.2121]^\top\).

Full solution

Arm-local vector to the tip: \([0.4,\;0,\;0] + R_x(45^\circ)[0,0,-0.3] = [0.4,\;0.2121,\;-0.2121]\).

Rotate by \(R_z(60^\circ)\): \(x = 0.4(0.5) - 0.2121(0.8660) = 0.0163\), \(y = 0.4(0.8660) + 0.2121(0.5) = 0.4525\). Add the post: \(z = 0.5 - 0.2121 = 0.2879\) m.

Common wrong answer: using \(+L_2\) gives z = 0.7121, a pendulum pointing up.

Close everything and write the Furuta ETS and its position formula from scratch in 4 minutes.

P2.2 · Two frames (notebook Question 3)derivespot the error

In the notebook figure, {B}’s origin is reached from {A} by 5 along yA, 3 along xA and 2 up zA. xB points down (−zA) and zB points along +yA. Find \({}^A\mathbf T_B\) and give an ETS for it.

Hint 1

The columns of \({}^A\mathbf R_B\) are B’s axes in A. You know two of them; the third is \(\mathbf y_B = \mathbf z_B\times\mathbf x_B\).

Hint 2

\(\mathbf y_B = \hat y_A \times(-\hat z_A) = -\hat x_A\).

Hint 3

Find a rotation that sends x to −z first (\(R_y(90^\circ)\) does), then fix z about the new x.

Full solution \[ {}^A\mathbf T_B=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1&0&3\\0&0&1&5\\-1&0&0&2\\0&0&0&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad \text{ETS: } t_x(3)\,t_y(5)\,t_z(2)\,R_y(90^\circ)\,R_x(-90^\circ) \]

Check: \(R_y(90^\circ)\) takes x to −z ✓. Its new x-axis is −zA; rotating −90° about it carries the current z (= +xA) to +yA ✓. Determinant +1 ✓. checked

Spot the error: a filled-in copy of this notebook answers ty(5) tx(3) Ry(90°) Rx(90°). It misses the 2 up zA, and \(R_x(+90^\circ)\) makes zB point along −yA.

P2.3 · Panda ETS (notebook Questions 1–2)derivecalculate

Using the Panda schematic (0.333, 0.316, 0.384, 0.0825, 0.088, 0.107 m), write the ETS from base to flange. What is the flange position at q = 0?

Hint 1

Each DH row in the table of section 5 is \(R_x(\alpha_{i-1})\,t_x(a_{i-1})\,R_z(q_i)\,t_z(d_i)\). Drop the zero terms.

Hint 2

At q = 0 the column is straight up: 0.333 + 0.316 + 0.384 = 1.033, then the wrist turns back down by 0.107.

Full solution

tz(0.333) Rz(q1) Rx(−90°) Rz(q2) Rx(90°) tz(0.316) Rz(q3) Rx(90°) tx(0.0825) Rz(q4) Rx(−90°) tx(−0.0825) tz(0.384) Rz(q5) Rx(90°) Rz(q6) Rx(90°) tx(0.088) Rz(q7) tz(0.107)

At q = 0: x = 0.0825 − 0.0825 + 0.088 = 0.088 m; z = 0.333 + 0.316 + 0.384 − 0.107 = 0.926 m; y = 0. checked against roboticstoolbox

Note: the filled-in notebook cell uses only Rx joints after the first. That is not the Panda, since its joints alternate between “about the link” and “across the link”.

P2.4 · PUMA 560 by ETS (notebook Question 5)deriveexplain

Write an ETS from base to wrist for the PUMA 560 (choose your own lengths, no offsets). How do you handle joints whose axes meet at one point?

Hint 1

Home pose: upper arm and forearm vertical. Waist about z; shoulder and elbow about a horizontal axis (take y); wrist roll about the forearm (z), bend (y), swivel (z).

Full solution

\(t_z(L_b)\,R_z(q_1)\,R_y(q_2)\,t_z(L_u)\,R_y(q_3)\,t_z(L_f)\,R_z(q_4)\,R_y(q_5)\,R_z(q_6)\), e.g. Lb = 1.0, Lu = 0.5, Lf = 0.3 m. Home position is (0, 0, 1.8) m. checked

Coincident joints: where axes intersect there is no translation between consecutive rotations. Waist and shoulder meet at one point (\(R_z R_y\) back to back), and the three wrist axes meet at the wrist centre (\(R_zR_yR_z\)). This is a spherical wrist. Its centre does not move when q4–q6 change checked, which is what makes PUMA IK solvable in closed form (W3).

Try it in the 3D explorer above (“PUMA-like arm”).

P2.5 · Why are 4 DH parameters enough?explain

A pose between two rigid bodies needs six numbers. Explain in 3 sentences why DH uses four, and give one weakness.

Model answer

DH restricts where frames go: in proximal DH, xi is perpendicular to zi+1 and intersects it. These two constraints remove two of the six freedoms, leaving a, α, d, θ. Weakness: for nearly parallel axes the common normal is ill-defined, so tiny geometry changes cause large parameter jumps (not continuous). Frames may also lie off the physical link.

P2.6 · Workspace by sampling (notebook Question 6)explainsketch

Describe how to plot a manipulator’s workspace from its FK, and sketch the Furuta pendulum’s workspace (no joint limits).

Model answer

Sample joint vectors uniformly within the joint limits, push each through FK, and plot the tool positions as a point cloud. For the Furuta pendulum, the tip lies on a circle of radius L2 centred at the arm’s end. That circle lies in the plane perpendicular to the arm, not in the vertical plane through the post. From the FK, \(x^2+y^2 = L_1^2 + L_2^2\sin^2\theta_2\) and \(z - L_0 = -L_2\cos\theta_2\), so \(\rho^2 + (z-L_0)^2 = L_1^2 + L_2^2\) where ρ is the horizontal distance from the post. Every tip position is the same distance \(\sqrt{L_1^2+L_2^2}\) from the top of the post. The workspace is a band of a sphere of that radius, centred at (0, 0, L0), between heights \(L_0 \pm L_2\). It is a surface, not a solid, because the arm has only two joints. For the example lengths: radius 0.5 m, heights 0.2 m to 0.8 m. checked

Common wrong answer: a torus. A torus would need the pendulum to swing in the radial plane.

Mini-quiz

Q1concept

What is the third column of \({}^A\mathbf R_B\), physically?

Answer

The unit z-axis of {B} expressed in {A}’s coordinates.

Q2calculate

\({}^A\mathbf T_B = R_x(90^\circ)\,t_z(1)\). Where is B’s origin in A?

Answer

\(R_x(90^\circ)[0,0,1]^\top = (0,-1,0)\). The translation is along the rotated z, which now points along −yA.

Q3spot the error

A student writes the proximal link transform as \(R_z(\theta_i)\,t_z(d_i)\,t_x(a_{i-1})\,R_x(\alpha_{i-1})\). What is wrong?

Answer

That is the distal order with proximal subscripts. Proximal is \(R_x(\alpha_{i-1})\,t_x(a_{i-1})\,R_z(\theta_i)\,t_z(d_i)\): twist and slide along the old x first, then rotate and slide along the new z.

Week 3 · Inverse kinematics

Which joint values put the tool where I want it?

IK runs FK backwards: from a desired pose to joint values. Unlike FK, the answer may not exist, may not be unique, and may need a numerical search. The exam skill is the closed-form derivation: project, apply the cosine rule, use atan2, list every branch.

Lecture: Inverse Kinematics62 slides · notebook “3 inverse kinematics”
Open in new tab ↗
How this is examined

Sample question 3 (W13 p.7): “Derive the inverse kinematics. You are given the position of the end effector (xT, yT, zT).” Sample question 2 (p.6): sketch the workspace. Both are solved in full on the Sample Qs tab.

Where the marks are (indicative): FK written first; a top-down view giving θ1; a side view reducing the rest to a planar 2R problem; the cosine rule for the elbow with ±; atan2 for the shoulder; the number of solutions and when none exist.

Where marks are lost: tan⁻¹(y/x) instead of atan2 (wrong quadrant); one branch only; mixing an interior triangle angle with a relative joint angle (the sign of a cosine flips); forgetting to subtract the base height or the last link before solving.

Practical (optional)

The W3 practical folder holds the PUMA 560 FK scripts (proximal DH and distal ETS), which pair with W2. rrp_ik.py in the lecture folder is, despite its name, a planar 2R arm (L1 = L2 = 1). It has the analytic IK (both elbows), its 2×2 Jacobian, and a Newton–Raphson solver. Its cos q2 is clipped to [−1, 1], so an unreachable target silently returns the nearest boundary pose.

Intuition first

Touch your nose two ways

Keep your fingertip on your nose and move your elbow: the hand stays put while the arm changes. A robot arm has the same freedom at its “elbow”, so most reachable points have an elbow-up and an elbow-down answer.

A triangle does the work

For two links, shoulder, elbow and tip form a triangle with known sides L1, L2 and the distance to the target. The cosine rule gives the elbow angle; the rest is pointing.

Split position from orientation

With a spherical wrist, the first three joints carry the wrist centre (like your shoulder and elbow placing your wrist). The last three only turn the hand. Two small problems instead of one big one.

Numerical IK = walking downhill

Measure how far the tool is from the goal, use the Jacobian as a local map of “which joint moves the tool where”, step, and repeat. Like adjusting a desk lamp by small nudges until the light lands on the page.

1 · The IK problem and its spaces pp. 7–11

Picture

Configuration (joint) space 𝒞 holds the joint vector q; for two revolute joints \(\mathcal C=\mathbb S^1\times\mathbb S^1\) (each angle in [0, 2π)). Task space 𝒯 holds the tool pose ξ, written as \({}^0\mathbf T_E\), as (x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw), or as position + quaternion (p.9). FK is \(\xi=\mathcal K(\mathbf q)\); IK is \(\mathbf q=\mathcal K^{-1}(\xi)\) (p.11). 𝒦 is a many-to-one, nonlinear map, which is why its inverse is hard.

Definitions are cheap marks: be able to say what 𝒞 and 𝒯 are for a given robot, and why IK can have 0, 1, several or infinitely many solutions.

2 · Does a solution exist? Workspace pp. 12–16

Picture

Reachable workspace: every point the tool can reach in at least one orientation. Dexterous workspace: every point it can reach in every orientation. For a full 3D pose you need the dexterous workspace (notebook Q1).

“Sketch the workspace” (W13 Q2) is this idea in 3D. Always give the radii and say why (cosine rule: distance ranges from |L1−L2| to L1+L2).

3 · Multiple solutions and how to choose pp. 17–20

Picture

A reachable point usually has several joint solutions (p.17). To pick one (p.18): the closest to the current configuration (smallest absolute or weighted joint change; prefer moving small distal joints over large proximal ones), or the one that avoids obstacles (p.19). Solution methods (p.20): closed form (algebraic, geometric, polynomial; non-iterative; all solutions known) or numerical (iterative; slower; handles long chains and returns a close-enough answer when no exact one exists, p.54).

A 6-DoF arm has no continuous redundancy for a 6-number pose (p.33), but it still has several discrete solutions. The PUMA 560 has up to 8: shoulder left/right × elbow up/down × wrist flip. added: standard result, Craig ch. 4

Slides vs slides

Slide 54 lists “unique solution to all positions” for closed form. Read it as “a definite, complete set of solutions”: slides 17 and 20 show that one point can have several solutions.

4 · Planar RP arm pp. 23–24

Derivation

A revolute joint q1 followed by a prismatic extension S along the link: tip \((x,y)=(S\cos q_1,\;S\sin q_1)\). Polar coordinates invert it directly:

\[ S=\sqrt{x^2+y^2},\qquad q_1=\operatorname{atan2}(y,x) \]

The slide writes \(\tan^{-1}(y/x)\) (p.24); use atan2 for the quadrant. If S may be negative, (−S, q1+π) is a second solution.

Worked example

(x, y) = (0.3, 0.4) m → S = 0.5 m, q1 = 53.130°. checked

5 · Planar RR arm, algebraic solution, and atan2 pp. 25–30

Derivation

FK (p.26): \(x=L_1c_1+L_2c_{12}\), \(y=L_1s_1+L_2s_{12}\). Square and add; cross terms collapse with \(c_1c_{12}+s_1s_{12}=\cos q_2\):

\[ x^2+y^2=L_1^2+L_2^2+2L_1L_2\cos q_2\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;\cos q_2=\frac{x^2+y^2-L_1^2-L_2^2}{2L_1L_2} \] \[ \sin q_2=\pm\sqrt{1-\cos^2q_2},\qquad q_2=\operatorname{atan2}(\sin q_2,\;\cos q_2) \]

The ± is the elbow: two solutions (p.28). If \(|\cos q_2|>1\) the point is out of reach.

For q1, expand the compound angles (p.30): \(x=(L_1+L_2c_2)c_1-(L_2s_2)s_1\), \(y=(L_2s_2)c_1+(L_1+L_2c_2)s_1\). This is the point (x, y) seen as the vector \((L_1+L_2c_2,\;L_2s_2)\) rotated by q1, so

\[ q_1=\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)-\operatorname{atan2}\big(L_2\sin q_2,\;L_1+L_2\cos q_2\big) \]

One q1 for each q2. The slide’s general tool for \(A\cos\varphi+B\sin\varphi=C\) gives the same result: \(\varphi=\operatorname{atan2}(C,\pm\sqrt{A^2+B^2-C^2})-\operatorname{atan2}(A,B)\).

atan2 (p.29) returns the angle of the point (x, y) in (−π, π], using both signs. \(\tan^{-1}(y/x)\) cannot tell (1, 1) from (−1, −1): both give 45°, but the second is −135°. checked

Exam recipe (any 2-link planar sub-problem)
  1. Write FK. Identify the shoulder point and the target in the plane (subtract offsets first).
  2. \(\cos q_2\) by square-and-add (or the cosine rule). Check \(|\cos q_2|\le1\).
  3. \(q_2=\operatorname{atan2}(\pm\sqrt{1-c_2^2},\,c_2)\): two branches.
  4. \(q_1=\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)-\operatorname{atan2}(L_2s_2,\,L_1+L_2c_2)\) for each branch.
  5. Check one branch by FK.
Worked example

L1 = 1.0 m, L2 = 0.7 m, target (1.2, 0.8) m. \(\cos q_2=(1.44+0.64-1-0.49)/1.4 = 0.421429\), so q2 = ±65.075°. atan2(0.8, 1.2) = 33.690°.

Elbow with q2 = +65.075°: q1 = 33.690° − 26.114° = 7.576°. With q2 = −65.075°: q1 = 33.690° + 26.114° = 59.804°. Both reproduce (1.2, 0.8). checked

6 · Planar RR arm, geometric solution p. 31

Derivation (triangle OAB)

O is the base, A the elbow, B the tip at distance \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\). The interior angle at A is \(\pi-q_2\) (q2 is measured from link 1’s extension). Cosine rule:

\[ x^2+y^2=L_1^2+L_2^2-2L_1L_2\cos(\pi-q_2)=L_1^2+L_2^2+2L_1L_2\cos q_2 \]

the same as the algebra. Sine rule for the angle μ at O between OA and OB: \(\dfrac{\sin\mu}{L_2}=\dfrac{\sin(\pi-q_2)}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}=\dfrac{\sin q_2}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\). With \(\sigma=\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)\), the slide’s answer is \(q_1=\sigma-\mu\).

Signs: μ takes the sign of q2. For the elbow drawn on the slide (q2 > 0) the tip is anticlockwise of link 1, so link 1 lies below the line OB. For the other branch μ < 0 and q1 = σ + |μ|. Computing μ = atan2(L2s2, L1+L2c2) handles both automatically. checked for both branches

Geometric answers earn full marks if the triangle is drawn and labelled. Write “interior angle at the elbow = π − q2” explicitly; that one line prevents the sign error below.

7 · Six-DoF arm with a spherical wrist: decouple position and orientation pp. 32–38

Picture

A spherical wrist has its last three axes meeting at one point, the wrist centre W (p.34). Rotating joints 4–6 cannot move W, so W’s position depends only on q1–q3. Solve q1–q3 from W, then q4–q6 from the remaining rotation.

Derivation

Step 0, wrist centre added: if the tool point lies a distance d6 beyond W along the approach axis \(\hat z_E\), then \(\mathbf p_W=\mathbf p_E-d_6\,{}^0\mathbf R_E\,[0\;0\;1]^\top\) (the third column of R scaled by d6).

Step 1 (top view, p.35): \(q_1=\operatorname{atan2}(y_W,x_W)\), second branch q1+π.

Step 2 (the arm’s vertical plane, p.36): shoulder height H, upper arm G, forearm F, \(r_W^2=x_W^2+y_W^2\). With q3 the relative elbow angle (anticlockwise positive, same as q2 in the 2R arm):

\[ \cos q_3=\frac{r_W^2+(z_W-H)^2-F^2-G^2}{2FG},\qquad q_3=\operatorname{atan2}\big(\pm\sqrt{1-\cos^2q_3},\cos q_3\big) \]

Step 3 (p.37): \(\sigma=\operatorname{atan2}(z_W-H,\;r_W)\), \(\mu=\operatorname{atan2}(F\sin q_3,\;G+F\cos q_3)\), and with signed angles \(q_2=\sigma-\mu\).

Step 4, wrist (p.38): compute \({}^0\mathbf R_3\) from q1–q3, then \({}^3\mathbf R_6=({}^0\mathbf R_3)^\top\,{}^0\mathbf R_6\), and read q4–q6 as Euler angles. For a Z–Y–Z wrist \({}^3\mathbf R_6=R_z(q_4)R_y(q_5)R_z(q_6)\) added:

\[ q_5=\operatorname{atan2}\!\big(\sqrt{r_{13}^2+r_{23}^2},\,r_{33}\big),\quad q_4=\operatorname{atan2}(r_{23},\,r_{13}),\quad q_6=\operatorname{atan2}(r_{32},\,-r_{31}) \]

The other sign of q5 is the wrist flip (q4, q6 each change by π). If q5 = 0 the wrist is singular: only q4+q6 is determined. checked: extraction and flip both reproduce R

Slides vs maths: elbow sign on pp. 36–37

Slide 36 writes \(\cos(\pi-q_3)\) on the left. By the cosine rule (the interior angle at the elbow is π − q3), the right-hand side equals \(+\cos q_3\), not \(\cos(\pi-q_3)\) checked. Slide 37’s \(q_2=\sigma+\mu\) is correct when q3 is read as a clockwise bend (the drawn elbow-up pose) and μ as a positive angle checked. In the exam, define your positive direction on the sketch and stay with it. Signed anticlockwise angles give the formulas above.

Worked example (position part)

H = 0.5, G = 0.4, F = 0.3 m; wrist centre W = (0.4813, 0.4039, 0.5974) m. Then q1 = 40°, rW = 0.6283 m, zW − H = 0.0974 m, cos q3 = 0.6428, q3 = ±50°.

q3 = −50° (elbow up) gives q2 = 30°; q3 = +50° (elbow down) gives q2 = −12.378°. With the second q1 branch (220°) that is 4 position solutions; times 2 wrist flips makes 8. checked

8 · Numerical IK: goal potential, Newton–Raphson, pseudo-inverse pp. 40–52

Derivation

IK as optimisation (p.41): \(\mathbf q^*=\arg\min_{\mathbf q}|\mathcal K(\mathbf q)\ominus\xi^*|\). The quantity being minimised is the goal potential \(G(\mathbf q)\). For position only (p.42), \(G=(x^*-x)^2+(y^*-y)^2\).

Newton–Raphson (pp. 45–47): linearise \(G(q)\approx G(q^k)+G'(q^k)(q-q^k)\), set it to 0: \(q^{k+1}=q^k-G'(q^k)^{-1}G(q^k)\). Stop when the relative change is below ε.

For IK (pp. 48–52) the derivative is the Jacobian \(\mathbf J=\partial\mathcal F/\partial\mathbf q\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). With error \(\mathbf e=\mathbf x^*-\mathcal F(\mathbf q^i)\), the update is

\[ \mathbf q^{i+1}=\mathbf q^i+\mathbf J^{\dagger}(\mathbf q^i)\,\mathbf e,\qquad \mathbf J^\dagger=\begin{cases}\mathbf J^{-1} & n=m\\ \mathbf J^\top(\mathbf J\mathbf J^\top)^{-1} & n>m\ (\text{“fat”: infinitely many }\Delta\mathbf q\text{, picks the smallest})\\ (\mathbf J^\top\mathbf J)^{-1}\mathbf J^\top & n<m\ (\text{“tall”: no exact }\Delta\mathbf q\text{, least squares})\end{cases} \]

pseudo-inverse forms checked against numpy Caveats (notebook Q4–Q6): G = 0 may be impossible (target outside the workspace); the method may stall in a local minimum or diverge near a singularity; the answer found depends on the initial guess.

Worked example: one Newton step

2R arm (1.0, 0.7) m, target (1.2, 0.8), start q0 = (0.5, 0.5) rad. FK gives (1.2558, 1.0685), so e0 = (−0.0558, −0.2685).

\[ \mathbf J(\mathbf q^0)=\begin{bmatrix}-L_1s_1-L_2s_{12} & -L_2s_{12}\\ L_1c_1+L_2c_{12} & L_2c_{12}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1.0685&-0.5890\\1.2558&0.3782\end{bmatrix} \]

\(\Delta\mathbf q=\mathbf J^{-1}\mathbf e^0=(-0.5341,\;1.0635)\), so q1 = (−0.0341, 1.5635) rad and |e1| = 0.2181 (down from 0.2742). It converges to the elbow branch (7.576°, 65.075°) in 5 iterations. checked

Calculation risk: J is 2×2 here, so invert it by hand: \(\mathbf J^{-1}=\frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}\). The explain-type question asks why numerical IK may fail. Name three reasons (unreachable, local minimum or singular J, initial guess).

9 · When does a closed form exist? pp. 55–56

Any 6-DoF serial chain of R and P joints is solvable, but not always analytically. A sufficient condition for a closed form: three neighbouring joint axes intersect at a point (p.56), e.g. a spherical wrist. This is Pieper’s result; three consecutive parallel axes also work added: Craig ch. 4.

Guided problems: solve on paper first

P3.1 · Two-link IK, both branchescalculate

L1 = 1.0 m, L2 = 0.7 m. Find all (q1, q2) that put the tip at (1.2, 0.8) m.

Hint 1

Square and add the FK equations to remove q1.

Hint 2

cos q2 = (x² + y² − L1² − L2²)/(2L1L2) = 0.421429.

Hint 3

q1 = atan2(0.8, 1.2) − atan2(0.7 sin q2, 1 + 0.7 cos q2).

Full solution

q2 = ±65.075°; q1 = 7.576° (for +65.075°) or 59.804° (for −65.075°). FK check: 1.0 cos 7.576° + 0.7 cos 72.651° = 0.9913 + 0.2087 = 1.2000 ✓.

Derive cos q2 and q1 for a 2R arm from FK in 4 minutes.

P3.2 · Planar RRR with tool orientation (notebook Q10)derivecalculate

A planar 3R arm (links L1, L2, L3, relative angles θ1, θ2, θ3) must place its tip at (x, y) with tool angle φ. Derive the IK. Then evaluate for L = (1.0, 0.7, 0.3) m, (x, y) = (1.2, 0.9) m, φ = 60°.

Hint 1

The last link’s direction is known (φ), so its start, the “wrist” point, is known too.

Hint 2

Wrist point \(=(x-L_3\cos\varphi,\;y-L_3\sin\varphi)\). Solve the 2R problem for θ1, θ2; then θ3 = φ − θ1 − θ2.

Full solution

Wrist point (1.0500, 0.6402) m. 2R IK gives θ2 = ±89.085°, θ1 = −3.319° or 66.061°. Then θ3 = 60° − θ1 − θ2 = −25.766° or 83.024°. Two solutions; both reproduce (1.2, 0.9, 60°). checked

P3.3 · One Newton–Raphson stepcalculate

For the 2R arm of P3.1, start at q = (0.5, 0.5) rad and take one Newton step towards (1.2, 0.8). Give Δq.

Hint 1

FK at q0 = (1.2558, 1.0685), so e = target − FK.

Hint 2

Solve J Δq = e with the 2×2 inverse formula.

Full solution

det J = (−1.0685)(0.3782) − (−0.5890)(1.2558) = −0.4041 + 0.7397 = 0.3355. \(\mathbf J^{-1}=\frac{1}{0.3355}\begin{bmatrix}0.3782&0.5890\\-1.2558&-1.0685\end{bmatrix}\); Δq = J⁻¹(−0.0558, −0.2685) = (−0.5341, 1.0635) rad. checked Common wrong answer: using Jᵀ instead of J⁻¹. That is gradient descent, which moves in a different direction.

P3.4 · Spherical-wrist arm, position (slides 35–37)derivecalculate

H = 0.5, G = 0.4, F = 0.3 m. The wrist centre is W = (0.4813, 0.4039, 0.5974) m. Find q1, q3 and q2 for the elbow-up solution.

Hint 1

q1 from the top view; then work in the (r, z) plane with z measured from the shoulder.

Hint 2

cos q3 = (rW² + (zW−H)² − F² − G²)/(2FG). Elbow up means the forearm bends down: q3 < 0.

Full solution

q1 = atan2(0.4039, 0.4813) = 40°. rW = 0.6283, zW−H = 0.0974. cos q3 = (0.3948 + 0.0095 − 0.09 − 0.16)/0.24 = 0.6428, so q3 = −50° (elbow up). σ = atan2(0.0974, 0.6283) = 8.811°; μ = atan2(0.3 sin(−50°), 0.4 + 0.3 cos 50°) = −21.189°; q2 = σ − μ = 30.0°. checked

P3.5 · How many solutions? (notebook Q12, Q13)explain

(a) The notebook’s 3-DoF arm: base rotation θ1, a horizontal joint θ2 offset by L2, and a slider d3. How many position solutions? (b) The PUMA 560 for a full pose?

Model answer

(a) Count branch by branch. θ1: facing the point, or turned by π (2 options). In the arm’s plane the slider axis stays a distance L2 from the θ2 axis, so the tip distance ρ from that axis gives \(|d_3|=\sqrt{\rho^2-L_2^2}\) and two (θ2, d3) pairs. That makes up to 4 if d3 may be negative, and 2 if the slider only extends (d3 ≥ 0). State the assumption: the figure’s joint limits decide. our model of the figure

(b) Up to 8: shoulder left/right × elbow up/down × wrist flip. standard result

P3.6 · Spot the errorspot the error

A student solving a 2R arm writes \(x^2+y^2=L_1^2+L_2^2-2L_1L_2\cos q_2\) and gets q2 = ±114.9° for the target of P3.1. What went wrong?

Answer

They used the cosine rule with the joint angle q2 instead of the interior angle π − q2. This flips the sign of cos q2: they found the supplement (180° − 65.075° = 114.925°). The same slip is printed on slide 36.

P3.7 · Numerical IK caveats (notebook Q4–Q6)explain

Is it always possible to reach G(q) = 0? Will the solver always find a solution that exists? Is it unique?

Model answer

No: outside the reachable workspace the minimum of G is positive. No: Newton steps can stall in a local minimum or blow up where J is singular, and the result depends on the start. No: a redundant arm has infinitely many solutions, and even a 6-DoF arm has several; the initial guess decides which one is found.

Mini-quiz

Q1concept

Why do we need the dexterous rather than the reachable workspace when a full pose is specified?

Answer

The reachable workspace only guarantees some orientation; a full pose fixes the orientation too, so the point must be reachable in that orientation.

Q2calculate

For L1 = 1, L2 = 0.7, is (0, 0.2) reachable?

Answer

No. Its distance 0.2 m is below |L1 − L2| = 0.3 m, so cos q2 = (0.04 − 1.49)/1.4 = −1.036 < −1.

Q3spot the error

“A tall Jacobian (n < m) uses J† = Jᵀ(JJᵀ)⁻¹.” True?

Answer

False. For tall J, JJᵀ (m×m) is singular; use (JᵀJ)⁻¹Jᵀ (least squares). Jᵀ(JJᵀ)⁻¹ is for fat J (n > m).

Week 4 · Parallel manipulators

Many legs, one platform: count the freedom, close the loops

A parallel robot holds its end effector with several chains at once. That makes it stiff, light and precise, but every loop adds constraint equations. This week has three exam skills: count mobility (plain and extended Grübler–Kutzbach), write loop-closure equations, and solve IK by splitting the robot into its legs.

Lecture: Parallel Manipulators76 slides · no notebook this week
Open in new tab ↗
How this is examined

Three of the ten sample questions come from here: Q5 four-bar IK (W13 pp. 9–11), Q6 planar mobility (pp. 12–13) and Q7 delta mobility, plain then extended (pp. 14–17). All three are solved on the Sample Qs tab.

Where the marks are (indicative): numbered links and joints on the figure; D chosen correctly (3 planar, 6 spatial); every joint’s DoF; the formula written before the numbers; for “extended”, naming what RC and RM are in this mechanism.

Where marks are lost: forgetting the ground link; a spherical joint counted as 1; D = 6 for a planar mechanism; quoting a mobility without saying whether it is plausible (a delta with 9 DoF should make you reach for RM).

Practical

No practical or notebook for this week. Slide 73 sets a homework (inverse kinematics of the Gough–Stewart platform); it is solved below as P4.5.

Intuition first

A table vs a crane

A serial arm is a crane: each joint carries everything after it, so errors and weight add up. A parallel robot is a table on several legs: each leg carries a share, so it is stiff and precise, but it cannot reach far.

Counting freedom like a budget

Each free body would have D freedoms (3 in a plane, 6 in space). Each joint takes some away and leaves Fi. Grübler–Kutzbach is the balance: what is left over is the mobility.

Spinning a pencil

A rod held by a ball joint at each end can spin about its own axis without moving anything else. That idle spin is a local mobility RM. The counting formula sees it as a real freedom, so it over-counts.

Cut the loop, then glue it

To analyse a closed loop, cut it at one link. You get two simple serial arms. The “glue” is the condition that both halves end at the same point with the same orientation: the loop-closure equations.
