1 · What a parallel mechanism is, and why use one pp. 9–19, 74

Picture

“The end effector is connected to the base by multiple parallel kinematic chains of links” (p.12). There are usually more joints than DoF, so several joints are passive (not motorised). Examples: Gough’s tyre tester (1950s), Stewart’s flight simulator (1965), the ABB FlexPicker delta (Clavel), surgical hexapods (pp. 13–18).

SerialParallel
Chainsopenclosed
Jointsall activeactive + passive
Forward kinematicssimplecomplex
Inverse kinematicscomplexsimple
Joint errorsaccumulatedo not accumulate
Workspacelargesmall
Payload-to-weightlowvery high
Moving inertiahighlow

Comparison as on slide 74 (p.74). Drawbacks: complex kinematics and a restricted workspace (p.19).

A scenario question (“which architecture for fast pick-and-place / a heavy flight simulator / a precise surgical tool?”) is answered from this table: delta, Stewart, hexapod, each justified by stiffness, low moving mass and non-accumulating errors.

2 · Workspace of parallel robots pp. 20–23

Four definitions (p.21): reachable (some orientation), dexterous (all orientations), constant-orientation (points reachable with one given orientation), orientation workspace (all orientations available at one given point). Two ways to compute it: discretisation, i.e. step each actuator by a small amount and take the boundary of the reached nodes (slow; accuracy limited by step size, p.22); or geometry, i.e. intersect the regions allowed by each actuator’s limits (p.23). For a two-leg planar mechanism with prismatic legs, each leg confines the point to an annulus between its minimum and maximum length about its base pivot. The workspace is the overlap of the annuli.

Sketch question: draw each leg’s annulus (rmin, rmax about its pivot), shade the intersection, and label it “reachable”.

3 · Mobility: Grübler–Kutzbach pp. 24–34

Derivation

Start with N bodies, each free with D DoF, then fix one (the ground): D(N − 1) freedoms. Each joint i removes D − Fi of them. So \(M=D(N-1)-\sum_i(D-F_i)\), which rearranges to the slide’s form (p.25):

\[ M=D\,(N-J-1)+\sum_{i=1}^{J}F_i,\qquad D=\begin{cases}3 & \text{planar}\\6 & \text{spatial}\end{cases},\quad N\text{ includes the ground},\quad F_R=F_P=1,\;F_U=2,\;F_S=3 \]
Exam recipe
  1. Decide planar or spatial (D = 3 or 6). Motion out of the drawing’s plane means spatial (“still 3D despite this depiction”, W13 p.14).
  2. Number every rigid body on the figure, ground = 1. A prismatic pair is two bodies.
  3. List every joint and its Fi. A joint connects exactly two bodies; if three bodies meet at one pin, that is two joints.
  4. Substitute. If M disagrees with the obvious motion, look for idle spins (RM) or redundant constraints (RC): section 4.
Worked counts from the slides
MechanismDNJΣFM
Planar 3-RPR (p.26; W13 Q6)38993(8−9−1)+9 = 3
Simplest delta, R–U–U legs (p.30)689(1+2+2)×3 = 156(8−9−1)+15 = 3
Common delta, parallelogram legs (p.33)61115(1+4×3)×3 = 396(11−15−1)+39 = 9 (!)
Planar four-bar added34441
Gough–Stewart 6-UPS added614186×(2+1+3) = 366(14−18−1)+36 = 6

all checked Why the simplest delta is not built: universal joints that are both stiff and play-free are hard to make, and play lowers the usable operating frequency (p.31).

Slides vs slides

A handwritten note on slide 29 reads D(N − J + 1). The printed formula (and every worked count) uses D(N − J − 1); with +1 the simplest delta would give 6(8−9+1)+15 = 15.

4 · Extended Grübler–Kutzbach: over-constraints and local mobility pp. 35–43

Equation (slide 35) \[ M=D(N-J-1)+\sum_{i=1}^{J}F_i+R_C-R_M,\qquad R_C=\sum_{i=1}^{J}F_i-\sum_{k=1}^{L}u_k \]

RM: local mobility, i.e. motions of internal parts that do not move the output (a rod spinning about its own axis between two ball joints). The plain formula counts them as DoF, so subtract them.

RC: over-constraints. Some joints repeat a constraint that another joint already imposes, so the plain formula “removes” freedoms twice. uk are the distinct platform DoFs that loop k allows; the sum counts each distinct DoF once across loops.

Common delta (slides 33–36)

Plain count 9, but the platform only translates (3 DoF). Each of the 6 parallelogram rods can spin about its own axis between its two spherical joints: RM = 6. No redundant constraints: RC = 0. So M = 9 + 0 − 6 = 3. checked

4RRR (slides 37–43)

Two square plates joined by four RR legs: N = 10 (base, platform, 8 leg links), J = 12, ΣF = 12. Plain: 6(10 − 12 − 1) + 12 = −6, which is impossible for a mechanism that moves.

Loop 1 (one pair of legs) lets the platform do {Ty, Tz, Rx}; loop 2 lets it do {Tx, Tz, Ry} (pp. 39–41). The distinct DoFs are {Tx, Ty, Tz, Rx, Ry}, so Σuk = 5 (Tz counted once). RC = 12 − 5 = 7, RM = 0. M = −6 + 7 − 0 = 1: the only motion common to both loops is Tz, so the platform can only move up and down (pp. 42–43). checked

“Explain” marks: the plain count assumes every constraint is independent and every DoF moves the output. RC fixes the first assumption, RM the second. Say which one applies, and why, for the mechanism in front of you.

5 · Active and passive joints, and loop-closure equations pp. 45–58

Derivation (four-bar)

Configuration \(\mathbf q=(\boldsymbol\theta,\boldsymbol\varphi)\): n active joints θ, m passive joints φ (p.45). Recipe (p.49): break the loop into serial chains, write the pose of the break point from each side, and equate. Choose the break so that the fewest equations are needed.

Break link 2 at K (p.54), with a and b the distances from K to link 2’s ends (L2 = a + b) and {D} at (L0, 0). Position and orientation of K must agree from both sides: three equations, one active (θ1) and three passive (φ1, φ2, φ3) unknowns.

\[ \begin{aligned} L_1\cos\theta_1+a\cos(\theta_1+\varphi_2)&=L_0+L_3\cos\varphi_1+b\cos(\varphi_1+\varphi_3)\\ L_1\sin\theta_1+a\sin(\theta_1+\varphi_2)&=L_3\sin\varphi_1+b\sin(\varphi_1+\varphi_3)\\ \theta_1+\varphi_2&=\varphi_1+\varphi_3+\pi \end{aligned} \]

Break link 2 at both ends (p.57): only its length must be preserved, giving one equation in θ1, φ1 (the slide calls it the Freudenstein equation):

\[ \eta_1(\theta_1,\varphi_1)=(L_1\cos\theta_1-L_0-L_3\cos\varphi_1)^2+(L_1\sin\theta_1-L_3\sin\varphi_1)^2-L_2^2=0 \]

both forms checked at two assembly modes A Gough–Stewart platform has 6 active (prismatic) and 30 passive joint variables in many loops; choosing which equations to use is not trivial (p.58).

6 · Forward kinematics: the hard direction pp. 59–67

Derivation

FK of a parallel robot means: given the active joints, solve the loop-closure equations for the passive joints, then compute the output pose. There is no general method as there is for serial arms (p.60). Solutions can be multiple, some imaginary, so numerical methods are often used (p.67).

Four-bar, by geometry added: with θ1 known, A = L1(cos θ1, sin θ1) and D = (L0, 0) are fixed. B lies on the circle of radius L2 about A and the circle of radius L3 about D. Two circles meet in two points, the two assembly modes, one point (a limit), or not at all (the linkage cannot be assembled at that θ1).

The slides’ route (pp. 62–66), given K = (x, y) and seeking δ = θ1+φ2: squaring and adding each chain’s equations gives two equations linear in cos δ and sin δ:

\[ A_1\cos\delta+B_1\sin\delta+C_1=0,\quad A_1=x-L_0,\;B_1=y,\;C_1=\frac{(x-L_0)^2+y^2+b^2-L_3^2}{2b} \] \[ A_2\cos\delta+B_2\sin\delta+C_2=0,\quad A_2=x,\;B_2=y,\;C_2=\frac{L_1^2-a^2-x^2-y^2}{2a} \]

By Cramer’s rule, \(\cos\delta=\dfrac{B_1C_2-B_2C_1}{A_1B_2-A_2B_1}\) and \(\sin\delta=\dfrac{A_2C_1-A_1C_2}{A_1B_2-A_2B_1}\), so \(\delta=\operatorname{atan2}(\sin\delta,\cos\delta)\). Consistency of the two requires \((A_1B_2-A_2B_1)^2=(A_1C_2-A_2C_1)^2+(B_1C_2-B_2C_1)^2\), which is slide 65’s condition on (x, y). constants C1, C2 and the identity checked

Slides vs maths: slide 65

The slide prints \(\delta=\tan^{-1}\!\big(\tfrac{A_1C_2-A_2C_1}{(B_1C_2-B_2C_1)+(A_1B_2-A_2B_1)}\big)\). With the tangent-half-angle substitution the correct result is \(\delta=2\tan^{-1}\!\big(\tfrac{A_2C_1-A_1C_2}{(B_1C_2-B_2C_1)+(A_1B_2-A_2B_1)}\big)\): opposite sign in the numerator and a factor of 2. In our test the slide form gives 0.300° where the true δ is −0.600° checked. Safest in the exam: use the atan2 of the Cramer’s-rule sine and cosine above.

Worked example (same linkage as Sample Q5)

L0 = 1.0, L1 = 0.5, L3 = 0.6, a = 0.2, b = 0.25 m (L2 = 0.45), θ1 = 70°. The two assembly modes:

ModeK (m)φ (coupler)φ1
B above line AD(0.3710, 0.4678)−0.600°129.175°
B below line AD(0.2756, 0.2993)−58.486°171.739°

This linkage is non-Grashof (shortest + longest = 0.45 + 1.0 > 0.5 + 0.6), so no link turns fully. The input link only rocks: it can be assembled only while |AD| ≤ L2 + L3, i.e. |θ1| ≤ 81.52°. checked

Four-bar: assembly modes, FK and IKdrawn to scale · L0 1.0, L1 0.5, L2 0.45 (a 0.2 + b 0.25), L3 0.6 m
Try: set θ1 = 70° and flip the mode: K jumps between the two rows of the table above. Push θ1 past ±81.5°: the circles stop meeting and the linkage cannot close. The IK readout recovers θ1 from K and φ alone (Sample Q5).

7 · Inverse kinematics: the easy direction pp. 68–73

Derivation

Given the pose of the output link, each leg is a serial chain whose end pose is known, so solve each leg separately. No loop-closure equations are needed (p.69). Each leg must not be redundant, or its solution is not unique.

Four-bar (pp. 70–72; Sample Q5): the coupler’s ends are A = K − a(cos φ, sin φ) and B = K + b(cos φ, sin φ). So θ1 = atan2(y − a sin φ, x − a cos φ), φ2 = φ − θ1, φ1 = atan2(y + b sin φ, x + b cos φ − L0), φ3 = φ + π − φ1 (mod 2π). The full worked answer, and a note on the sign printed on W13 slide 11, are on the Sample Qs tab.

Gough–Stewart leg (homework, p.73): leg i joins base point \(\mathbf b_i\) (in {B}) to platform point \(\mathbf p_i\) (in {P}). Given \({}^B\mathbf T_P=[\mathbf R\;|\;\mathbf t]\):

\[ \mathbf l_i=\mathbf t+\mathbf R\,\mathbf p_i-\mathbf b_i,\qquad d_i=\lVert\mathbf l_i\rVert\ (\text{active prismatic}),\qquad \hat{\mathbf n}_i=\mathbf l_i/d_i \]

The passive joint angles follow from the leg direction \(\hat{\mathbf n}_i\): the spherical joint at the base takes the leg’s azimuth and elevation, and the universal joint at the platform takes the angle between \(\hat{\mathbf n}_i\) and the platform axes \(\mathbf R\). One unique answer per leg: this is why parallel IK is “simple”.

Worked example: Stewart leg lengths

Base points on a 1.0 m circle at −10°, 10°, 110°, 130°, 230°, 250°; platform points on a 0.5 m circle at −50°, 50°, 70°, 170°, 190°, 290°. Home pose (platform level, 1.0 m above the base): all six legs are 1.2182 m long.

Pose \(t(0.05,-0.02,1.0)\,R_z(5^\circ)\,R_y(3^\circ)\): legs = 1.1597, 1.1974, 1.2170, 1.2812, 1.2152, 1.2504 m. checked

Delta robot: IK in 3Dbase radius 0.20 m · platform 0.05 m · arm 0.20 m · rods 0.45 m
blue = actuated arms · grey = parallelogram rods · x red y green z blue
Try: move the platform with the sliders. The three motor angles come from closed-form IK (each arm alone, like the four-bar). Every rod length is checked live to be 0.45 m: that is the loop closure. Note how the platform never tilts. Each pair of rods is a parallelogram, which keeps the platform parallel to the base. That is why plain G–K’s 9 becomes 3.

Guided problems: solve on paper first

P4.1 · Mobility of the 4RRRcalculateexplain

Two square plates are joined by four identical RR legs (slides 37–43). Compute the plain G–K mobility, explain why it is wrong, and find the true mobility with the extended equation.

Hint 1

N = 10, J = 12, all revolute, D = 6.

Hint 2

Write the platform DoFs each pair of legs allows; count the union, not the sum.

Full solution

Plain: 6(10 − 12 − 1) + 12 = −6. That is impossible for a moving mechanism, so constraints are being double-counted. Loop DoFs: {Ty, Tz, Rx} and {Tx, Tz, Ry}; union = 5. RC = 12 − 5 = 7, RM = 0, so M = −6 + 7 = 1 (pure Tz).

P4.2 · Loop closure for the four-barderive

Break the four-bar at both ends of link 2 and write the single constraint equation. How many unknowns does it link?

Hint

The two cut points U (end of link 1) and V (end of link 3) must stay L2 apart.

Full solution

U = (L1cos θ1, L1sin θ1), V = (L0 + L3cos φ1, L3sin φ1), and |U − V|² = L2² gives η1 above. It links one active and one passive variable (θ1, φ1). Given θ1, solving it gives two φ1 (the two assembly modes).

P4.3 · Four-bar FK numberscalculate

For the linkage in the worked example with θ1 = 70°, find the coupler angle φ for the assembly mode with B below line AD.

Hint 1

A = (0.1710, 0.4698); |AD| = 0.9529 m.

Hint 2

Intersect the circle of radius 0.45 about A with the circle of radius 0.6 about D, and take the lower point.

Full solution

Along AD from A: x = (L2² − L3² + |AD|²)/(2|AD|) = (0.2025 − 0.36 + 0.9080)/1.9058 = 0.3938 m, h = √(0.45² − 0.3938²) = 0.2178 m. B = A + 0.3938 û − 0.2178 n̂ = (0.4062, 0.0862). φ = atan2(By − Ay, Bx − Ax) = −58.486°. Then K = A + 0.2(cos φ, sin φ) = (0.2756, 0.2993) m. checked

P4.4 · Why is the delta’s platform always level?explainsketch

Explain, with a sketch of one leg, why a delta platform translates but never rotates, and connect it to the mobility count.

Model answer

Each forearm is a parallelogram: two equal, parallel rods with spherical joints at the four corners. A parallelogram keeps its top and bottom edges parallel, so each leg keeps one platform edge parallel to its upper-arm axis. Three legs at 120° lock all three rotations, leaving 3 translations. Plain G–K counts each rod’s idle spin as a DoF (9), so subtract RM = 6 to get 3.

P4.5 · Gough–Stewart IK (homework, slide 73)derivecalculate

Each leg is S (base, passive), P (active), U (platform, passive). Given \({}^B\mathbf T_P\), determine all joint variables. Then compute leg 1 for the worked-example geometry at the home pose (platform 1.0 m above the base, no rotation).

Hint 1

Write platform point i in {B}: \(\mathbf t+\mathbf R\mathbf p_i\). The leg vector is that minus \(\mathbf b_i\).

Hint 2

Leg 1: b1 = (cos(−10°), sin(−10°), 0); p1 = 0.5(cos(−50°), sin(−50°), 0).

Full solution

\(\mathbf l_1=(0.3214-0.9848,\;-0.3830+0.1736,\;1.0)=(-0.6634,\,-0.2094,\,1.0)\) m; d1 = √(0.4401 + 0.0438 + 1) = 1.2182 m. Passive angles: the base spherical joint aligns the leg with \(\hat{\mathbf n}_1=\mathbf l_1/d_1\) (azimuth atan2(−0.2094, −0.6634) = −162.48°, elevation asin(1.0/1.2182) = 55.17°). The roll about the leg axis is shared between the S and U joints and does not affect d1. d checked

P4.6 · Spot the errorspot the error

“The slider-crank (ground, crank, connecting rod, slider; 3 revolute joints and 1 prismatic) has M = 6(4 − 4 − 1) + 4 = −2, so it is a structure.” What is wrong?

Answer

It is planar, so D = 3: M = 3(4 − 4 − 1) + 4 = 1. A slider-crank has one DoF (crank angle ↔ slider position).

Mini-quiz

Q1concept

Why is FK hard and IK easy for parallel robots, the opposite of serial ones?

Answer

FK needs the passive joints, which are found only by solving the coupled nonlinear loop-closure equations (multiple, possibly imaginary solutions). IK gives each leg’s end pose directly, so each leg is a small independent serial IK.

Q2calculate

A spatial mechanism has N = 6, J = 7, joints: 5 R, 1 U, 1 S. Plain G–K mobility?

Answer

ΣF = 5 + 2 + 3 = 10; M = 6(6 − 7 − 1) + 10 = −2. Report it, then look for over-constraints (RC) before concluding it is a structure.

Q3concept

Name the two meanings of RM and RC in one line each.

Answer

RM: internal motions that do not move the output (subtract). RC: constraints counted twice because they repeat each other (add back).

Week 5 · Trajectories

How does the arm get there, and when?

A path says where the robot goes. A trajectory also says when: position, velocity and acceleration of every joint against time. This week builds trajectories from simple pieces: cubics, quintics, and straight lines with parabolic ends. Then it asks whether to build them in joint space or in task space, and what goes wrong in each.

Lecture: Trajectories69 slides · Dr KM Digumarti · notebook “5 Trajectories”
Open in new tab ↗
How this is examined

Sample questions 8 and 9 (W13 p.18, p.19; full solutions in Q8 and Q9): two cubics joined at a via point with continuous acceleration, and a rest-to-rest cubic for a prismatic joint (0.02 m to 0.15 m in 0.8 s). Expect a variation of one of these with new numbers, or a parabolic-blend calculation like the p.37 example.

Where the marks are (indicative; marks not published): the conditions written as a list (four for a cubic, eight for two cubics); the general coefficients or the matrix equation; correct substitution of numbers with units; a check that \(q(t_F)=q_F\) and \(\dot q(t_F)\) is right; for blends, the existence test \(a\ge 4\Delta q/t_F^2\) and the choice of root.

Where marks are lost: dividing by \(t_F^2\) where \(t_F^3\) belongs; forgetting that each segment of a via-point trajectory has its own clock; using a strict inequality (the slide says \(\ge\)); taking the wrong root of the blend quadratic; quoting a Cartesian straight line as if joint-linear motion gave it.

Practical (optional, no coding in the exam)

The practical file ik_2r_plain_python.py is plain numpy for a planar 2R arm (l1 = 1.0, l2 = 0.8): analytical IK with both elbow branches, and a Newton–Raphson IK from a starting guess. It is the “IK at each sample” step of the Cartesian recipe below. The lecture notebook calls rtb.quintic, rtb.trapezoidal, rtb.mstraj and rtb.ctraj; none of those cells has a saved output, so no toolbox numbers are quoted here as results.

Intuition first

Path = route, trajectory = timetable

A route on a map says “Brisbane, Gympie, Rockhampton”. A timetable says “Gympie at 10:40, moving at 90 km/h”. The robot needs the timetable, because motors are driven by what to do now.

A cubic is a smooth lift ride

A lift starts and stops gently. Four facts fix the ride: where and when it starts and ends, and how fast it moves at each end. Four facts, four coefficients. Rest-to-rest means both end speeds are zero.In the notebook: the cubic is found by solving a 4×4 matrix with np.linalg.solve.

Via points: ride over the hills

A cyclist going up then down stops pedalling at the crest: slope zero. On a steady climb she keeps the average of the slopes either side. That is the lecturer’s simple rule. A smoother ride matches acceleration too, but then the speeds are forced by the whole route.

Parabolic blends: a car on a motorway

Floor the pedal at a constant rate, cruise, brake at the same rate. Speed against time is a trapezoid. If the trip is too short for the chosen acceleration, no cruise fits; there is a minimum acceleration for a given distance and time.

Straight in the joints is not straight in space

Two joints turning at steady rates draw an arc, not a line. To go straight in space you must solve IK at many points along the line, and the arm may not be able to follow (hole, singularity, wrong elbow).

1 · Path, trajectory, and where to build it pp. 6–14, pp. 42–45

Picture

A trajectory is a time sequence of position (and velocity and acceleration) for every degree of freedom (p.7). A path is the same set of poses with no timing. The task: given an initial and a final pose of the tool, work out the motion in between (p.10).

Teach mode (p.9): an operator jogs the robot (teach pendant, or by hand) and the joint positions are stored and replayed. No kinematics are needed. It suits a repeated task with few uncertainties, such as pick and place on an assembly line.

Two ways to generate a trajectory. Joint space (p.12): turn the start and end poses into joint angles with IK, then interpolate each joint. There are infinitely many curves between the same two points (p.13). Task space (p.43): describe the tool motion directly, then use IK along it.

Comparison
Joint spaceTask (Cartesian) space
You specify\(\mathbf q(t)\), one curve per jointpose of {T} relative to {S} against time
Costcheap: no IK along the waymore computation: IK at every sample (p.43)
Tool pathwhatever the joint curves produce (not a line)exactly what you asked for (line, circle, ellipse)
Good forfree motion between pointsa specified path; avoiding an obstacle (p.43)
What goes to the motorsalways joint positions, velocities and accelerations (p.68)

Describing the tool {T} relative to the station {S} (p.45) has two benefits: the description is decoupled from the manipulator (the same description works for different robots), and it adapts to a moving {S}, such as a conveyor belt.

A short “explain” item: compare joint and task space on cost, path shape, and obstacle control, and finish with “either way the motors receive joint commands”. A common wrong claim is that Cartesian commands go straight to the motors; they do not.

2 · Cubic polynomial trajectories pp. 15–20

Picture

A polynomial of order \(N\) has \(N+1\) coefficients, so it needs \(N+1\) conditions: \(q(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}a_kt^k\) (p.15). Starting at rest, moving, and stopping at rest at the goal gives four conditions (start and end position, start and end velocity). The simplest polynomial with four coefficients is a cubic. In the widget above, the default curve is exactly the slide example.

Derivation

Let \(t_0=0\) (shift the clock otherwise, see below). With \(T=t_F\) and \(\Delta q=q_F-q_0\):

\[ q=a_0+a_1t+a_2t^2+a_3t^3,\qquad \dot q=a_1+2a_2t+3a_3t^2,\qquad \ddot q=2a_2+6a_3t \]

Four conditions: \(q(0)=q_0\), \(q(T)=q_F\), \(\dot q(0)=\dot q_0\), \(\dot q(T)=\dot q_F\) (zero for rest-to-rest). In matrix form (notebook cell 16 does this for the example):

\[ \begin{bmatrix}1&0&0&0\\1&T&T^2&T^3\\0&1&0&0\\0&1&2T&3T^2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a_0\\a_1\\a_2\\a_3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}q_0\\q_F\\\dot q_0\\\dot q_F\end{bmatrix} \]

Solve by hand. The first and third rows give \(a_0=q_0\) and \(a_1=\dot q_0\). Let \(r=\Delta q-\dot q_0T\) and \(s=\dot q_F-\dot q_0\). The other two rows are \(a_2T^2+a_3T^3=r\) and \(2a_2T+3a_3T^2=s\). Multiply the first by \(2/T\) and subtract it from the second: \(a_3T^2=s-2r/T\). Back-substitute:

\[ a_2=\frac{3\Delta q-(2\dot q_0+\dot q_F)T}{T^2},\qquad a_3=\frac{-2\Delta q+(\dot q_0+\dot q_F)T}{T^3} \]

checked symbolically and numerically For rest to rest (\(\dot q_0=\dot q_F=0\)): \(a_2=3\Delta q/T^2\), \(a_3=-2\Delta q/T^3\). Consequences: the velocity is a parabola with peak \(1.5\,\Delta q/T\) at \(t=T/2\); the acceleration is a straight line, \(+6\Delta q/T^2\) at the start and \(-6\Delta q/T^2\) at the end, zero at \(T/2\) (p.19). Note that the acceleration is not zero at the ends, so it jumps there (that is what a quintic fixes, section 4).

If \(t_0\ne0\): use \(\tau=t-t_0\) and \(T=t_F-t_0\) in the formulas above. Each segment of a multi-point trajectory gets its own clock \(\tau\in[0,T_k]\), which is how the sample solutions (Q8) write it.

More than one joint (p.20, notebook Q1): each joint gets its own cubic, solved independently with its own \(q_0,q_F\). Give all joints the same \(T\) so they start and stop together. A program then evaluates every joint at the controller’s path-update rate.

Exam recipe
  1. State the assumptions: \(t_0=0\), start and end at rest unless told otherwise.
  2. Write \(q,\dot q\) and the four conditions as a list.
  3. \(a_0=q_0\), \(a_1=\dot q_0\) straight away.
  4. Rest to rest: \(a_2=3\Delta q/T^2\), \(a_3=-2\Delta q/T^3\). Otherwise use the general pair above.
  5. Write \(q(t)\) with units: \(a_k\) is in °/s\(^k\) or m/s\(^k\).
  6. Check \(q(T)=q_F\) and \(\dot q(T)=\dot q_F\).
Worked example (slides pp. 17–19, notebook cell 15)

One revolute joint, rest at 10°, to 50° in 2 s, stop. \(\Delta q=40^\circ\), \(T=2\) s. \(a_0=10^\circ\), \(a_1=0\), \(a_2=3(40)/4=30^\circ/\mathrm{s}^2\), \(a_3=-2(40)/8=-10^\circ/\mathrm{s}^3\). So \(q(t)=10+30t^2-10t^3\). Peak speed \(1.5(40)/2=30\) °/s at \(t=1\) s; acceleration \(\ddot q=60-60t\), from +60 to −60 °/s² (the three plots on p.19). checked

Non-zero end velocity. 20° to 80° in 3 s, \(\dot q_0=0\), \(\dot q_F=10\) °/s: \(a_2=[3(60)-(0+10)(3)]/9=16.667\), \(a_3=[-2(60)+(0+10)(3)]/27=-3.333\). Check: \(q(3)=20+16.667(9)-3.333(27)=80\) and \(\dot q(3)=2(16.667)(3)-3(3.333)(9)=10\). checked

Calculation, usually with new numbers (sample Q9 is a rest-to-rest cubic for a prismatic joint). The trap is the denominators: \(t_F^2\) for \(a_2\) and \(t_F^3\) for \(a_3\). Units follow: m/s² and m/s³ for a prismatic joint.

3 · Via points: velocities, the simple rule, continuous acceleration pp. 21–28

Picture

To pass through intermediate (via) points, use a cubic between each adjacent pair (p.21). If every cubic starts and ends at rest, the robot stops at every via point (p.25: “Is this desirable?” Usually not). Each cubic needs a velocity at each end, so the real question is what velocity to give at the via points. There are three options (p.26):

  1. the user specifies them;
  2. the system computes them with a simple formula;
  3. the system computes them so that the acceleration is continuous.
Option 2: the simple rule (p.27)

Slope of each straight chord: \(s_k=\Delta q_k/\Delta t_k\). At a via point, if the slopes either side change sign, the velocity is zero (the curve peaks or dips there). Otherwise it is the average of the two slopes. The first and last velocities are zero (the figure on p.27 shows flat tangents at \(q_0\) and \(q_F\); the slide does not say so in words, so state it as an assumption). Each segment is then the closed-form cubic of section 2 with those end velocities.

Worked example (notebook Q2, “Question 2” data)

Points 10, 50, 20, 40, 45° at 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 s. Slopes: \(+8,\ -6,\ +4,\ +1\) °/s. At qA: +8 then −6, sign change, so 0. At qB: −6 then +4, sign change, 0. At qC: +4 and +1, same sign, average \(2.5\) °/s. At q0, qF: 0. checked

segment (own clock, T = 5 s)\(a_0\)\(a_1\)\(a_2\)\(a_3\)
q0 → qA1004.8−0.64
qA → qB500−3.60.48
qB → qC2001.9−0.22
qC → qF402.5−0.40.02

(units °, °/s, °/s², °/s³). Example, last segment: \(\Delta q=5\), \(a_2=[15-(2\cdot2.5+0)5]/25=-0.4\), \(a_3=[-10+(2.5)5]/125=0.02\); \(q(5)=40+12.5-10+2.5=45\) ✓. Position and velocity are continuous at every via point, but the acceleration jumps: end of one segment minus start of the next is −2.4, +3.4 and −2.0 °/s² at qA, qB, qC. checked

Option 3: continuous acceleration (p.26, homework p.28, notebook Q3)

The homework asks for two cubics through \(q_0,q_{via},q_F\) with \(\dot q_0=\dot q_F=0\) and “constant acceleration at the via point”. The unknown is the via velocity \(w\). Read “constant” as continuous: the acceleration at the end of segment 1 equals that at the start of segment 2. (If \(a_{via}\) were also prescribed, with \(w\) free, you would have too many conditions; this is the reading the lecturer’s sample answer uses, Q8.)

Count: two cubics have 8 unknowns. Conditions: 4 positions (start, via twice, end), 2 end velocities, velocity continuity, acceleration continuity: 8. Solvable.

Short route. Let \(d_1=q_{via}-q_0\), \(d_2=q_F-q_{via}\), durations \(T_1,T_2\). Use the closed-form cubic with end velocities \((0,w)\) for segment 1 and \((w,0)\) for segment 2. Then \(\ddot q_1(T_1)=2a_2+6a_3T_1=\dfrac{-6d_1+4wT_1}{T_1^2}\) and \(\ddot q_2(0)=2a_2'=\dfrac{6d_2-4wT_2}{T_2^2}\). Setting them equal and solving for \(w\):

\[ \dot q_{via}=\frac{3\,\big[T_1^2\,(q_F-q_{via})+T_2^2\,(q_{via}-q_0)\big]}{2\,T_1T_2\,(T_1+T_2)},\qquad T_1=T_2=T:\ \ \dot q_{via}=\frac{3(q_F-q_0)}{4T} \]

checked symbolically and with the 8×8 system The equal-time result agrees with the lecturer’s coefficient \(a_{21}=3(\theta_g-\theta_0)/(4t_f)\) in Q8. The via velocity does not depend on \(q_{via}\) when the times are equal. The shared acceleration at the via point is \(3(q_0+q_F-2q_{via})/T^2\) (equal times).

Many via points. Continuity of acceleration at each interior point gives one linear equation per interior velocity (a tridiagonal system), where \(h\) are the segment durations and \(s\) the chord slopes:

\[ \frac{w_{i-1}}{h_{i-1}}+2\Big(\frac1{h_{i-1}}+\frac1{h_i}\Big)w_i+\frac{w_{i+1}}{h_i}=3\Big(\frac{s_{i-1}}{h_{i-1}}+\frac{s_i}{h_i}\Big) \]

This is a spline. The slides do not give it; it is for understanding only.

For the Q2 data with zero end velocities it gives via velocities \(0,\ 2.304,\ -3.214,\ 4.554,\ 0\) °/s, a very different answer from the simple rule. checked

Worked example (sample Q8 numbers, and an unequal-time variant)

\(q_0=10^\circ,\ q_{via}=40^\circ,\ q_F=20^\circ\), \(T_1=T_2=1\) s: \(\dot q_{via}=3(10)/4=7.5\) °/s; segment 1: \(10+0t+82.5t^2-52.5t^3\); segment 2: \(40+7.5t-75t^2+47.5t^3\). Shared acceleration \(3(10+20-80)/1=-150\) °/s². checked

Now \(T_1=1\) s, \(T_2=2\) s (same angles): \(\dot q_{via}=3[1(-20)+4(30)]/(2\cdot1\cdot2\cdot3)=300/12=25\) °/s. Segment 1: \(10+65t^2-35t^3\); segment 2: \(40+25t-40t^2+11.25t^3\); shared acceleration −80 °/s². checked

Exam recipe
  1. Write unknowns and conditions (8 for two cubics; velocity and acceleration continuity at the via point).
  2. Give each segment its own clock \(\tau\) and duration.
  3. Use the closed-form cubic with end velocities \((0,w)\) and \((w,0)\) so only \(w\) is unknown.
  4. Equate end-of-1 and start-of-2 accelerations; solve for \(w\).
  5. Substitute back, then check \(q_1(T_1)=q_{via}\), \(q_2(T_2)=q_F\) and the accelerations match.
Two question types. (a) “Apply the simple rule to these points”: compute the slopes, decide sign change, write the velocities (the Q2 numbers above). (b) “Two cubics with continuous acceleration”: sample Q8. State the 8 conditions first; most marks are there. A trap is calling a trajectory that stops at every via point “smooth”; it is smooth in position but wasteful.

4 · Quintic polynomials, and why polynomials are inefficient pp. 29–30

Picture

A quintic has six coefficients, so it takes six conditions: position, velocity and acceleration at both ends (p.29). The extra two conditions let you set the end accelerations (usually zero), so the acceleration no longer jumps at the start and stop.

p.30 (hand sketch): the velocity of any polynomial trajectory is a hump that touches its peak briefly, while a trapezoid holds the peak speed for most of the motion. With a generous blend acceleration a trapezoid covers the same distance in the same time at a peak speed much closer to the mean, so it asks less of the motor. The notebook (cell 28) makes the same point and leads into linear trajectories.

Derivation \[ q=a_0+a_1t+\dots+a_5t^5,\quad \dot q=a_1+2a_2t+3a_3t^2+4a_4t^3+5a_5t^4,\quad \ddot q=2a_2+6a_3t+12a_4t^2+20a_5t^3 \]

Conditions: \(q,\dot q,\ddot q\) at \(t=0\) and \(t=T\). With zero end accelerations: \(a_0=q_0\), \(a_1=\dot q_0\), \(a_2=0\), and

\[ a_3=\frac{20\Delta q-(8\dot q_F+12\dot q_0)T}{2T^3},\quad a_4=\frac{-30\Delta q+(14\dot q_F+16\dot q_0)T}{2T^4},\quad a_5=\frac{12\Delta q-6(\dot q_F+\dot q_0)T}{2T^5} \]

checked symbolically Rest to rest: \(a_3=10\Delta q/T^3\), \(a_4=-15\Delta q/T^4\), \(a_5=6\Delta q/T^5\). These closed forms are mine (the slides only list the conditions); use the 6×6 matrix in an exam. Peak speed is \(1.875\,\Delta q/T\) at \(T/2\), and peak acceleration magnitude \(10\Delta q/(\sqrt3\,T^2)\approx5.77\,\Delta q/T^2\).

Worked example

0° to 15° in 1 s, rest to rest. Quintic: \(a_3=150\), \(a_4=-225\), \(a_5=90\) (units °/s³, °/s⁴, °/s⁵). Peak speed \(1.875(15)=28.125\) °/s; end accelerations 0. Cubic for the same move: peak speed \(1.5(15)=22.5\) °/s, end accelerations \(\pm6(15)=\pm90\) °/s². The mean speed is 15 °/s, so mean/peak is 66.7 % for the cubic and 53.3 % for the quintic. A trapezoid’s peak speed lies between \(\Delta q/T\) (ratio near 100 %, large \(a\)) and \(2\Delta q/T\) (the triangle, smallest \(a\)). checked

Notebook cell 29 prints qd.mean()/qd.max()*100 for traj_B (quintic 0→15 in 1 s, \(\dot q_0=10\), \(\dot q_F=5\), 50 samples). The notebook has no saved output. From the closed form above I compute 68.5 % (and 52.3 % for the zero-end-velocity case traj_A, which differs from 53.3 % because the 50-sample mean is not the exact mean). computed here

Counting questions: linear 2 coefficients, cubic 4, quintic 6; each extra order buys one more boundary condition per end. “Why use a quintic?” Acceleration continuity at the ends (smaller jerk, less vibration). “Why not use a polynomial everywhere?” Peak speed is high for the time taken, so a trapezoid is more efficient.

5 · Linear segments with parabolic blends (LSPB) pp. 31–37

Picture

A straight line \(q=a_0+a_1t\) has constant velocity, which a real joint cannot reach instantly from rest (p.31). So add a blend at each end: constant acceleration \(+a\) for a time \(t_B\), a coast at constant speed \(v\), then \(-a\) for \(t_B\) (pp.32–34). Velocity against time is a trapezoid. Position is parabola, line, parabola.

Derivation (slides pp. 33–36)

Take \(t_0=0\). With \(a\) the blend acceleration magnitude, \(v\) the coast speed, \(t_B\) the blend duration:

\[ q_{B1}=q_0+\tfrac12at_B^2,\qquad q_{B2}=q_{B1}+v\,(t_F-2t_B),\qquad q_F=q_{B2}+v\,t_B-\tfrac12at_B^2,\qquad v=a\,t_B \]

\(q_{B1}\) is the position at the end of blend 1, \(q_{B2}\) the position at the start of blend 2 (time \(t_F-t_B\)). The slide labels equations 1 and 3 “second order polynomial in time” and equation 2 “linear in time”. Eliminate \(q_{B1},q_{B2},v\):

\[ a\,t_B^2-a\,t_F\,t_B+(q_F-q_0)=0\ \Rightarrow\ t_B=\frac{t_F}{2}\pm\frac{\sqrt{a^2t_F^2-4a(q_F-q_0)}}{2a} \]

Take the root that is positive and smaller than \(t_F\) (in fact smaller than \(t_F/2\), the minus sign, because two blends must fit in the time). A real root exists only if the discriminant is non-negative:

\[ a^2t_F^2-4a\,\Delta q\ \ge 0\iff a\ \ge\ \frac{4\,\Delta q}{t_F^2} \]

The slide uses “≥” (non-strict). At equality \(t_B=t_F/2\), the coast phase has length zero and the profile is a triangle with peak \(2\Delta q/t_F\). Below the minimum there is no real root: that motion cannot be done in time \(t_F\). A motor sets a maximum \(a\). The coast speed is \(v=at_B=\tfrac12\big[a t_F-\sqrt{a^2t_F^2-4a\Delta q}\big]\), always in \((\Delta q/t_F,\,2\Delta q/t_F]\). Bigger \(a\) gives a shorter blend and a lower coast speed. checked

If you choose \(v\) instead of \(a\) (the toolbox does this, V=, notebook cell 40): \(\Delta q=v(t_F-t_B)\) gives \(t_B=t_F-\Delta q/v\) and \(a=v/t_B=v^2/(vt_F-\Delta q)\). This needs \(\Delta q/t_F\lt v\le2\Delta q/t_F\). For 120° in 2 s and \(V=70\): \(t_B=2-120/70=0.2857\) s, \(a=245\) °/s². checked

Slides vs notebook (the t₀ caveat)

The slides (pp.33–34) and notebook (cell 35) write a general-\(t_0\) form: \(q_{B1}=q_0+a(t_B-t_0)^2/2\) and \(a t_B^2-a(t_F-t_0)t_B+(q_F-q_0-at_0^2/2)=0\), then say “if \(t_0=0\)”. The general form is inconsistent: \(q_{B2}\) still uses \(t_F-2t_B\) and \(v=at_B\), which only hold for \(t_0=0\). Test: the p.37 motion shifted to start at \(t_0=1\) s and end at \(t_F=3\) s is the same motion and must give the same \(t_B=0.2254\) s. The slide’s quadratic gives roots 2.049 and −0.049 instead. Correct general form: replace \(t_F\) by the duration \(T=t_F-t_0\) everywhere: \(a t_B^2-aTt_B+\Delta q=0\), with \(t_B\) a duration. Every example on the slides has \(t_0=0\), so no slide answer changes. checked

Exam recipe (p.37)
  1. List \(\Delta q\), \(t_0=0\), \(t_F\), \(a\).
  2. Existence: compute \(4\Delta q/t_F^2\) and test \(a\ge\) it. If not, say “no solution; needs a larger \(a\) or a longer \(t_F\)”.
  3. \(t_B=\tfrac{t_F}{2}-\tfrac{\sqrt{a^2t_F^2-4a\Delta q}}{2a}\) (the smaller root).
  4. \(v=at_B\).
  5. Check: \(2\cdot\tfrac12at_B^2+v(t_F-2t_B)=\Delta q\).
Worked example (slide p.37; the slide gives no final answer)

120° in 2 s, \(a=300\) °/s². Step 1: \(4(120)/2^2=120\), and \(300\ge120\) ✓. Step 2: \(a^2t_F^2-4a\Delta q=360000-144000=216000\), \(\sqrt{\cdot}=464.76\), \(t_B=1-464.76/600=0.2254\) s (the + root, 1.7746 s, exceeds \(t_F/2\): rejected). Step 3: \(v=300(0.2254)=67.62\) °/s. Check: blends cover \(2\times7.62=15.24^\circ\), coast covers \(67.62\times1.5492=104.76^\circ\), total 120.00° ✓. checked

Edge cases: \(a=120\): \(t_B=1\) s, \(v=120\) °/s, no coast. \(a=100\): discriminant \(4\,(10^4)-4(100)(120)=-8000\lt 0\), no real root. checked

The standard calculation, and a classic spot-the-error item (strict “>” versus “≥”, wrong root, \(t_F^2\) forgotten in the minimum). Also explain in words why a minimum exists: the joint must accelerate up to \(v\) and brake again within \(t_F\). The gentlest way to cover \(\Delta q\) in \(t_F\) is the triangle: accelerate for half the time, brake for half, which needs exactly \(a=4\Delta q/t_F^2\).

6 · Several segments with blends pp. 38–41

Picture

With via points \(q_i,q_j,q_k,\dots\) the joint moves in straight segments and blends through each corner (p.38). Starting and ending at rest and passing exactly through every via point without stopping is over-constrained (notebook cell 42), so the path passes near the via points, not through them. The blend rounds each corner.

Symbols (p.39): \(t_{djk}\) total duration between \(q_j\) and \(q_k\); \(t_{jk}\) duration of the linear part; \(t_j\) duration of the blend at \(q_j\); \(v_{jk}\) slope of the linear part; \(a_j\) blend acceleration at \(q_j\). Given (p.40): the via points, the segment durations \(t_{djk}\), the acceleration magnitudes \(a_j\). Find: the blend times. The slides refer to Craig §7.3 for the solution (and to Corke §3.3.3 and mstraj for quintic blends, p.41).

Craig’s solution (not on the slides; for understanding)

Each via time is the centre of its blend. For \(n\) points, with \(\mathrm{sgn}\) giving the sign of the acceleration:

First segment: \(\ddot\theta_1=\mathrm{sgn}(\theta_2-\theta_1)|\ddot\theta_1|\), \(t_1=t_{d12}-\sqrt{t_{d12}^2-2(\theta_2-\theta_1)/\ddot\theta_1}\), \(v_{12}=\dfrac{\theta_2-\theta_1}{t_{d12}-\tfrac12t_1}\).

Interior segments: \(v_{jk}=\dfrac{\theta_k-\theta_j}{t_{djk}}\); at a via point \(j\): \(\ddot\theta_j=\mathrm{sgn}(v_{jk}-v_{ij})|\ddot\theta_j|\), \(t_j=\dfrac{v_{jk}-v_{ij}}{\ddot\theta_j}\).

Last segment: \(\ddot\theta_n=\mathrm{sgn}(\theta_{n-1}-\theta_n)|\ddot\theta_n|\), \(t_n=t_{d(n-1)n}-\sqrt{t_{d(n-1)n}^2+2(\theta_n-\theta_{n-1})/\ddot\theta_n}\), \(v_{(n-1)n}=\dfrac{\theta_n-\theta_{n-1}}{t_{d(n-1)n}-\tfrac12t_n}\).

Then the linear duration is \(t_{jk}=t_{djk}-\tfrac12t_j-\tfrac12t_k\) (full \(t_1\) or \(t_n\) at the ends). The first-segment formula comes from the slide’s single-segment algebra, with the end of segment 1 placed at the middle of the next blend: \(\theta_2-\theta_1=a t_1t_{d12}-\tfrac12at_1^2\). Because the path is a rounded corner, it misses the via point by \(|\Delta v|\,t_j/8=a_jt_j^2/8\).

Worked example (mine, built from the formulas above)

Points 0°, 40°, 10°; \(t_{d12}=t_{d23}=2\) s; every blend acceleration magnitude 50 °/s². Blend 1: \(t_1=2-\sqrt{4-2(40)/50}=0.4508\) s; \(v_{12}=40/(2-0.2254)=22.54\) °/s. Last blend: \(\ddot\theta_3=+50\), \(t_3=2-\sqrt{4+2(-30)/50}=0.3267\) s; \(v_{23}=-30/(2-0.1633)=-16.33\) °/s. Via blend: \(\ddot\theta_2=-50\), \(t_2=(-16.33-22.54)/(-50)=0.7775\) s. Linear durations 1.160 s and 1.285 s. The joint misses \(\theta_2=40^\circ\) by \(50(0.7775)^2/8=3.78^\circ\) (it reaches 36.22° at the via time). Checked by integrating the whole profile: it ends at 10° with zero velocity. checked

This is an explain-level topic in the slides (symbols and set-up only). Be ready to say: what is given and what is found; why via points are only approached; that each blend’s acceleration limit sets its duration. Do not expect the full Craig derivation unless the paper supplies it.

7 · Task-space straight lines and their three problems pp. 44–47

Picture

Frames (p.44): base {B}, wrist {W}, tool {T}, station {S}, goal {G}, camera {C}. The trajectory is {T} relative to {S}. Linear interpolation in joint space does not give a straight tool path; a straight tool path needs IK at every sample (p.46).

Numbers for that arc: the start joint angles are \((51.07^\circ,\,95.83^\circ)\), the end \((-38.93^\circ,\,95.83^\circ)\). Halfway in joint space the tool is at \((3.359,\,3.359)\) m, not at the line’s midpoint \((2.375,\,2.375)\) m: 1.39 m off the line. checked

Three problems with Cartesian straight lines (p.47)
  1. Intermediate points may lie outside the workspace. Both ends can be reachable while the line crosses the hole near the base. Example: \(L_1=1\), \(L_2=0.7\) m (inner radius \(|L_1-L_2|=0.3\) m). The line \(y=0.2\) from \((-1,0.2)\) to \((1,0.2)\) has reachable ends (distance 1.02 m) but its middle \((0,0.2)\) is only 0.2 m from the base: unreachable. checked
  2. The path may pass through a singularity. The Jacobian determinant of a planar 2R is \(L_1L_2\sin q_2\), zero when the arm is fully stretched or folded. To keep a given tool speed the joint rates grow like \(1/\sin q_2\). Example with \(L_1=L_2=1\) m and the tool moving along x at 1 m/s through \((x,0)\): at \(x=1.0\) the largest joint rate is 1.16 rad/s, at 1.9 it is 3.20, at 1.99 it is 10.0 and at 1.999 it is 31.6 rad/s. A real joint cannot do that. checked
  3. Start and goal are reachable only in different configurations. If A needs the elbow on one side and B on the other, a straight line between them would need the arm to switch branch part-way (a joint jump, or a pass through a singularity). See Q4 of the notebook (section 8).
A scenario question: “a robot must weld a straight seam from A to B, list what can go wrong”. Answer all three with one sentence of cause each: hole or limit, singularity (joint rates blow up), different IK branch. Add the fix: replan in joint space around the problem, or change the base position or the path.

8 · The Cartesian recipe and the planar RR example pp. 48–65, p.68

Recipe (p.48)
  1. Given a tool trajectory in Cartesian coordinates, sample it at a few points.
  2. Use IK at each sample to get joint positions.
  3. Fit a curve to each joint’s samples (a cubic in the example; quintic if needed, p.60).
  4. Resample the fitted curves at the controller rate; optionally use FK to draw the resulting tool path (pp.62–64).

Why not run IK at every fine sample? Numerical IK output is not smooth (notebook cells 67–69, Puma 560 with ikine_GN), so fit first, then resample.

Worked example (pp. 49–64, notebook cells 51–59)

Planar RR, \(L_1=4\) m, \(L_2=3\) m. Start \((0,\ L_1+0.25L_2)=(0,4.75)\), end \((4.75,0)\), constant 3 m/s along the straight line.

  1. Path. \(y=-x+4.75\). Length \(\sqrt{4.75^2+4.75^2}=6.7175\) m, time \(6.7175/3=2.2392\) s (the slide rounds to 2.24 s).
  2. Sample 11 points (10 sections), \(t_i=i\,t_F/10\) (the slide writes \(0.224\,i\)): \(x(t)=3t/\sqrt2\), \(y(t)=4.75-3t/\sqrt2\) (p.53).
  3. IK (p.56): \(\cos q_2=\dfrac{x^2+y^2-L_1^2-L_2^2}{2L_1L_2}\), \(q_2=\operatorname{atan2}(+\sqrt{1-\cos^2q_2},\cos q_2)\), \(q_1=\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)-\operatorname{atan2}(L_2\sin q_2,\ L_1+L_2\cos q_2)\). At the start: \(q_1=0.8914\) rad (51.07°), \(q_2=1.6725\) rad (95.83°); at the end \(q_1=-0.6794\) rad (−38.93°), same \(q_2\). The line stays between radius 3.36 m and 4.75 m, inside the annulus \(1\le r\le7\) m, so there is no workspace problem. checked
  4. Cubic fit (p.59): \(q_1(t)\approx0.1346t^3-0.3375t^2-0.6182t+0.8858\), \(q_2(t)\approx0.0000t^3-0.4032t^2+0.9029t+1.6674\) rad. The fit misses the samples by up to 0.008 rad (0.46°). checked
  5. Resample to 50 points and apply FK: the fitted-curve tool path wanders up to 37 mm from the true line (6.7 m long). A quintic fit is more than 5 times closer; the slide’s remark (p.60) that one cubic may not suffice is right. checked

Four observations (cell 60): Cartesian generation costs more but is more intuitive; motors always get joint commands; accuracy depends on the fit and the number of samples; any shape (circle, square, 3D) works the same way.

Slides vs recomputation (p.59)

The slide gives \(q_1=0.1347t^3-0.3376t^2-0.6181t+0.8858\) and \(q_2=0.0004t^3-0.4043t^2+0.9036t+1.6674\). Recomputing with the notebook’s own code (11 equal samples over 2.2392 s) gives the \(q_1\) above (agrees to 0.0001) but \(q_2\) with a cubic term of 0.0000, \(-0.4032\), \(0.9029\). That is expected: \(q_2\) is symmetric (equal at both ends, 1.6725 rad), so a cubic fit must have a zero cubic term. The slide’s \(q_2\) is reproduced only if the samples span about 2.247 s, so it was probably made with a slightly different sampling. Treat the slide’s \(q_2\) digits beyond 0.01 as not exact; the shape and the method are what matter. checked

Two more points from the slides

Poses cannot be interpolated like numbers (p.65): positions and angles can be, but not translation matrices or rotation matrices directly. The toolbox’s ctraj interpolates a pose properly (notebook cells 63–66, from \(\mathrm{Trans}(0.4,-0.2,0)R_x(3)\) to \(\mathrm{Trans}(0.4,0.2,0)R_x(1)\), 2 s, step 0.02 s).

Summary (p.68): start and goal are usually given in Cartesian space as the pose of {T} with respect to {S}; the path between can be made in joint or task space; either way, the motors receive joint positions, velocities and accelerations.

Typical questions: write the line equation, its length and the travel time; give \(x(t_i),y(t_i)\) for one sample; do the IK for one sample (both branches); explain why we fit and resample; say what “higher-order fit” buys.

Guided problems: solve on paper first

P5.1 · Rest-to-rest cubiccalculatederive

A revolute joint starts at rest at 20° and must stop at 80° after exactly 3 s. Find \(a_2\) and \(a_3\) of the cubic (take \(t_0=0\)) and the peak speed.

Hint 1: conditions

Four: \(q(0)=20\), \(q(3)=80\), \(\dot q(0)=0\), \(\dot q(3)=0\). So \(a_0=20\) and \(a_1=0\).

Hint 2: the two unknowns

Rest to rest: \(a_2=3\Delta q/T^2\) and \(a_3=-2\Delta q/T^3\) with \(\Delta q=60^\circ\), \(T=3\) s.

Hint 3: peak speed

The velocity \(2a_2t+3a_3t^2\) peaks where \(\ddot q=0\), at \(t=T/2\).

Full solution

\(a_2=3(60)/9=20\) °/s². \(a_3=-2(60)/27=-4.4444\) °/s³. So \(q(t)=20+20t^2-4.4444t^3\).

Peak speed at \(t=1.5\) s: \(\dot q=2(20)(1.5)+3(-4.4444)(2.25)=60-30=30\) °/s, which equals \(1.5\Delta q/T=1.5(60)/3\). End accelerations \(\pm6\Delta q/T^2=\pm40\) °/s². Check \(q(3)=20+180-120=80\) ✓. checked

Common wrong answer: \(a_3=-13.33\) from dividing by \(T^2\).

Close everything and derive \(a_2,a_3\) for rest to rest from the four conditions, in 4 minutes.

P5.2 · More than one joint (notebook Question 1)explaincalculate

“What if the robot has more than one joint?” A three-joint arm must move from rest to rest in 2 s, with joint changes of +40°, +90° and −20°. How do you generate the trajectory, and what are \(a_2\), \(a_3\) and the peak speed of joint 2?

Hint 1

One cubic per joint (p.20), solved independently, all with the same \(T=2\) s.

Full solution

Each joint \(i\) has \(q_i(t)=q_{i0}+a_{2,i}t^2+a_{3,i}t^3\) with \(a_{2,i}=3\Delta q_i/T^2\), \(a_{3,i}=-2\Delta q_i/T^3\). With \(T=2\): joint 1 \((30,-10)\), joint 2 \((67.5,-22.5)\), joint 3 \((-15,5)\). Peak speeds \(1.5\Delta q_i/T=30,\ 67.5,\ -15\) °/s (joint 3 moves backwards). checked

Why the same \(T\): all joints start and stop together, so the arm moves as one. A controller evaluates every cubic at its path-update rate and sends the joint set to the servos. The joints do not coordinate their geometry: the tool path between the two poses is whatever the joint curves produce, not a straight line.

P5.3 · Via-point rule on real numbers (notebook Question 2)calculatespot the error

Points on the trajectory are 10, 50, 20, 40, 45° at times 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 s. Use the “change of sign gives zero, otherwise the average” rule, with zero velocity at both ends. Find the velocity at qC (t = 15 s) and the cubic for the last segment in its own clock \(\tau=t-15\). Then say whether the acceleration is continuous at qB.

Hint 1: slopes

Slopes of the four chords: \(+8,\ -6,\ +4,\ +1\) °/s.

Hint 2: last segment

From 40° at 2.5 °/s to 45° at 0 °/s in \(T=5\) s: use the general cubic with \(\Delta q=5\).

Full solution (with a script)

Velocities: q0 0; qA: +8, −6 change sign → 0; qB: −6, +4 change sign → 0; qC: +4, +1 → 2.5; qF 0. Last segment: \(a_0=40\), \(a_1=2.5\), \(a_2=[3(5)-(2\cdot2.5+0)5]/25=-0.4\), \(a_3=[-2(5)+(2.5+0)5]/125=0.02\). Check \(q(5)=40+12.5-10+2.5=45\) ✓, \(\dot q(5)=2.5-4+1.5=0\) ✓. checked

Other segments (local clock): \((10,0,4.8,-0.64)\), \((50,0,-3.6,0.48)\), \((20,0,1.9,-0.22)\).

import numpy as np
t = np.array([0, 5, 10, 15, 20.]); q = np.array([10, 50, 20, 40, 45.])
s = np.diff(q) / np.diff(t)                       # chord slopes
v = np.zeros(len(q))
for i in range(1, len(q) - 1):                    # interior via points only
    v[i] = 0 if s[i-1] * s[i] < 0 else (s[i-1] + s[i]) / 2
for k in range(len(q) - 1):                       # one cubic per segment, own clock tau
    T, d = t[k+1] - t[k], q[k+1] - q[k]
    a = [q[k], v[k], (3*d - (2*v[k] + v[k+1])*T) / T**2, (-2*d + (v[k] + v[k+1])*T) / T**3]
    tau = np.linspace(0, T, 50)
    pos = a[0] + a[1]*tau + a[2]*tau**2 + a[3]*tau**3
    vel = a[1] + 2*a[2]*tau + 3*a[3]*tau**2
    acc = 2*a[2] + 6*a[3]*tau                     # plot (t[k] + tau, pos / vel / acc)

Acceleration at qB: end of segment 2 is \(2(-3.6)+6(0.48)(5)=7.2\) °/s²; start of segment 3 is \(2(1.9)=3.8\). Not equal: the acceleration jumps by 3.4 °/s². The simple rule gives continuous position and velocity only. checked

Common wrong answer: velocity at qC taken as zero “because the path flattens at the end”. Zero is only for a sign change.

P5.4 · Continuous acceleration at the via point (notebook Question 3, slide p.28)derivecalculate

Two cubics join \(q_0\), \(q_{via}\), \(q_F\) with zero end velocities and the same acceleration on both sides of the via point. (a) Count unknowns and conditions. (b) Find the via velocity for \(q_0=10^\circ\), \(q_{via}=40^\circ\), \(q_F=20^\circ\) with \(T_1=T_2=1\) s. (c) Repeat with \(T_1=1\) s, \(T_2=2\) s.

Hint 1

Unknowns 8; conditions: 4 positions, 2 end velocities, 1 velocity continuity, 1 acceleration continuity.

Hint 2: the shortcut

Use the closed-form cubic with end velocities \((0,w)\) and \((w,0)\). Then \(\ddot q_1(T_1)=(-6d_1+4wT_1)/T_1^2\) and \(\ddot q_2(0)=(6d_2-4wT_2)/T_2^2\).

Hint 3

Equal times: \(w=3(q_F-q_0)/(4T)\).

Full solution

(a) 8 unknowns (\(a_{10}\dots a_{13}\), \(a_{20}\dots a_{23}\)); 8 conditions as in hint 1.

Derivation: with \(d_1=q_{via}-q_0\), \(d_2=q_F-q_{via}\), equate \((-6d_1+4wT_1)/T_1^2=(6d_2-4wT_2)/T_2^2\). Then \(4w(1/T_1+1/T_2)=6(d_1/T_1^2+d_2/T_2^2)\), so \(w=\dfrac{3(T_1^2d_2+T_2^2d_1)}{2T_1T_2(T_1+T_2)}\).

(b) \(w=3(10)/4=7.5\) °/s; segments \(10+82.5t^2-52.5t^3\) and \(40+7.5t-75t^2+47.5t^3\) (the lecturer’s sample Q8 answer with these numbers, Q8).

(c) \(d_1=30\), \(d_2=-20\): \(w=3[1(-20)+4(30)]/[2(1)(2)(3)]=300/12=25\) °/s. Segments \(10+65t^2-35t^3\) and \(40+25t-40t^2+11.25t^3\). The acceleration on both sides is −80 °/s² (check: \(2(65)+6(-35)(1)=-80\) and \(2(-40)=-80\)). checked

Reading of “constant acceleration”: I take it as continuous. If \(a_{via}\) were prescribed as an extra given, the system would be over-determined; I flagged this in the derivation above.

Write the eight conditions for two cubics from memory, then solve for \(w\) with equal times.

P5.5 · Blend example (slide p.37)calculate

A joint moves a total of 120° in 2 s. Acceleration and deceleration are 300 °/s². Find the blend time and the constant (coast) velocity.

Hint 1: existence

Is \(300\ge4(120)/2^2\)?

Hint 2: root

\(t_B=1-\sqrt{300^2(4)-4(300)(120)}/600\). Which root is smaller than \(t_F/2\)?

Full solution

Step 1: \(4(120)/4=120\); \(300\ge120\) ✓. Step 2: \(\sqrt{360000-144000}=\sqrt{216000}=464.76\); \(t_B=1-464.76/600=0.2254\) s. Step 3: \(v=300(0.2254)=67.62\) °/s. Check: \(2\cdot\tfrac12(300)(0.2254)^2+67.62(2-0.4508)=15.24+104.76=120\) ✓. The slide gives no final number, so this is my computation. checked

Common wrong answer: \(t_B=1.7746\) s (+ root), which also makes \(v=532\) °/s, far above the average of 60 °/s.

P5.6 · Is that blend possible?spot the errorexplain

Three student claims about a 120° move in 2 s. Which are wrong, and why? (a) “With \(a=120\) °/s² the profile has a coast phase.” (b) “With \(a=100\) °/s², \(t_B=1-\sqrt{-8000}/200\), so take the real part, \(t_B=1\) s.” (c) “A larger \(a\) makes the coast velocity larger.”

Hint

Minimum \(a=4\Delta q/t_F^2=120\). What is \(t_B\) at equality?

Model answer

(a) Wrong. At \(a=120\) the discriminant is 0, \(t_B=t_F/2=1\) s, the coast lasts \(t_F-2t_B=0\); the profile is a triangle with peak \(2\Delta q/t_F=120\) °/s. (b) Wrong. \(a=100\lt 120\) has a negative discriminant (\(-8000\)): no real \(t_B\), so no such motion exists; you cannot take the real part. Fix: raise \(a\) to at least 120 or lengthen \(t_F\). (c) Wrong. \(v=\tfrac12[at_F-\sqrt{a^2t_F^2-4a\Delta q}]\) falls from 120 toward the mean speed 60 °/s as \(a\) grows: 120 at \(a=120\), then 82.9 at 150 and 67.6 at 300. Both a strict “>” in the existence test and “larger \(a\) gives faster” are classic traps. checked

P5.7 · The t₀ caveatspot the errorcalculate

The p.37 motion (120°, \(a=300\) °/s²) now starts at \(t_0=1\) s and ends at \(t_F=3\) s. A student plugs \(t_0=1\), \(t_F=3\) into the slide’s general quadratic \(at_B^2-a(t_F-t_0)t_B+(q_F-q_0-at_0^2/2)=0\). What do they get, and what is the correct \(t_B\)?

Hint

It is the same motion, only shifted in time. Should \(t_B\) change?

Full solution

Slide quadratic: \(300t_B^2-600t_B+(120-150)=0\), i.e. \(300t_B^2-600t_B-30=0\), roots 2.049 and −0.049. Neither is 0.2254 s, and 2.049 s is not even smaller than \(t_F-t_0=2\) s. Correct: use the duration \(T=t_F-t_0=2\) s: \(300t_B^2-600t_B+120=0\), \(t_B=0.2254\) s, \(v=67.62\) °/s, unchanged by a time shift. checked

P5.8 · Sketch the three profilessketch

For a 10° to 50° move in 2 s, sketch \(q,\dot q,\ddot q\) against time for (i) the cubic, (ii) the quintic, (iii) an LSPB for the same move with \(a=100\) °/s². Mark the key values.

Hint

Draw the three rows on a shared time axis. Mark values at \(t=0\), \(1\) and \(2\) s.

What the sketches show

(i) Cubic: \(q\) an S-curve from 10 to 50; \(\dot q\) a parabola, 0 → 30 °/s at 1 s → 0; \(\ddot q\) a straight line from +60 to −60 °/s², zero at 1 s. (ii) Quintic: same S-curve but steeper in the middle; \(\dot q\) a narrower, taller bell peaking at \(1.875(40)/2=37.5\) °/s; \(\ddot q\) starts and ends at 0, with extremes \(\pm57.7\) °/s². checked (iii) LSPB with \(a=100\) (minimum \(4(40)/4=40\) ✓): \(t_B=1-\sqrt{10^4(4)-4(100)(40)}/200=1-\sqrt{24000}/200=0.2254\) s, \(v=22.54\) °/s; \(q\) parabola–line–parabola; \(\dot q\) a trapezoid; \(\ddot q\) three flat levels \(+100,0,-100\) with jumps at \(t_B\) and \(t_F-t_B\).

Key distinctions the sketch must show: acceleration zero at the ends only for the quintic; the trapezoid has a flat top; the cubic acceleration is linear.

Draw all nine small plots in 4 minutes with values on the axes.

P5.9 · The other IK solution (notebook Question 4)explaincalculate

In the RR example the notebook uses the \(+\sqrt{\cdot}\) IK solution (\(q_2\gt 0\)). What happens if we use the other one? Give the start joint angles for the other solution (\(L_1=4\), \(L_2=3\), start tool point (0, 4.75)).

Hint 1

The other branch has \(\sin q_2\to-\sin q_2\), so \(q_2\to-q_2\).

Hint 2

\(q_1=\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)-\operatorname{atan2}(L_2\sin q_2,L_1+L_2\cos q_2)\). The second term changes sign with \(q_2\).

Full solution

At (0, 4.75): \(\cos q_2=(22.5625-25)/24=-0.1016\), so \(q_2=\pm95.83^\circ\). For \(q_2=-95.83^\circ\): \(\mu=\operatorname{atan2}(3\sin q_2,4+3\cos q_2)=\operatorname{atan2}(-2.984,3.695)=-38.93^\circ\), so \(q_1=90^\circ-(-38.93^\circ)=128.93^\circ\). (The + branch has \(q_1=90-38.93=51.07^\circ\).) At the end point (4.75, 0): \(q_1=38.93^\circ\), \(q_2=-95.83^\circ\). checked

What happens. The tool path is identical (both branches reproduce every sampled point, checked by FK) but the arm is mirrored about the line from the base to the tool: the elbow is on the other side. Joint curves differ: \(q_2\to-q_2\) at every sample and \(q_1=2\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)-q_1^{+}\). The fit, resample and FK steps work the same way, with different coefficients. What you must not do is switch branches part-way: in the example, jumping at sample 5 would change \(q_1\) from 0.165 rad to 1.608 rad and \(q_2\) from 2.157 to −2.179 in one step, which no joint can do. Choose the branch from the start configuration, joint limits, or obstacles, and keep it for the whole path. If start and goal can only be reached in different branches, the straight Cartesian line is impossible (problem 3 of p.47).

P5.10 · Joint-linear is not Cartesian-linear (slide p.46)calculatesketch

The RR arm (\(L_1=4\), \(L_2=3\)) moves from joint angles \((51.07^\circ,95.83^\circ)\) to \((-38.93^\circ,95.83^\circ)\) with each joint changing linearly in time. Where is the tool at the halfway time? How far is that from the straight-line midpoint (2.375, 2.375)?

Hint 1

Halfway joint angles are the averages: \(q_1=6.07^\circ\), \(q_2=95.83^\circ\).

Hint 2

FK: \(x=L_1\cos q_1+L_2\cos(q_1+q_2)\), \(y=L_1\sin q_1+L_2\sin(q_1+q_2)\).

Full solution

\(x=4\cos6.07^\circ+3\cos101.9^\circ=3.9775-0.6188=3.3588\); \(y=4\sin6.07^\circ+3\sin101.9^\circ=0.4233+2.9355=3.3588\). Distance from the line \(x+y=4.75\): \((3.3588+3.3588-4.75)/\sqrt2=1.391\) m. Because \(q_2\) is the same at both ends it never changes, so the tool stays at distance \(\sqrt{L_1^2+L_2^2+2L_1L_2\cos q_2}=4.75\) m from the base: it moves on an arc, not a chord. checked

Sketch: arc from (0, 4.75) to (4.75, 0) bulging away from the origin, the straight line inside it (figure in section 7).

P5.11 · Quintic by hand (slide p.29)derivecalculate

Move 0° to 15° in 1 s, rest to rest, zero end accelerations, with a quintic. Find \(a_3,a_4,a_5\) and the peak speed, and compare with the cubic for the same move.

Hint 1

Zero start conditions give \(a_0=a_1=a_2=0\). The three end conditions give a 3×3 system for \(a_3,a_4,a_5\).

Hint 2

At \(T=1\): \(a_3+a_4+a_5=15\); \(3a_3+4a_4+5a_5=0\); \(6a_3+12a_4+20a_5=0\).

Full solution

Eliminate: from the third equation \(a_5=-(6a_3+12a_4)/20\); substituting gives \(a_4=-1.5a_3\) and \(a_5=0.6a_3\); the first equation gives \(a_3(1-1.5+0.6)=15\), \(a_3=150\), \(a_4=-225\), \(a_5=90\). Velocity \(450t^2-900t^3+450t^4\) peaks at \(t=0.5\): \(450(0.25)-900(0.125)+450(0.0625)=28.125\) °/s. Cubic: peak \(22.5\) °/s and end accelerations \(\pm90\) °/s²; quintic ends at 0 but has the higher peak speed (and peak acceleration 86.6 °/s²). checked

P5.12 · Choosing the coast velocity (toolbox trapezoidal, notebook cells 37–40)calculate

The toolbox lets you set the coast velocity \(V\) instead of \(a\). For 0° to 120° in 2 s with \(V=70\) °/s, find \(t_B\) and the blend acceleration.

Hint

The coast covers \(v(t_F-2t_B)\) and each blend \(\tfrac12vt_B\), so \(\Delta q=v(t_F-t_B)\).

Full solution

\(t_B=t_F-\Delta q/V=2-120/70=0.2857\) s; \(a=V/t_B=245\) °/s². Valid because \(60\lt 70\le120\). Check: \(70(2-0.2857)=120\) ✓. The notebook saved no output for this cell, so this is my calculation. checked

P5.13 · Six-DoF trajectory: jtraj versus ctraj (notebook Question 5)explain

A Puma 560 moves from \(\mathrm{Trans}(0.4,-0.2,0)\,R_x(3)\) to \(\mathrm{Trans}(0.4,0.2,0)\,R_x(1)\) in 2 s at 0.5 s steps. Generate a trajectory in joint space with jtraj, plot joint positions, velocities and accelerations, and compare with the ctraj solution. What do you observe?

Model answer (not run; expected behaviour)

Method. Convert both poses to joint vectors with IK, then jtraj(q0, qF, t) interpolates each joint with a smooth polynomial that starts and ends at rest (Corke §7.3: a quintic). Plot \(q,\dot q,\ddot q\) for the six joints. With 0.5 s steps over 2 s there are only 5 samples (4 if the end is excluded), so smoothness is hard to see; use a finer step for the plots.

Comparison. jtraj: smooth bell-shaped joint velocities, zero speed at both ends; the tool path between the poses is curved. ctraj: the tool path is a straight line in x, y, z with orientation interpolated; after IK the joint curves are not simple and may be less smooth (notebook cells 67–69: the numerical IK output was not very smooth, so fit and resample). Rule: joint space is cheap and smooth; task space gives the tool path you asked for at higher cost. I did not run the notebook; no outputs are saved.

P5.14 · Write the letter R, and a legged robot (notebook Questions 6 and 7)explainderive

(a) Generate a trajectory for the letter “R” from the toolbox font and compute the joint angles for a six-DoF arm. (b) A legged robot (ANYmal) leg is a 3-DoF manipulator. Generate a circular foot trajectory in Cartesian space and find the joint angles. Give the procedure and the pitfalls.

Model answer (procedure, not run)

Procedure (the p.48 recipe). (1) Get or write the Cartesian points: for the letter, the font gives 2D stroke coordinates; scale and place them on a plane in front of the arm, with the pen orientation fixed. For the leg, sample the circle \(x=x_c+r\cos\phi\), \(y=y_c+r\sin\phi\) in the plane of motion with \(\phi=2\pi t/T\) (constant speed, or a speed profile). (2) Do IK at each sample: a 6-DoF arm with spherical wrist has the closed-form split into position (3 joints) and orientation (3 joints); a 3-DoF leg is an RRR chain (hip, thigh, shank). (3) Fit a curve to each joint, or just use the dense samples. (4) Resample at the controller rate; FK to check the drawn shape.

Pitfalls. Keep the same IK branch (e.g. knee bent forwards or backwards) all the way. Keep every sample inside the workspace (circle radius small enough for the leg’s reach). A pen lift between strokes of the letter is a separate, via-point move. Avoid singular poses (a fully stretched leg or folded wrist). Corners of the letter (R has sharp turns) need blends or via-point velocities, or the arm will overshoot or stop at each one.

P5.15 · Scenario: a welding seamexplaincalculate

A robot with \(L_1=1\) m and \(L_2=0.7\) m must move its tool in a straight line along \(y=0.2\) m from \((-1,\,0.2)\) to \((1,\,0.2)\). Is the task feasible as stated? Which of the three problems on slide 47 does it hit? Give two fixes. Then, for a 2R at the stretched pose, what happens to the joint rates?

Hint

Reach is the annulus \(|L_1-L_2|\le r\le L_1+L_2\), i.e. 0.3 m to 1.7 m from the base.

Model answer

Ends: \(r=\sqrt{1+0.04}=1.02\) m, inside the annulus, so each is reachable. Middle \((0,0.2)\): \(r=0.2\lt 0.3\), inside the hole. So the line leaves the workspace in the middle: problem 1 (intermediate points outside the workspace). Fixes: move the seam or the base so the nearest distance is at least 0.3 m (for example shift to \(y=0.4\)); or split the motion into two via points and go round the hole in joint space; or use a robot with a smaller inner radius. checked

Stretched or folded arm: \(\det J=L_1L_2\sin q_2\to0\), so for a given tool speed the joint rates grow like \(1/\sin q_2\) (problem 2): with \(L_1=L_2=1\) m and 1 m/s along x, the largest rate is 1.16 rad/s at \(x=1\) and 31.6 rad/s at \(x=1.999\). The Cartesian speed must be reduced near the boundary. checked

P5.16 · Slide questionsexplain

Answer the lecturer’s own questions: (a) p.15: “How many conditions on motion does a start-at-rest, stop-at-rest statement specify, and what is the simplest function?” (b) p.25: “If every cubic stops at each via point, is this desirable?” (c) p.45: “What are the benefits of describing the trajectory as {T} relative to {S}?” (d) p.50: “What is the equation of the path?”

Model answers

(a) Four (start and end position, start and end velocity); a cubic. (b) Usually not: the robot slows to zero at every via point, which wastes time and energy; use via velocities (the simple rule or continuous acceleration). (c) The description is decoupled from the manipulator (the same one works for different robots) and follows a moving {S} such as a conveyor. (d) \(y=-x+4.75\) (slope \(-1\), through (0, 4.75) and (4.75, 0)). checked

Mini-quiz

Q1concept

How many boundary conditions does a quintic need, and which ones? How many does a cubic need?

Answer

Quintic: six, position, velocity and acceleration at both ends. Cubic: four, position and velocity at both ends.

Q2calculate

A joint must move 90° in 1.5 s with a trapezoidal velocity profile. What is the smallest blend acceleration that works, and what is the coast phase then?

Answer

\(a_{min}=4(90)/1.5^2=160\) °/s². At that value \(t_B=0.75\) s, so there is no coast phase (a triangle with peak \(2\Delta q/t_F=120\) °/s).

Q3spot the error

“If each joint changes linearly with time, the tool moves in a straight line.” True?

Answer

False. Joint-linear motion gives a curved tool path in general (p.46). In the RR example the tool moves on an arc of radius 4.75 m, 1.39 m off the straight line at its midpoint.

Week 6 · Velocity kinematics and statics

How fast does the tool move when the joints move?

Forward kinematics gives where the tool is. Velocity kinematics gives how fast it moves for given joint rates, through one matrix, the Jacobian \(\mathbf J(\mathbf q)\). The same matrix explains where the arm gets stuck (singularities), how well it can move in each direction (manipulability), and how joint torques turn into tool forces (statics, \(\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf J^\top\mathbf F\)).

Lecture: Velocity Kinematics62 slides · Dr KM Digumarti · notebook “6 velocity kinematics” · plus the 1-page “Cross Product Clarification”
Open in new tab ↗
How this is examined

None of the ten W13 sample questions is on velocity kinematics (the only “velocity” items there are wheeled-robot kinematics, W13 pp.20–21). So expect a new short question of the derive, calculate, sketch or explain type. The most likely forms: the Jacobian of a planar RR arm at a given \(\mathbf q\) (in frame {0} or in the tool frame); the determinant and the poses where it vanishes; joint rates for a wanted tool velocity; joint torques for a tool force; a sketch of the velocity ellipse near and far from a singularity.

Where the marks are (indicative; marks not published): the FK written first; the derivative taken correctly (each column is one joint’s effect); the Jacobian assembled with the linear rows above the angular rows; the frame of expression stated; the determinant factorised; the singular poses named with a sentence on what is lost; units on every answer (m/s, rad/s, N·m).

Where marks are lost: using joint angles instead of running sums (\(q_1+q_2\), not \(q_2\)); mixing frame {0} and frame {E} (the Jacobian rotates, \(\det\) does not); using \(\mathbf J\mathbf F\) instead of \(\mathbf J^\top\mathbf F\); putting the inverse in the force ellipsoid; forgetting that a tall Jacobian needs a pseudo-inverse; writing degrees where a calculator expects radians.

Practical (optional, no coding in the exam)

The lecture notebook builds everything from scratch: skew, vex, skewa, vexa; the helpers ρ (rotation block) and τ (translation column); one derivative function per elementary transform (dTRx, dTRy, dTRz, dTtx, dTty, dTtz with an isflip flag); dT_dqj, Jv_j, Jω_j and jacob0. It then compares with the toolbox’s jacob0 and jacobe. Questions 1 and 4 are given for the planar RR arm; questions 2 and 3 (PUMA 560) have no code. All four are solved below. The notebook has no saved outputs.

Intuition first

The Jacobian is an exchange-rate table

It converts joint speeds into hand speeds, like a currency table. The rates change with the pose: the same turn of the shoulder moves a stretched hand a long way and a tucked hand a short way.

One column = one dial

On a mixing desk, turning one dial alone changes the sound in one particular way. Column \(j\) of \(\mathbf J\) is exactly what the tool does when only joint \(j\) moves at unit speed. Move several dials: add the effects.In the practical: Jv_j and Jω_j build one column at a time.

A singularity is a locked door hinge line

Push a door along the line of its hinges and nothing turns. A fully stretched arm is the same: no joint can move the hand along the arm. Near that pose, a tiny hand motion demands a huge joint speed.

The ellipsoid is a squashed ball

Put every unit-size joint-speed combination into the Jacobian and the ball of choices comes out as an egg. The hand is fast along the long axis and slow along the short one. A collapsed egg is a singularity.

Speed and force trade off

A long lever moves far but pushes weakly. Where the hand can move fast, it can push only weakly, and the reverse. The force egg has the same axes as the velocity egg, but with reciprocal lengths.
