Set the friction factor to 0 and (c) gets worse (22.6 mrad) than a 7% mass error: friction matters. Finally set the controller period to 50 ms with the exact model: (c) RMS 3.29 mrad.

1 · Partitioned control of a non-linear single-input system pp. 5–11

Picture

The controller is cut into two parts (p.10). The model-based part (\(\alpha\), \(\beta\)) knows the physics and cancels it. The servo part (\(f'\)) sees only a perfect unit mass and steers it with the usual PD law. The slide’s summary (p.49): the model-based part cancels the non-linearity, the servo part ensures stability.

Derivation: cubic spring

Slide 8: a mass-spring-damper is linear, \(m\ddot x + b\dot x + kx = f\) (m kg, b N·s/m, k N/m, f N, x m). Slide 9 makes the spring cubic, so the plant is non-linear:

\[ m\ddot x + b\dot x + kx^{3} = f \qquad (k\ \text{in N/m}^3) \]

Step 1: isolate the acceleration term, \(m\,\ddot x + (b\dot x + kx^3) = f\). Step 2: partition \(f = \alpha f' + \beta\) with \(\alpha = m\) and \(\beta = b\dot x + kx^3\) (p.10). Step 3: substitute,

\[ m\ddot x + \beta = m f' + \beta \;\Rightarrow\; \ddot x = f'. \]

The plant now looks like a pure double integrator, whatever the spring does. \(f'\) (“f-prime”) is a commanded acceleration in m/s². Step 4: the servo law is the Week 8 law,

\[ f' = \ddot x_d + k_v\dot e + k_p e,\qquad e = x_d - x \;\Rightarrow\; \ddot e + k_v\dot e + k_p e = 0 . \]

Critical damping needs \(k_v = 2\sqrt{k_p}\) (Week 8; slide 8 only says “like being critically damped”). Units: \(k_p\) in s⁻², \(k_v\) in s⁻¹. Check: \(\alpha f'\) is kg·m/s² = N. ✓

Limitation (p.15): you must know the structure (cubic spring, Coulomb friction) and the parameters (\(k\), \(b_c\), …). In practice they are not always known. Section 4 shows what that costs.

Exam recipe
  1. Write the plant with the acceleration term isolated: (coefficient)·\(\ddot x\) + (everything else) = input.
  2. \(\alpha\) = the coefficient of \(\ddot x\). \(\beta\) = everything else, including every non-linear term and every sign.
  3. Servo: \(f' = \ddot x_d + k_v\dot e + k_p e\) with \(e = x_d - x\) (desired minus actual).
  4. Law: \(f = \alpha f' + \beta\). Write \(\beta\) in terms of the measured \(x,\dot x\), not the desired ones.
  5. Show the closed loop: \(\ddot x = f'\), hence \(\ddot e + k_v\dot e + k_p e = 0\).
  6. Sanity check units: \(\alpha f'\) must have the units of \(f\).
Worked example (numbers are mine; the slides are symbolic)

m = 2 kg, b = 4 N·s/m, k = 50 N/m³, \(k_p = 100\) s⁻², \(k_v = 20\) s⁻¹. Now: x = 0.10 m, ẋ = 0.30 m/s; desired \(x_d = 0.12\) m, \(\dot x_d = 0.40\) m/s, \(\ddot x_d = 0.50\) m/s².

\(e = 0.02\) m, \(\dot e = 0.10\) m/s. \(f' = 0.50 + 20(0.10) + 100(0.02) = 4.5\) m/s². \(\beta = 4(0.30) + 50(0.10)^3 = 1.25\) N. \(f = 2(4.5) + 1.25 = 10.25\) N.

Plant: \(\ddot x = (f - b\dot x - kx^3)/m = (10.25 - 1.2 - 0.05)/2 = 4.5\) m/s² \(= f'\). ✓ Then \(\ddot e = 0.5 - 4.5 = -4.0\), and \(\ddot e + 20(0.10) + 100(0.02) = -4 + 2 + 2 = 0\). ✓ checked

Typical question: “Given \(m\ddot x + b\dot x + kx^3 = f\) (or another EoM), write the partitioned law.” Marks are for \(\alpha = m\), \(\beta\) = the rest, and the servo with \(\ddot x_d\). Trap: the law uses \(f'\), an acceleration, inside \(\alpha f'\). Do not add \(k_p e\) to \(f\) directly without multiplying by \(\alpha\).

2 · A single link with gravity and friction pp. 12–15

Picture

One rigid link of length L, pivoted at the origin, with a point mass m at its tip. The angle q is measured counter-clockwise from the horizontal (p.12). Gravity pulls the mass down with force mg. Its lever arm about the pivot is the horizontal distance \(L\cos q\), so the gravity torque is \(mgL\cos q\): largest when the link is horizontal (q = 0), zero when vertical (q = 90°).

Derivation: equation of motion (Lagrangian, as on the handwritten slide 13)

Tip position \(x = L\cos q,\ y = L\sin q\), so \(\dot x = -L\sin q\,\dot q\) and \(\dot y = L\cos q\,\dot q\) (m, m/s). Kinetic and potential energy:

\[ K = \tfrac12 m(\dot x^2+\dot y^2) = \tfrac12 mL^2\dot q^2,\qquad P = mgy = mgL\sin q,\qquad \mathcal L = K - P . \]

The generalised torque is \(Q = \dfrac{d}{dt}\dfrac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\dot q} - \dfrac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial q}\). Here \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\dot q = mL^2\dot q\), so its derivative is \(mL^2\ddot q\), and \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial q = -mgL\cos q\). Hence \(Q = mL^2\ddot q + mgL\cos q\). Friction opposes motion, so the actuator torque must also overcome it (p.12): viscous \(\tau_v = b_v\dot q\) and Coulomb \(\tau_c = b_c\,\mathrm{sgn}(\dot q)\):

\[ \tau = mL^2\ddot q + b_v\dot q + b_c\,\mathrm{sgn}(\dot q) + mgL\cos q \qquad\text{(N·m)} \]

checked (Lagrangian result, symbolically) Units: m kg, L m, \(b_v\) N·m·s/rad, \(b_c\) N·m, g = 9.81 m/s². added If the link also has its own mass or inertia, \(mL^2\) becomes the total inertia about the pivot.

Partition (p.14): \(\tau = \alpha\tau' + \beta\) with

\[ \alpha = mL^2,\qquad \beta = b_v\dot q + b_c\,\mathrm{sgn}(\dot q) + mgL\cos q,\qquad \tau' = \ddot q_d + k_v\dot e + k_p e,\quad e = q_d - q . \]

Substituting into the EoM gives \(mL^2\ddot q = mL^2\tau'\), so \(\ddot q = \tau'\) and \(\ddot e + k_v\dot e + k_p e = 0\) again.

added \(\mathrm{sgn}(\dot q)\) jumps at \(\dot q = 0\). With a noisy velocity measurement the term chatters between \(\pm b_c\). Practical implementations smooth it (the widget above uses \(\tanh(\dot q/0.01)\) in plant and controller alike).

Exam recipe
  1. Get the EoM (Lagrangian if not given): \(K\), \(P\), then \(\tfrac{d}{dt}\partial\mathcal L/\partial\dot q - \partial\mathcal L/\partial q\).
  2. Add friction torques on the side that the actuator must overcome.
  3. \(\alpha\) = coefficient of \(\ddot q\); \(\beta\) = the rest (velocity terms, gravity, friction).
  4. \(\tau' = \ddot q_d + k_v\dot e + k_p e\).
  5. \(\tau = \alpha\tau' + \beta\). Quote it with the measured \(q,\dot q\) inside \(\beta\).
  6. Check: at rest on the path (\(e = 0\), \(\ddot q_d = 0\), \(\dot q = 0\)) the torque must equal the gravity torque \(mgL\cos q\).
Worked example

m = 2 kg, L = 0.5 m, \(b_v = 0.3\) N·m·s/rad, \(b_c = 0.2\) N·m, g = 9.81 m/s². State: q = 30°, \(\dot q\) = 1 rad/s. Desired \(\ddot q_d\) = 2 rad/s², e = 0.05 rad, \(\dot e\) = −0.1 rad/s; \(k_p\) = 64 s⁻², \(k_v\) = 16 s⁻¹.

\(\alpha = 2(0.5)^2 = 0.5\) kg·m². \(\tau' = 2 + 16(-0.1) + 64(0.05) = 3.6\) rad/s². \(\beta = 0.3(1) + 0.2(+1) + 2(9.81)(0.5)\cos30^\circ = 0.5 + 8.4957 = 8.9957\) N·m. \(\tau = 0.5(3.6) + 8.9957 = 10.7957\) N·m.

Check with the plant: \(\ddot q = (\tau - \beta)/\alpha = 1.8/0.5 = 3.6 = \tau'\). ✓ checked

Slides vs slides

Friction is written \(\mathbf f(\dot{\mathbf q})\) on p. 19 and on the “true” side of p. 27, but \(\hat{\mathbf f}(\mathbf q,\dot{\mathbf q})\) in \(\hat\beta\) (p. 27), in the error equation (p. 28) and on the practical sheet. The friction in this deck (viscous, Coulomb) depends on velocity only, so both mean the same. The extra \(\mathbf q\) is generality (a friction that varies with position). Write \(\mathbf f(\mathbf q,\dot{\mathbf q})\) if the question does, otherwise \(\mathbf f(\dot{\mathbf q})\). Slide 18 also writes the generalised force as F where p. 19 writes Q; same object.

Calculation: given the EoM and a state, compute \(\tau\). Common slips: using degrees in \(\cos q\) on a radian calculator, forgetting that \(\mathrm{sgn}(\dot q)\) takes the sign of the velocity (not of q or e), and using \(\ddot q_d\) in \(\beta\). Explain: “why does the law need the parameters?” (p. 15).

3 · The n-joint manipulator: computed torque pp. 16–21

Picture

Every line in the block diagram is now an \(n\times1\) vector (p.17). The model-based part has two jobs: multiply the commanded accelerations by the inertia matrix \(\mathbf M(\mathbf q)\), and add the velocity, gravity and friction torques. The first job undoes the coupling: pushing joint 1 also needs torque on joints 2 and 3 (the off-diagonal terms of \(\mathbf M\)), and \(\mathbf M\) supplies exactly that.

Derivation

The manipulator dynamics from Week 8 (p.19), all \(n\times1\) except \(\mathbf M\) (\(n\times n\)):

\[ \mathbf Q = \mathbf M(\mathbf q)\ddot{\mathbf q} + \mathbf C(\mathbf q,\dot{\mathbf q}) + \mathbf g(\mathbf q) + \mathbf f(\dot{\mathbf q}) \]

Partition \(\mathbf Q = \boldsymbol\alpha\mathbf Q' + \boldsymbol\beta\) with \(\boldsymbol\alpha = \mathbf M(\mathbf q)\), \(\boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf C + \mathbf g + \mathbf f\), and servo \(\mathbf Q' = \ddot{\mathbf q}_d + \mathbf K_v\dot{\mathbf E} + \mathbf K_p\mathbf E\) (pp. 18–19). Substituting: \(\mathbf M\ddot{\mathbf q} + \boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf M\mathbf Q' + \boldsymbol\beta\). \(\mathbf M\) is symmetric positive definite, hence invertible, so \(\ddot{\mathbf q} = \mathbf Q'\) and

\[ \ddot{\mathbf E} + \mathbf K_v\dot{\mathbf E} + \mathbf K_p\mathbf E = \mathbf 0 \quad(\text{slide }21). \]

With diagonal gains each row is independent: \(\ddot e_i + k_{v,i}\dot e_i + k_{p,i}e_i = 0\). A coupled, non-linear robot becomes \(n\) separate linear second-order systems. checked (20 random states on the 3-link arm)

Three facts the slides stress (p.18, p.20): \(\boldsymbol\alpha\) is chosen to decouple the n equations and is not diagonal; \(\mathbf K_v,\mathbf K_p\) are usually diagonal; the model-based box “linearises the system”, the servo box “stabilises the closed-loop system”.

Exam recipe
  1. Write the EoM as \(\mathbf M\ddot{\mathbf q} + \mathbf C + \mathbf g + \mathbf f = \mathbf Q\) and identify the matrices.
  2. \(\boldsymbol\alpha = \mathbf M(\mathbf q)\) (full matrix), \(\boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf C + \mathbf g + \mathbf f\).
  3. \(\mathbf Q' = \ddot{\mathbf q}_d + \mathbf K_v\dot{\mathbf E} + \mathbf K_p\mathbf E\); choose \(\mathbf K\) diagonal, e.g. \(k_p=\omega_n^2\), \(k_v = 2\omega_n\).
  4. \(\mathbf Q = \mathbf M(\mathbf q)\,\mathbf Q' + \boldsymbol\beta\).
  5. State the closed loop \(\ddot{\mathbf E} + \mathbf K_v\dot{\mathbf E} + \mathbf K_p\mathbf E = \mathbf 0\) and say “decoupled because the gains are diagonal”.
  6. Qualify: “only if the model is exact and the law runs continuously”.
Worked example: why \(\boldsymbol\alpha\) is not diagonal (practical arm, initial pose)

For the 3-link arm of the practical sheet at \(\mathbf q = (0, 0, 90^\circ)\) (derived in problem P9.2) \(\mathbf M = \begin{bmatrix}103&31&1\\31&13&1\\1&1&1\end{bmatrix}\) kg·m². Ask for a unit acceleration of joint 1 only, \(\mathbf Q' = (1,0,0)\) rad/s². Then \(\mathbf Q - \boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf M\mathbf Q' = (103, 31, 1)\) N·m. To accelerate joint 1 by 1 rad/s² and keep joints 2 and 3 still, the controller must also apply 31 N·m at joint 2 and 1 N·m at joint 3. A \(\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf M)\) would skip those. checked

Explain / spot-the-error: “the closed loop is linear and decoupled” is true only for a perfect model (slide 21). “\(\alpha\) is diagonal because \(K_p,K_v\) are” is false. If asked “what does the red box do and the green box do?”: red (model-based) linearises, green (servo) stabilises.

4 · When the ideal fails: imprecise model and discretisation pp. 22–28

Picture

Two things break the clean result \(\ddot E + K_v\dot E + K_pE = 0\) (p.22). (1) The model is inexact: friction is hard to model, the robot wears, a grasped object shifts the mass (p.26). (2) The law runs on a computer: sensors are sampled, torques updated at discrete times, and the dynamics computation takes finite time (p.23). The dynamics part is the slow one; error × gain is quick (p.24).

The slide’s fix for (2) (p.25): move the model-based block to the outer loop. Its input is the desired trajectory \(\ddot{\mathbf q}_d,\dot{\mathbf q}_d,\mathbf q_d\), so it can be evaluated ahead of time or at a slower rate, and the fast servo loop (\(K_p,K_v\) on the measured error) runs inside. reading of the diagram The cancellation is then only approximate (the model is evaluated along the plan, not the actual state), so the servo has to mop up the difference.

Derivation: error equation with hats (slide 28)

Hats mean estimates. The law uses \(\boldsymbol\alpha = \hat{\mathbf M}(\mathbf q)\), \(\boldsymbol\beta = \hat{\mathbf C} + \hat{\mathbf g} + \hat{\mathbf f}\) (p.27) with the same servo \(\mathbf Q'\). The true plant is \(\mathbf M\ddot{\mathbf q} + \mathbf C + \mathbf g + \mathbf f = \mathbf Q\). Equate the two:

\[ \mathbf M\ddot{\mathbf q} + \mathbf C + \mathbf g + \mathbf f = \hat{\mathbf M}\big(\ddot{\mathbf q}_d + \mathbf K_v\dot{\mathbf E} + \mathbf K_p\mathbf E\big) + \hat{\mathbf C} + \hat{\mathbf g} + \hat{\mathbf f}. \]

Add and subtract \(\hat{\mathbf M}\ddot{\mathbf q}\) on the left, move the hatted torques across, multiply by \(\hat{\mathbf M}^{-1}\) and use \(\ddot{\mathbf E} = \ddot{\mathbf q}_d - \ddot{\mathbf q}\):

\[ \ddot{\mathbf E} + \mathbf K_v\dot{\mathbf E} + \mathbf K_p\mathbf E = \hat{\mathbf M}^{-1}\Big[(\mathbf M-\hat{\mathbf M})\ddot{\mathbf q} + (\mathbf C-\hat{\mathbf C}) + (\mathbf g-\hat{\mathbf g}) + (\mathbf f-\hat{\mathbf f})\Big] \quad(\text{slide }28). \]

checked (20 random states, 2-link arm with mismatched masses) Read it as a servo loop driven by a forcing term: each model mismatch pushes on the error. If every hat is exact the right side is zero. The error no longer decays to zero; for a bounded forcing it settles at roughly (forcing)/\(k_p\), so a bigger \(k_p\) shrinks it (at the price of noise sensitivity and torque limits). Note the \(\ddot{\mathbf q}\) on the right is the actual acceleration.

Single link with only the mass wrong, \(\hat m = km\) (added: the special case of the slide’s equation). Here \(\alpha = mL^2\), \(\hat\alpha = kmL^2\), and \(\beta-\hat\beta = (m-\hat m)gL\cos q\). Dividing the bracket by \(\hat\alpha\):

\[ \ddot e + k_v\dot e + k_p e = \frac{m-\hat m}{\hat m}\Big[\ddot q + \frac gL\cos q\Big] . \]

checked (20 random states) The coefficient \((m-\hat m)/\hat m\) is the relative error in mass; the bracket is the acceleration the mass actually has plus the gravity acceleration at the pivot. If \(\hat m\lt m\) gravity is under-compensated, the link sags, and \(e = q_d - q\) becomes positive.

Exam recipe
  1. Write the law with hats: \(\boldsymbol\alpha = \hat{\mathbf M}\), \(\boldsymbol\beta = \hat{\mathbf C}+\hat{\mathbf g}+\hat{\mathbf f}\).
  2. Equate to the true dynamics and isolate \(\ddot{\mathbf E} + \mathbf K_v\dot{\mathbf E} + \mathbf K_p\mathbf E\).
  3. Quote the slide-28 right side, term by term (mass, Coriolis, gravity, friction mismatch).
  4. For a numeric case, plug in the mismatch: \((m-\hat m)/\hat m\) and the bracket.
  5. Static error: set \(\ddot e = \dot e = 0\), \(\ddot q = 0\): \(e_{ss} \approx \dfrac{m-\hat m}{\hat m}\dfrac{g}{L}\dfrac{\cos q}{k_p}\).
  6. Discretisation: say the model part is slow, so run it in the outer loop; the servo loop stays fast.
Worked example: the practical’s 2.8 kg (single link: m = 3 kg, L = 3 m, \(k_p=100\) s⁻², \(k_v=20\) s⁻¹)

\(\hat m = 2.8\) kg, so \((m-\hat m)/\hat m = 0.2/2.8 = 1/14 = 0.0714\). \(g/L = 9.81/3 = 3.27\) rad/s². Holding the link horizontal (q = 0, \(\ddot q = 0\)): forcing \(= 0.0714(3.27) = 0.2336\) rad/s², so \(e_{ss} = 0.2336/100 = 2.34\) mrad \(= 0.134^\circ\). Holding it vertical (q = 90°): \(\cos q = 0\), no lever arm, so the static error from mass mismatch is essentially zero. checked, including a simulation of the hold

Typical question: “the mass is estimated 5% too small; write the closed-loop error equation and say what happens”. State: forcing term non-zero, error does not decay to zero, steady-state error proportional to the mismatch and inversely to \(k_p\), larger when the link is horizontal. Trap: “the servo law fixes any model error” (it reduces it, it does not remove it).

5 · Control in Cartesian space pp. 29–33

Picture

Tasks are given as paths of the tool, \(\mathbf x(t)\). The joint-space controller of Section 3 needs the whole plan in joint space. Slide 30 does that with a trajectory generator that converts \((\mathbf x_d,\dot{\mathbf x}_d,\ddot{\mathbf x}_d)\) into \((\mathbf q_d,\dot{\mathbf q}_d,\ddot{\mathbf q}_d)\). Slide 31 lists the three conversions and says all are computationally intensive:

\[ \mathbf q = \mathcal K^{-1}(\mathbf x),\qquad \dot{\mathbf q} = \mathbf J^{-1}(\mathbf q)\dot{\mathbf x},\qquad \ddot{\mathbf q} = \tfrac{d}{dt}\big(\mathbf J^{-1}\big)\dot{\mathbf x} + \mathbf J^{-1}\ddot{\mathbf x}. \]

The alternative (p.32): write the dynamics in Cartesian space, \(\mathcal F = \mathbf M_x(\mathbf q)\ddot{\mathbf x} + \mathbf C_x(\mathbf q,\dot{\mathbf q}) + \mathbf g_x(\mathbf q)\), solve for the control force/wrench \(\mathcal F\) from the Cartesian error, then convert to joint torques with \(\mathbf Q = \mathbf J^\top(\mathbf q)\,\mathcal F\). Feedback is cheap and forward: \(\mathbf x = \mathcal K(\mathbf q)\) (forward kinematics) and \(\dot{\mathbf x} = \mathbf J(\mathbf q)\dot{\mathbf q}\) (p.33).

Derivation

The Cartesian law mirrors the joint law (p.33): servo on \(\mathbf e_x = \mathbf x_d - \mathbf x\), then \(\mathbf M_x\), then add the model terms:

\[ \mathcal F = \mathbf M_x(\mathbf q)\big(\ddot{\mathbf x}_d + \mathbf K_v\dot{\mathbf e}_x + \mathbf K_p\mathbf e_x\big) + \mathbf c_x(\mathbf q,\dot{\mathbf q}) + \mathbf g_x(\mathbf q),\qquad \mathbf Q = \mathbf J^\top(\mathbf q)\,\mathcal F, \]

so \(\ddot{\mathbf e}_x + \mathbf K_v\dot{\mathbf e}_x + \mathbf K_p\mathbf e_x = \mathbf 0\) in Cartesian coordinates (exact model).

added Why \(\mathbf Q = \mathbf J^\top\mathcal F\): virtual work. A small joint motion \(\delta\mathbf q\) moves the tool by \(\delta\mathbf x = \mathbf J\delta\mathbf q\). Equal work gives \(\mathbf Q^\top\delta\mathbf q = \mathcal F^\top\delta\mathbf x = \mathcal F^\top\mathbf J\delta\mathbf q\), so \(\mathbf Q = \mathbf J^\top\mathcal F\) for any \(\delta\mathbf q\). This is the statics result from W6.

added Where the Cartesian terms come from (standard result, not on the slides): from \(\ddot{\mathbf x} = \mathbf J\ddot{\mathbf q} + \dot{\mathbf J}\dot{\mathbf q}\) get \(\ddot{\mathbf q} = \mathbf J^{-1}(\ddot{\mathbf x} - \dot{\mathbf J}\dot{\mathbf q})\). Substitute in the joint dynamics and premultiply by \(\mathbf J^{-\top}\): \(\mathbf M_x = \mathbf J^{-\top}\mathbf M\mathbf J^{-1}\), \(\mathbf c_x = \mathbf J^{-\top}(\mathbf C - \mathbf M\mathbf J^{-1}\dot{\mathbf J}\dot{\mathbf q})\), \(\mathbf g_x = \mathbf J^{-\top}\mathbf g\). checked (numerically, 2-link arm) So these still need \(\mathbf J\) to be invertible: near a singularity \(\mathbf M_x\) blows up (some tool direction cannot be accelerated), even though \(\mathbf J^\top\mathcal F\) itself is always fine.

Slides vs textbook

Slide 31 prints the third line as \(\dot J^{-1}(\mathbf q)\dot{\mathbf x} + J^{-1}(\mathbf q)\ddot{\mathbf x}\), with the dot over J. The correct term is the time derivative of the inverse: \(\tfrac{d}{dt}(\mathbf J^{-1}) = -\mathbf J^{-1}\dot{\mathbf J}\mathbf J^{-1}\). Derivation: \(\dot{\mathbf x} = \mathbf J\dot{\mathbf q}\Rightarrow\ddot{\mathbf q} = \mathbf J^{-1}(\ddot{\mathbf x} - \dot{\mathbf J}\dot{\mathbf q}) = \mathbf J^{-1}\ddot{\mathbf x} - \mathbf J^{-1}\dot{\mathbf J}\mathbf J^{-1}\dot{\mathbf x}\). “Inverse of \(\dot{\mathbf J}\)” would be wrong (and \(\dot{\mathbf J}\) is usually not even invertible). checked by finite differences

Exam recipe
  1. State why: joint-space needs \(\mathcal K^{-1}\), \(\mathbf J^{-1}\) and \(\tfrac d{dt}\mathbf J^{-1}\) along the whole path (slide 31).
  2. Write the Cartesian plant \(\mathcal F = \mathbf M_x\ddot{\mathbf x} + \mathbf C_x + \mathbf g_x\).
  3. Servo on Cartesian error, \(\mathcal F = \mathbf M_x(\ddot{\mathbf x}_d + \mathbf K_v\dot{\mathbf e} + \mathbf K_p\mathbf e) + \mathbf c_x + \mathbf g_x\).
  4. Map to joints: \(\mathbf Q = \mathbf J^\top\mathcal F\). Feedback: \(\mathbf x = \mathcal K(\mathbf q)\), \(\dot{\mathbf x} = \mathbf J\dot{\mathbf q}\).
  5. For a numeric \(\mathbf Q = \mathbf J^\top\mathcal F\): build \(\mathbf J\) at the pose, transpose, multiply; cross-check joint 1 with \(x F_y - yF_x\).
Worked example: \(\mathbf Q = \mathbf J^\top\mathcal F\) for a 2-link arm (\(l_1 = l_2 = 1\) m)

The position Jacobian is \(\mathbf J = \begin{bmatrix}-l_1s_1 - l_2s_{12} & -l_2s_{12}\\ l_1c_1 + l_2c_{12} & l_2c_{12}\end{bmatrix}\). At \(\mathbf q = (30^\circ, 60^\circ)\): \(s_1 = 0.5\), \(c_1 = 0.8660\), \(s_{12} = 1\), \(c_{12} = 0\), so \(\mathbf J = \begin{bmatrix}-1.5&-1\\0.8660&0\end{bmatrix}\). A tool force \(\mathcal F = (3, -4)\) N gives

\[ \mathbf Q = \mathbf J^\top\mathcal F = \begin{bmatrix}-1.5&0.8660\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3\\-4\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-4.5-3.4641\\-3\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-7.9641\\-3.0000\end{bmatrix}\ \text{N·m}. \]

Cross-check by moments. The tool is at \((\cos30^\circ + \cos90^\circ,\ \sin30^\circ + \sin90^\circ) = (0.8660,\ 1.5)\) m and joint 2 at (0.8660, 0.5) m. Torque about joint 1: \(xF_y - yF_x = 0.8660(-4) - 1.5(3) = -7.9641\) N·m ✓. About joint 2, \(\mathbf r = (0, 1)\): \(0\cdot(-4) - 1\cdot 3 = -3\) N·m ✓. checked

Likely a calculation (\(\mathbf Q = \mathbf J^\top\mathcal F\)) or an explain (“why is Cartesian-space control attractive / what is expensive in the joint-space version?”). Trap: using \(\mathbf J\) instead of \(\mathbf J^\top\), or the inverse. Dimension check: \(\mathbf J\) is 2×2 here, force 2×1, torque 2×1.

6 · Force control pp. 34–44

Picture

Goal (p.35): make the end effector push on the environment with a desired force. Model (p.36): a mass m pushed by the control force f against a wall, which behaves as a spring \(f_e = k_e x\). An unknown disturbance \(f_{dist}\) also acts on the mass. The handwritten balance is \(f - f_e - f_{dist} = m\ddot x\).

Derivation: the ideal law, and why it fails

Plant (p.37): \(f = m\ddot x + f_{dist} + f_e\). Because \(f_e = k_ex\), \(x = k_e^{-1}f_e\) and \(\ddot x = k_e^{-1}\ddot f_e\), so \(f = mk_e^{-1}\ddot f_e + f_{dist} + f_e\). Now the controlled quantity is the force, and the same partition applies with \(\alpha = mk_e^{-1}\) (units kg·m/N = s²) and \(\beta = f_{dist} + f_e\):

\[ f = mk_e^{-1}\big[\ddot f_d + k_v\dot E + k_pE\big] + f_{dist} + f_e,\qquad E = f_d - f_e \]

with \(f_d\) the desired interaction force. Substituting gives \(\ddot f_e = f'\), i.e. \(\ddot E + k_v\dot E + k_pE = 0\) (p.38). But \(\beta\) contains \(f_{dist}\), which we do not know, so the law is infeasible. Two ways out (p.39). Write \(\alpha = mk_e^{-1}\).

Option 1: drop \(f_{dist}\), keep \(f_e\): \(f = \alpha[\ddot f_d + k_v\dot E + k_pE] + f_e\). Equate to the plant \(f = \alpha\ddot f_e + f_{dist} + f_e\): \(\alpha(\ddot E + k_v\dot E + k_pE) = f_{dist}\), so

\[ \ddot E + k_v\dot E + k_pE = \frac{f_{dist}}{mk_e^{-1}} \;\Rightarrow\; E_{ss} = \frac{f_{dist}}{mk_e^{-1}k_p}\quad(\ddot E = \dot E = 0). \]

Option 2: replace \(f_{dist} + f_e\) by \(f_d\): \(f = \alpha[\ddot f_d + k_v\dot E + k_pE] + f_d\). Equating: \(\alpha(\ddot E + k_v\dot E + k_pE) = f_{dist} + f_e - f_d = f_{dist} - E\), so

\[ \ddot E + k_v\dot E + \Big(\frac{1}{mk_e^{-1}} + k_p\Big)E = \frac{f_{dist}}{mk_e^{-1}} \;\Rightarrow\; E_{ss} = \frac{f_{dist}}{1 + mk_e^{-1}k_p}. \]

checked (both closed loops and steady states, symbolically and by simulation) Let \(x = mk_e^{-1}k_p\) (dimensionless: kg·(m/N)·s⁻² = 1). Then \(E_1 = f_{dist}/x\), \(E_2 = f_{dist}/(1+x)\), and \(E_2/E_1 = x/(1+x) < 1\): Option 2 is always better, and much better when \(x\) is small, which is exactly a stiff environment (\(k_e\) large \(\Rightarrow x\) small) (p.40). Physically, as \(k_p\to0\) Option 2 still pushes with \(f_d\), so the contact force is \(f_d - f_{dist}\) and \(E\to f_{dist}\); Option 1 gets \(E\to\infty\).

Practical implementation (pp. 41–43). The full law needs \(\dot f_e\). Differentiating a noisy force measurement is “not a good idea” (p. 42), and \(\ddot f_d,\dot f_d\) are zero for a constant \(f_d\). Since \(\dot E = \dot f_d - k_e\dot x = -k_e\dot x\), replace the derivative of the force by the measured velocity: with Option 2,

\[ f = m\big[k_e^{-1}k_pE - k_v\dot x\big] + f_d . \]

checked (equal to Option 2 for constant \(f_d\)) This is the form on p. 43: outer loop \(k_p/k_e\) on the force error, inner velocity loop \(k_v\), and \(f_d\) fed forward. Stiffness is usually unknown; \(k_e\) is “usually chosen to be a high value” and the controller is designed to be robust to small changes (p.44). likely reason, inferred \(k_e\) enters only through the gain \(k_p/k_e\), so a high assumed value gives a lower, safer loop gain.

Slides vs slides

Slide 38 writes the closed loop with bold \(\mathbf K_v,\mathbf K_p\) and slide 39 (Option 2) writes capital \(K_v\) where Option 1 has \(k_v\). The system is scalar, so these are the plain gains \(k_v,k_p\). The steady-state formulas on slides 39–40 are consistent with the closed-loop equations printed beside them.

Exam recipe
  1. Write the plant with \(f_e = k_ex\) substituted, so the acceleration is \(k_e^{-1}\ddot f_e\).
  2. \(\alpha = mk_e^{-1}\), \(\beta = f_{dist} + f_e\); \(E = f_d - f_e\). Note \(\beta\) is infeasible (\(f_{dist}\) unknown).
  3. Option 1: delete \(f_{dist}\). Option 2: replace \(f_{dist}+f_e\) by \(f_d\).
  4. Equate to the plant, get \(\alpha(\ddot E + k_v\dot E + k_pE) = \) (right-hand side), then set derivatives to 0.
  5. \(E_1 = f_{dist}/(mk_e^{-1}k_p)\), \(E_2 = f_{dist}/(1+mk_e^{-1}k_p)\). Compare: \(E_2\lt E_1\).
  6. Sanity check: \(x = mk_e^{-1}k_p\) is dimensionless; E has the units of force.
Worked example

m = 2 kg, \(f_{dist}\) = 5 N, \(k_p\) = 100 s⁻². Stiff wall, \(k_e\) = 1000 N/m: \(mk_e^{-1} = 0.002\) s², \(x = 0.2\). \(E_1 = 5/0.2 = 25\) N, \(E_2 = 5/1.2 = 4.17\) N. Soft wall, \(k_e\) = 20 N/m: \(mk_e^{-1} = 0.1\) s², \(x = 10\). \(E_1 = 0.5\) N, \(E_2 = 5/11 = 0.455\) N.

Reading: on a stiff wall Option 1 is useless at this gain (25 N is larger than any sensible \(f_d\), the contact would be lost), while Option 2 stays below \(f_{dist}\). To get Option 2 to 1% of the disturbance you would need \(x = 99\), i.e. \(k_p = 99/0.002 = 49\,500\) s⁻². checked

Calculation or explain: “state the steady-state error of each option and say which is better for a stiff environment”. Trap: swapping the two formulas, forgetting the “1 +”, or saying Option 1 is better because it uses the measured \(f_e\). Also expect “why is \(\tfrac{d}{dt}f_e\) a bad idea?” (noise amplified by differentiation).

7 · Hybrid force and position control pp. 45–47

Picture

Many tasks need both (p.46: a humanoid pressing and wiping a wall). Along the wall normal the hand must push with a force; along the wall it must follow a path. The hybrid controller runs both laws and uses a diagonal 0/1 selection matrix for each to pass, axis by axis, only the output that applies (p.47).

Derivation

The commanded Cartesian force is the sum of the two filtered outputs:

\[ \mathcal F = \mathbf S\,\mathcal F_{pos} + \mathbf S'\,\mathcal F_{force}, \]

where \(\mathcal F_{pos}\) comes from the Cartesian position law of Section 5 and \(\mathcal F_{force}\) from a force law as in Section 6. \(\mathbf S\) and \(\mathbf S'\) are diagonal with 0 or 1 entries, “complementary to each other”, saying for each degree of freedom whether it is in position or force mode (slide 47). inferred Complementary means \(\mathbf S' = \mathbf I - \mathbf S\), so each axis is controlled by exactly one law. The slide does not write this relation. It also says “joint” in the last bullet although the diagram is in Cartesian space.

For the wall in the slide with the wall normal along \(x\) (axis labels are my choice): position control in \(y,z\), force control in \(x\):

\[ \mathbf S = \mathrm{diag}(0,1,1),\qquad \mathbf S' = \mathrm{diag}(1,0,0). \]

A full pose has six Cartesian degrees of freedom (three forces, three moments), and \(\mathbf S\) is then 6×6. The surface constraint decides: translation along the normal and rotations that tilt the hand off the surface are blocked (so they can be force/moment-controlled); sliding along the surface and the rotation about the normal are free (position-controlled).

Exam recipe
  1. Name the constraint surface and its normal direction.
  2. Directions the surface blocks: force control, \(\mathbf S'\) entry 1 (and \(\mathbf S\) entry 0).
  3. Free directions: position control, \(\mathbf S\) entry 1 (and \(\mathbf S'\) entry 0).
  4. Write \(\mathbf S\) and \(\mathbf S' = \mathbf I - \mathbf S\) as diagonal matrices in the stated order of axes.
  5. Write \(\mathcal F = \mathbf S\mathcal F_{pos} + \mathbf S'\mathcal F_{force}\) and \(\mathbf Q = \mathbf J^\top\mathcal F\).
  6. Feedback: position law uses \(\mathbf x\); force law uses the measured \(\mathcal F_E\).
Worked example

With the wall normal along \(x\): position law outputs \(\mathcal F_{pos} = (5, 3, -2)\) N, force law outputs \(\mathcal F_{force} = (8, 40, 7)\) N. Then

\[ \mathcal F = \mathrm{diag}(0,1,1)\begin{bmatrix}5\\3\\-2\end{bmatrix} + \mathrm{diag}(1,0,0)\begin{bmatrix}8\\40\\7\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0\\3\\-2\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}8\\0\\0\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}8\\3\\-2\end{bmatrix}\ \text{N}. \]

The 5 N of the position law along \(x\) and the 40 N and 7 N of the force law along \(y,z\) are discarded: each axis obeys one law only. checked

Scenario: “a robot polishes a flat table / presses a stamp / turns a crank; choose S and S′”. Name the normal, put the normal in force mode, everything else in position mode. Draw the p. 47 diagram if asked to sketch. Trap: swapping S and S′ (S goes with the position law in the diagram).

8 · Putting it together: which law, when? p. 49

Decision table
SituationLawClosed loop (exact model)
Scalar plant, non-linear (spring, friction)\(f = \alpha f' + \beta\), \(f' = \ddot x_d + k_v\dot e + k_pe\)\(\ddot e + k_v\dot e + k_pe = 0\)
n-joint arm, joint space\(\mathbf Q = \mathbf M\mathbf Q' + \mathbf C + \mathbf g + \mathbf f\)\(\ddot{\mathbf E} + \mathbf K_v\dot{\mathbf E} + \mathbf K_p\mathbf E = \mathbf 0\), decoupled
Model inexactsame law with hatsRHS \(=\hat{\mathbf M}^{-1}[(\mathbf M-\hat{\mathbf M})\ddot{\mathbf q} + \dots]\ne0\) (slide 28)
Path given in task space\(\mathcal F = \mathbf M_x(\dots) + \mathbf c_x + \mathbf g_x\), \(\mathbf Q = \mathbf J^\top\mathcal F\)\(\ddot{\mathbf e}_x + \mathbf K_v\dot{\mathbf e}_x + \mathbf K_p\mathbf e_x = \mathbf 0\)
Contact force wantedOption 2: \(f = mk_e^{-1}[\dots] + f_d\)\(E_{ss} = f_{dist}/(1 + mk_e^{-1}k_p)\)
Force on some axes, motion on others\(\mathcal F = \mathbf S\mathcal F_{pos} + \mathbf S'\mathcal F_{force}\)each axis follows its own law

Not in this deck (do not expect it from these slides): Lyapunov stability proofs, impedance/admittance control, and the gain-selection rule (Week 8).

Guided problems: solve on paper first

Problems P9.1–P9.7 are the practical sheet’s items (a)–(i) in order, solved as exam questions. The sheet gives no trajectory duration; I assume T = 2 s (speeds scale as 1/T, accelerations as 1/T²) and gains \(k_p = 100\) s⁻², \(k_v = 20\) s⁻¹ (critical damping). Gravity acts along −y with g = 9.81 m/s² (the arm moves in a vertical plane), and the joint angles \(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3\) are the figure’s: \(\theta_1\) from the horizontal, the others relative to the previous link.

P9.1 · Practical (a): the joint trajectorycalculatederivesketch

The 3-link arm (L = 3, 2, 1 m) starts at rest at pose (x, y, φ) = (5, 1, 90°) and must stop at (−3, 3, 180°). Find the start and goal joint angles (take the elbow branch with \(\theta_2\ge0\)), then the rest-to-rest cubic for each joint over T = 2 s. Give the goal angles \(\theta_1,\theta_3\) in degrees and the peak speed of joint 1 in rad/s. Sketch q(t), \(\dot q\)(t), \(\ddot q\)(t) for joint 1.

Hint 1: remove the last link

The wrist is the point where link 3 starts: \((x - L_3\cos\varphi,\ y - L_3\sin\varphi)\). Then it is a 2-link IK, and \(\theta_3 = \varphi - \theta_1 - \theta_2\).

Hint 2: 2-link IK

\(\cos\theta_2 = (w_x^2 + w_y^2 - L_1^2 - L_2^2)/(2L_1L_2)\), \(\theta_1 = \operatorname{atan2}(w_y,w_x) - \operatorname{atan2}(L_2\sin\theta_2,\ L_1 + L_2\cos\theta_2)\).

Hint 3: rest-to-rest cubic

With \(\dot q(0) = \dot q(T) = 0\): \(q(t) = q_0 + \Delta\,(3s^2 - 2s^3)\), \(s = t/T\), \(\Delta = q_f - q_0\). Peak speed at \(t = T/2\).

Full solution

Start. Wrist = \((5 - 0,\ 1 - 1) = (5, 0)\) m. \(\cos\theta_2 = (25 - 9 - 4)/12 = 1\), so \(\theta_2 = 0\): the arm is fully stretched along x, \(\theta_1 = \operatorname{atan2}(0,5) - 0 = 0\), \(\theta_3 = 90^\circ - 0 = 90^\circ\). Start \(\mathbf q_0 = (0, 0, 90^\circ)\). FK check: \(x = 3 + 2 + 0 = 5\), \(y = 0 + 0 + 1 = 1\) ✓.

Goal. Wrist = \((-3 - \cos180^\circ,\ 3 - \sin180^\circ) = (-2, 3)\) m, \(|w|^2 = 13\). \(\cos\theta_2 = (13 - 9 - 4)/12 = 0\), so \(\theta_2 = 90^\circ\). \(\theta_1 = \operatorname{atan2}(3,-2) - \operatorname{atan2}(2, 3) = 123.69^\circ - 33.69^\circ = 90^\circ\). \(\theta_3 = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - 90^\circ = 0\). Goal \(\mathbf q_f = (90^\circ, 90^\circ, 0)\). FK check: link 1 up to (0, 3), link 2 along 180° to (−2, 3), link 3 along 180° to (−3, 3) ✓. checked The other elbow, \(\theta_2 = -90^\circ\), gives \((157.38^\circ, -90^\circ, 112.62^\circ)\); the sheet does not say which branch, and the integers make \((90^\circ,90^\circ,0)\) the intended one.

Cubics. \(\Delta = (90^\circ, 90^\circ, -90^\circ) = (\pi/2, \pi/2, -\pi/2)\). With \(a_0 = q_0\), \(a_1 = 0\): \(a_2 = 3\Delta/T^2\), \(a_3 = -2\Delta/T^3\). For joints 1 and 2: \(a_2 = 1.1781\) rad/s², \(a_3 = -0.3927\) rad/s³. For joint 3 the signs flip: \(a_2 = -1.1781\), \(a_3 = +0.3927\). Peak speed \(1.5\Delta/T = 1.1781\) rad/s at t = 1 s; peak acceleration \(6\Delta/T^2 = 2.3562\) rad/s² at t = 0 (and \(-2.3562\) at t = T). checked

Sketch (joint 1). q(t): an S-curve from 0 to 90°, flat at both ends, midpoint 45° at t = 1 s. \(\dot q\): a parabola, 0 at both ends, peak 1.18 rad/s at t = 1 s. \(\ddot q\): a straight line from +2.36 to −2.36 rad/s², crossing 0 at t = 1 s. Note the acceleration is non-zero at t = 0 and T: it jumps when the trajectory stops, which the servo sees as a step.

Remarks. The start pose is a singularity (\(\det\mathbf J\propto\sin\theta_2 = 0\)), so Cartesian-space control with \(\mathbf J^{-1}\) cannot start here; the joint-space law of this problem has no such trouble. A joint-space cubic does not move the tool in a straight line: at t = 1 s the joints are (45°, 45°, 45°), the tool is at (1.414, 4.828) m with φ = 135°, nowhere near the straight-line midpoint (1, 2). checked

Common wrong answer: dividing by T instead of using \(1.5\Delta/T\) for the peak speed (0.785 rad/s).

Close everything and derive the rest-to-rest cubic coefficients and the peak speed from the four boundary conditions in 3 minutes.

P9.2 · Practical (b), (c): Lagrangian model and the matrices at the startderivecalculate

Point masses \(m_1=3,\ m_2=2,\ m_3=1\) kg at the distal ends of links of lengths 3, 2, 1 m. Obtain \(\mathbf Q = \mathbf M(\mathbf q)\ddot{\mathbf q} + \mathbf C(\mathbf q,\dot{\mathbf q}) + \mathbf g(\mathbf q)\) (ignore friction). Evaluate \(\mathbf M\), \(\mathbf C\), \(\mathbf g\) at the start, \(\mathbf q_0 = (0,0,90^\circ)\), \(\dot{\mathbf q} = \mathbf 0\).

Hint 1: positions of the three masses

\(p_1 = L_1(c_1,s_1)\); \(p_2 = p_1 + L_2(c_{12},s_{12})\); \(p_3 = p_2 + L_3(c_{123},s_{123})\), with \(c_{12} = \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)\) etc.

Hint 2: what you need from \(K\) and \(P\)

\(K = \sum\tfrac12 m_i|\dot p_i|^2\), \(P = g\sum m_iy_i\). Then \(M_{ij} = \partial^2K/\partial\dot q_i\partial\dot q_j\) and \(g_i = \partial P/\partial q_i\).

Hint 3: at the start

\(c_2 = 1\), \(c_3 = 0\), \(c_{23} = \cos90^\circ = 0\); since \(\dot{\mathbf q} = \mathbf 0\), \(\mathbf C = \mathbf 0\).

Full solution

Let \(A = (m_2+m_3)L_1L_2 = 18\), \(B = m_3L_1L_3 = 3\), \(D = m_3L_2L_3 = 2\) (kg·m²). The inertia matrix (symmetric):

\[ \begin{aligned} M_{11} &= (m_1+m_2+m_3)L_1^2 + (m_2+m_3)L_2^2 + m_3L_3^2 + 2Ac_2 + 2Bc_{23} + 2Dc_3 = 67 + 36c_2 + 6c_{23} + 4c_3\\ M_{12} &= (m_2+m_3)L_2^2 + m_3L_3^2 + Ac_2 + Bc_{23} + 2Dc_3 = 13 + 18c_2 + 3c_{23} + 4c_3\\ M_{13} &= m_3L_3^2 + Bc_{23} + Dc_3 = 1 + 3c_{23} + 2c_3\\ M_{22} &= (m_2+m_3)L_2^2 + m_3L_3^2 + 2Dc_3 = 13 + 4c_3,\quad M_{23} = m_3L_3^2 + Dc_3 = 1 + 2c_3,\quad M_{33} = m_3L_3^2 = 1 \end{aligned} \]

Velocity terms, with \(s_2 = \sin\theta_2\), \(s_{23} = \sin(\theta_2+\theta_3)\), \(s_3 = \sin\theta_3\):

\[ \begin{aligned} C_1 &= -As_2(2\dot q_1\dot q_2 + \dot q_2^2) - Bs_{23}\big(2\dot q_1(\dot q_2+\dot q_3) + (\dot q_2+\dot q_3)^2\big) - Ds_3\big(2(\dot q_1+\dot q_2)\dot q_3 + \dot q_3^2\big)\\ C_2 &= (As_2 + Bs_{23})\dot q_1^2 - Ds_3\big(2(\dot q_1+\dot q_2)\dot q_3 + \dot q_3^2\big),\qquad C_3 = Bs_{23}\dot q_1^2 + Ds_3(\dot q_1+\dot q_2)^2 \end{aligned} \]

Gravity (\(g_i = \partial P/\partial q_i\), g = 9.81 m/s²):

\[ \begin{aligned} g_1 &= g\big[6(3)c_1 + 3(2)c_{12} + 1(1)c_{123}\big],\quad g_2 = g\big[3(2)c_{12} + 1(1)c_{123}\big],\quad g_3 = g\,(1)(1)\,c_{123}\end{aligned} \]

checked (M, C and g against a symbolic Lagrangian derivation at random poses)

At the start. With \(c_2 = 1\), \(c_3 = c_{23} = 0\):

\[ \mathbf M = \begin{bmatrix}103&31&1\\31&13&1\\1&1&1\end{bmatrix}\ \text{kg·m}^2,\qquad \mathbf C = \begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathbf g = 9.81\begin{bmatrix}18+6+0\\6+0\\0\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}235.44\\58.86\\0\end{bmatrix}\ \text{N·m}. \]

Sanity check: \(g_1\) is the torque of all three weights about joint 1, all at horizontal distances 3, 5, 5 m (the arm lies along x, last link points up): \(9.81(3\cdot3 + 2\cdot5 + 1\cdot5) = 9.81\cdot24\) ✓. \(g_3 = 0\): the last link points straight up, so its weight has no lever arm. checked Inverse-dynamics demand at t = 0 on the T = 2 s cubic: \(\mathbf Q = \mathbf M\ddot{\mathbf q}_d + \mathbf g = (548.8,\ 160.2,\ 2.4)\) N·m.

If gravity were perpendicular to the arm’s plane (horizontal arm on a table), \(\mathbf g = \mathbf 0\); the sheet lists \(\mathbf g\) as a term, so I take a vertical plane.

P9.3 · Practical (d), (e): the partitioned law for the first linkderivecalculate

Ignore friction and consider joint 1 only. State what “the desired position is known, at each time step the next position” means, then write the partitioned control law. Treat the first link on its own (m₁ = 3 kg at the tip, L₁ = 3 m, which is why the sheet quotes “3 kg”) and give \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) at q₁ = 0 and the torque needed at t = 0 on the T = 2 s cubic when the error is zero.

Hint 1: what is q_d?

\(q_d(t)\), \(\dot q_d(t)\), \(\ddot q_d(t)\) come from the cubic of P9.1, evaluated at the next servo time \(t_{k+1}\).

Hint 2: the model

\(\tau = m_1L_1^2\ddot q + m_1gL_1\cos q\) (no friction).

Full solution

(d) The reference supplies \(q_d,\dot q_d,\ddot q_d\) at every servo step. “The next position” is the cubic sampled at the next sample time; the servo law uses the error \(e = q_d - q\) and \(\dot e = \dot q_d - \dot q\), and \(\ddot q_d\) as feed-forward.

(e) EoM: \(\tau = mL^2\ddot q + mgL\cos q\). Partition: \(\alpha = m_1L_1^2 = 3(9) = 27\) kg·m², \(\beta = m_1gL_1\cos q = 88.29\cos q\) N·m, \(\tau' = \ddot q_d + k_v\dot e + k_pe\). Law:

\[ \tau = 27\big(\ddot q_d + 20\,\dot e + 100\,e\big) + 88.29\cos q\quad\text{(N·m, with q in rad)}. \]

At t = 0 on the cubic: \(q = 0\), \(e = \dot e = 0\), \(\ddot q_d = 2.3562\): \(\tau(0) = 27(2.3562) + 88.29 = 63.62 + 88.29 = 151.91\) N·m. checked

The other reading. If “the first link” means joint 1 of the full arm (joints 2, 3 held), then \(\alpha = M_{11} = 103\) kg·m² and \(\beta = g_1 = 235.44\) N·m at the start (\(C_1 = 0\)). The structure is identical; only the numbers change, and holding joints 2, 3 would need their own torques. The sheet’s “2.8 kg” (against \(m_1 = 3\)) fits the single-link reading best.

Common wrong answer: using \(\alpha = m_1L_1\) (units kg·m, not kg·m²) or leaving \(\mathrm{cos}\,q\) out of \(\beta\).

P9.4 · Practical (f): the forward-dynamics simulatorderiveexplain

Describe, as an algorithm, a program that takes joint torque as input and returns positions and velocities. Why forward dynamics for simulation but inverse dynamics for control? Then: for P9.3, with the true model and zero error at t = 0, what joint acceleration does the simulator return?

Hint 1: the equation to integrate

Solve the EoM for the acceleration: \(\ddot{\mathbf q} = \mathbf M^{-1}(\mathbf Q - \mathbf C - \mathbf g - \mathbf f)\).

Hint 2: state

Stack \(\mathbf x = [\mathbf q;\dot{\mathbf q}]\), \(\dot{\mathbf x} = [\dot{\mathbf q};\ \ddot{\mathbf q}]\) and integrate.

Full solution

Algorithm (state \(\mathbf x_k = [\mathbf q_k;\dot{\mathbf q}_k]\), step \(h\)):

for k = 0, 1, 2, ...
    Q = controller(t_k, q_k, qdot_k)               # partitioned law, from the *model*
    qddot = solve(M_true(q_k), Q - C_true - g_true - f_true)   # forward dynamics (solve, do not invert)
    (q_{k+1}, qdot_{k+1}) = integrate(q_k, qdot_k, qddot, h)   # RK4, or semi-implicit Euler for small h
    log q_{k+1}, qdot_{k+1}, e = q_d(t_{k+1}) - q_{k+1}

Why. The plant maps torque to motion, so simulating it is forward dynamics: input \(\mathbf Q\), output \(\ddot{\mathbf q}\). The controller needs the torque that produces a desired acceleration, which is inverse dynamics: input \(\ddot{\mathbf q}\), output \(\mathbf Q\). Computed torque is inverse dynamics inside the controller; the simulator is forward dynamics standing in for the real robot.

Numbers. \(\ddot q(0) = (\tau - \beta)/\alpha = (151.91 - 88.29)/27 = 2.3562\) rad/s², exactly \(\ddot q_d(0)\) as the closed-loop theory says. checked

Keep the controller’s model and the simulator’s “true” model separate in the code: part (h) works only because the two differ.

P9.5 · Practical (g): the error plotcalculatesketch

The simulator of P9.4 runs with the exact model and the law of P9.3 (\(k_p=100\), \(k_v=20\)). (i) What does e(t) look like if the link starts on the trajectory? (ii) If it starts 0.1 rad behind (e(0) = 0.1 rad, \(\dot e(0) = 0\)), what is e at t = 0.1 s? (iii) What does a slow controller (torque updated every 50 ms) do?

Hint 1

Exact model: \(\ddot e + 20\dot e + 100e = 0\). Its roots: \(s^2 + 20s + 100 = (s+10)^2\).

Hint 2

A double root at \(-\omega\) gives \(e(t) = (c_1 + c_2t)e^{-\omega t}\). Fit \(e(0) = e_0\), \(\dot e(0) = 0\).

Full solution

(i) \(e(t)\equiv0\): the model part cancels the plant exactly, \(\ddot q = \ddot q_d\) at every instant. In my simulation (RK4, step 0.1 ms, law evaluated continuously) the largest error before t = 1.99 s is below \(10^{-10}\) rad, i.e. numerical noise. Expect a flat line at zero (a classic “is the plot broken?” moment).

(ii) Roots \(s = -10\) twice. \(e = (c_1 + c_2t)e^{-10t}\); \(e(0) = c_1 = 0.1\); \(\dot e(0) = c_2 - 10c_1 = 0\Rightarrow c_2 = 1\). So \(e(t) = 0.1(1 + 10t)e^{-10t}\), \(e(0.1) = 0.1(2)e^{-1} = 0.0736\) rad. Also \(e(0.25) = 0.0287\), \(e(0.5) = 0.00404\) rad: no overshoot, settling in about 0.5 s. checked against the simulation

(iii) The law only changes every 50 ms, the torque is stale in between, and the cancellation is imperfect: the error is small but not zero. In my simulation the peak error is 0.26 mrad with a 10 ms update and 1.13 mrad with a 50 ms update, against about 0 for continuous control. checked This is the discretisation problem of slides 23–25: the slower the model-based part runs, the larger the residual error.

Sketch: (i) a flat line at 0; (ii) a monotone decay from 0.1 to 0, tangent to zero slope at t = 0; (iii) small ripples (sawtooth) of 1 mrad riding on the reference acceleration.

P9.6 · Practical (h): an imprecise mass of 2.8 kgcalculateexplain

The controller now uses \(\hat m = 2.8\) kg while the simulated link has m = 3 kg (L = 3 m, \(k_p=100\), \(k_v=20\)). (i) Write the closed-loop error equation. (ii) With the link held at q_d = 0 (horizontal), what steady-state error does it predict, in mrad? (iii) What happens to that error if the link is held vertical? (iv) Give the sign of e and say why.

Hint 1

Use the scalar form: right side \(=\dfrac{m-\hat m}{\hat m}\big[\ddot q + \dfrac gL\cos q\big]\).

Hint 2

Static: \(\ddot q = \dot e = \ddot e = 0\), so \(k_pe_{ss} = \dfrac{m-\hat m}{\hat m}\dfrac gL\cos q\).

Full solution

(i) \(\ddot e + 20\dot e + 100e = \dfrac{0.2}{2.8}\Big[\ddot q + 3.27\cos q\Big] = 0.0714\big[\ddot q + 3.27\cos q\big]\) (slide 28 specialised to a mass error; the \(\ddot q\) is the actual acceleration).

(ii) At q = 0, \(\cos q = 1\): \(e_{ss} = 0.0714(3.27)/100 = 2.336\times10^{-3}\) rad \(= 2.34\) mrad \(= 0.134^\circ\). A simulation with the link held at q_d = 0 reaches the same value to 7 digits. checked

(iii) At q = 90°, \(\cos q = 0\): the gravity mismatch has no lever arm and the static error vanishes (to ~\(10^{-19}\) rad here). Mass error only matters through \(\hat\alpha\) when the link accelerates.

(iv) \(e>0\): \(\hat m\lt m\) means gravity is under-compensated, the link sags below the reference, and \(e = q_d - q\) is positive.

On the cubic trajectory (T = 2 s). The simulated error peaks at 3.35 mrad (0.19°) at t ≈ 0.47 s, when the acceleration is still large and the link is still near horizontal. At t = 2 s (link vertical) it is −1.21 mrad, caused by the deceleration term \(\tfrac{1}{14}\ddot q\), then it dies out at rest (4×10⁻¹¹ rad at 4 s). The forcing at t = 0 is \(\tfrac1{14}(2.3562 + 3.27) = 0.4019\) rad/s². checked

Full-arm reading. If joint 1’s \(m_1\) is 2.8 kg in the full 3-link model: \(\hat M_{11} = 103 - 0.2(9) = 101.2\), \(\hat g_1 = 235.44 - 0.2(9.81)(3) = 229.554\) N·m, static forcing \((g_1-\hat g_1)/\hat M_{11} = 0.0582\) rad/s² at the start. checked

P9.7 · Practical (i): all jointsderiveexplain

Extend the law to the full 3-link arm. Then suppose a student uses \(\boldsymbol\alpha = \mathrm{diag}(M_{11},M_{22},M_{33})\) instead of the full \(\mathbf M\), with everything else exact. At t = 0 on the T = 2 s cubic (\(\ddot{\mathbf q}_d = (2.3562, 2.3562, -2.3562)\) rad/s², zero error), how big is the forcing on the joint-1 error equation?

Hint 1

Use the slide-28 pattern with \(\hat{\mathbf M} = \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf M)\): row 1 of \(\hat{\mathbf M}^{-1}(\mathbf M-\hat{\mathbf M})\ddot{\mathbf q}\).

Hint 2

Off-diagonals of row 1 are \(M_{12} = 31\) and \(M_{13} = 1\); the actual \(\ddot{\mathbf q} = \ddot{\mathbf q}_d\) at t = 0 (zero error).

Full solution

The law. \(\mathbf Q = \mathbf M(\mathbf q)\big(\ddot{\mathbf q}_d + \mathbf K_v\dot{\mathbf E} + \mathbf K_p\mathbf E\big) + \mathbf C(\mathbf q,\dot{\mathbf q}) + \mathbf g(\mathbf q)\), with \(\mathbf K_p = 100\,\mathbf I\), \(\mathbf K_v = 20\,\mathbf I\), and \(\mathbf M,\mathbf C,\mathbf g\) from P9.2 re-evaluated at every step from the measured \(\mathbf q,\dot{\mathbf q}\). Closed loop: \(\ddot{\mathbf E} + 20\dot{\mathbf E} + 100\mathbf E = \mathbf 0\), three decoupled critically damped loops (slide 21). checked on random states

What is new compared with one joint. (1) \(\boldsymbol\alpha\) is a full matrix: the off-diagonal entries are the inertial coupling. (2) \(\mathbf C\) and \(\mathbf g\) change with the whole pose, not only with joint 1. (3) Cost: \(\mathbf M,\mathbf C,\mathbf g\) must be recomputed every update, which is why slides 23–25 move them to a slower outer loop. (4) All three torques must be applied together; joint 1 cannot be controlled alone.

Numbers. Row 1 of \((\mathbf M - \mathrm{diag}\mathbf M)\ddot{\mathbf q}\) is \(31(2.3562) + 1(-2.3562) = 30(2.3562) = 70.69\). Divide by \(\hat M_{11} = 103\): forcing \(= 0.6863\) rad/s², about 29% of the commanded \(\ddot q_{d,1}\) (2.36), which at \(k_p = 100\) leaves a tracking error of order \(0.6863/100 = 6.9\) mrad. checked

Common wrong answer: “\(\mathbf K_p,\mathbf K_v\) are diagonal, therefore \(\boldsymbol\alpha\) is”. Diagonal gains give decoupling only because \(\boldsymbol\alpha = \mathbf M\) is full.

P9.8 · Spot the error: three claims about computed torquespot the error

A study note says: (1) “Computed torque guarantees \(\ddot E + K_v\dot E + K_pE = 0\) for any robot.” (2) “Since \(K_p\) and \(K_v\) are diagonal, \(\alpha\) is diagonal.” (3) “\(f' = \ddot x_d + k_v\dot e + k_pe\) has units of force, so \(f = f' + \beta\).” Find the error in each and correct it.

Model answer

(1) It holds only if the model is exact (and the law runs continuously). With hats the right-hand side is the slide-28 term \(\hat{\mathbf M}^{-1}[\dots]\ne0\). “Guarantees” and “any” are the absolute words to distrust. (2) \(\boldsymbol\alpha = \mathbf M(\mathbf q)\) is a full matrix (slide 18); diagonal gains plus full \(\mathbf M\) are what give decoupled errors. (3) \(f'\) is an acceleration (m/s²); the law is \(f = \alpha f' + \beta\) with \(\alpha = m\) (kg), so \(\alpha f'\) is in newtons.

P9.9 · Force control: which option, and how big is the error?calculateexplain

A 2 kg end effector presses on a wall of stiffness \(k_e = 1000\) N/m with \(k_p = 100\) s⁻². An unknown disturbance of 5 N acts on it. Using the Option 2 law, find the steady-state force error. Then say which option you would use, and why.

Hint 1

\(x = mk_e^{-1}k_p\). Check it is dimensionless.

Hint 2

Option 2: \(E_{ss} = f_{dist}/(1 + x)\).

Full solution

\(mk_e^{-1} = 2/1000 = 0.002\) s². \(x = 0.002(100) = 0.2\). \(E_2 = 5/(1 + 0.2) = 4.17\) N; Option 1 would give \(5/0.2 = 25\) N. Use Option 2: it always has the smaller error (\(E_2/E_1 = x/(1+x)\)), and the gap is largest on a stiff wall (small \(x\)). Both still leave a steady error because \(f_{dist}\) is not cancelled; with this wall even Option 2 stays near \(f_{dist}\) unless \(k_p\) is raised greatly (to get 1% of 5 N you need \(k_p = 49\,500\) s⁻²). In implementation use \(f = m[k_e^{-1}k_pE - k_v\dot x] + f_d\) (slide 43) so that the force is never differentiated. checked

P9.10 · Cartesian control: Q from a tool forcecalculateexplain

A 2-link planar arm with \(l_1 = l_2 = 1\) m is at \(\mathbf q = (30^\circ, 60^\circ)\). The Cartesian controller commands the tool force \(\mathcal F = (3, -4)\) N. Find the joint torques, and explain in one line why slide 31’s joint-space route is costlier.

Hint 1

\(\mathbf Q = \mathbf J^\top\mathcal F\) with the position Jacobian of Section 5.

Hint 2

At this pose \(s_{12} = 1\), \(c_{12} = 0\).

Full solution

\(\mathbf J = \begin{bmatrix}-1.5&-1\\0.8660&0\end{bmatrix}\), \(\mathbf Q = \mathbf J^\top\mathcal F = (-1.5\cdot3 + 0.8660\cdot(-4),\ -1\cdot3 + 0) = (-7.9641,\ -3.0)\) N·m. Cross-check with moments: the tool is at (0.8660, 1.5) m, so \(xF_y - yF_x = 0.8660(-4) - 1.5(3) = -7.9641\) ✓. checked

Joint-space route: before any control can run, the whole Cartesian path needs \(\mathcal K^{-1}\) (inverse kinematics, possibly multi-valued and iterative), \(\mathbf J^{-1}\) and the derivative of \(\mathbf J^{-1}\) at every point (slide 31). The Cartesian route only needs forward kinematics and \(\mathbf J\) on the feedback side and one transpose to get torques.

P9.11 · Hybrid control: choose S and S′sketchexplaincalculate

A robot wipes a horizontal table, pressing with a constant 10 N. Use axes (x, y, z) with z vertical. Write S and S′ for the three translational directions, say which law feeds which, and compute \(\mathcal F\) when the position law outputs (12, −3, 9) N and the force law outputs (1, 2, 10) N. Sketch the controller diagram.

Hint 1

The table blocks motion along its normal, z. Sliding along x and y is free.

Full solution

Normal z is force-controlled; x, y are position-controlled: \(\mathbf S = \mathrm{diag}(1,1,0)\) (applied to the position law), \(\mathbf S' = \mathbf I - \mathbf S = \mathrm{diag}(0,0,1)\) (applied to the force law; complementary, inferred). Then

\[ \mathcal F = \mathbf S\begin{bmatrix}12\\-3\\9\end{bmatrix} + \mathbf S'\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\10\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}12\\-3\\0\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\10\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}12\\-3\\10\end{bmatrix}\ \text{N}. \]

The force law’s \(f_d\) is 10 N along z. Draw the slide-47 diagram: position law (\(\ddot x_d,\dot x_d,x_d\), feedback \(x\)) → S; force law (\(\mathcal F_d\), feedback \(\mathcal F_E\)) → S′; both into a sum → \(\mathcal F\) → arm; “constraints” into both S and S′. checked

P9.12 · Sketch and label the computed-torque diagramsketchexplain

Draw the MIMO computed-torque block diagram (slide 20). Mark which part linearises and which stabilises, and state what each feedback path carries.

Model answer

Blocks, left to right: inputs \(\ddot{\mathbf q}_d,\dot{\mathbf q}_d,\mathbf q_d\); servo = sum of \(\ddot{\mathbf q}_d\), \(\mathbf K_v\dot{\mathbf E}\), \(\mathbf K_p\mathbf E\) giving \(\mathbf Q'\); multiply by \(\mathbf M(\mathbf q)\); add \(\mathbf C(\mathbf q,\dot{\mathbf q}) + \mathbf g(\mathbf q) + \mathbf f(\dot{\mathbf q})\); output \(\mathbf Q\) into the manipulator, giving \(\mathbf q,\dot{\mathbf q}\). Two feedback paths: \(\mathbf q,\dot{\mathbf q}\) subtract from \(\mathbf q_d,\dot{\mathbf q}_d\) to form \(\mathbf E,\dot{\mathbf E}\) (servo); \(\mathbf q,\dot{\mathbf q}\) also feed the model blocks \(\mathbf M\), \(\mathbf C+\mathbf g+\mathbf f\). The model-based group (\(\mathbf M\) and the \(\mathbf C+\mathbf g+\mathbf f\) path) “linearises the system”; the servo group (\(\mathbf K_p,\mathbf K_v\) and the error loops) “stabilises the closed-loop system”. See the figure in Section 1.

Mini-quiz

Q1concept

In computed-torque control, what does the model-based part do and what does the servo part do?

Answer

The model-based part (\(\alpha\), \(\beta\)) cancels the non-linear dynamics so the system looks like \(\ddot q = q'\); the servo part (\(\ddot q_d + k_v\dot e + k_pe\)) makes that linear system stable and tracking (slide 49). The first linearises, the second stabilises.

Q2calculate

A single link has m = 1.5 kg, L = 0.4 m, no friction, and is at q = 60° with \(\ddot q_d = 0\), e = 0.1 rad, \(\dot e = 0\), \(k_p = 25\) s⁻², \(k_v = 10\) s⁻¹. Find the commanded torque.

Answer

\(\alpha = 1.5(0.16) = 0.24\) kg·m². \(\tau' = 0 + 0 + 25(0.1) = 2.5\) rad/s². \(\beta = 1.5(9.81)(0.4)\cos60^\circ = 2.943\) N·m. \(\tau = 0.24(2.5) + 2.943 = 3.543\) N·m. checked

Q3spot the error

A student writes the Option 2 steady-state force error as \(f_{dist}/(mk_e^{-1}k_p)\) and concludes that Option 2 gets better as the wall gets stiffer. What is wrong?

Answer

That is Option 1’s formula. Option 2 is \(f_{dist}/(1 + mk_e^{-1}k_p)\). For a stiffer wall (\(k_e\) larger) \(x = mk_e^{-1}k_p\) shrinks, so both errors grow; but Option 2 saturates at \(f_{dist}\) while Option 1 grows without bound. So Option 2 is the better option on a stiff wall, but its error does not improve as the wall stiffens.

Week 10 · Wheeled robots: kinematics

How fast must each wheel spin to move the robot like this?

A wheeled robot’s chassis moves with velocity (u, v, θ̇) in its own frame. Each wheel only cares about the velocity of its contact point along its driving direction. One formula, the generalised wheel model, turns that sentence into a row of a matrix. Stack one row per wheel and you have the robot’s kinematics.

Lecture: Wheeled Robots71 slides · practical sheet “Mobile robot kinematics”
Open in new tab ↗
How this is examined

Sample question 10 (W13 pp. 20–21) is practical Q1 word for word: the three-wheel omnidirectional robot. It is solved in full on the Sample Qs tab, with the generalised model the lecturer put on the next slide.

Where the marks are (indicative): each wheel’s position (Cx, Cy), drive angle β and roller angle γ written down; the generalised model quoted; one row per wheel; the stacked matrix; the inverse (or rank argument) and what it means (holonomic or not).

Where marks are lost: the sign of the Cy term (it is −θ̇ Cy in the x-row); using R(θ) where R⁻¹(θ) is needed; γ for a standard wheel (it is 0, and that wheel also cannot slide sideways); forgetting the no-slide equation, which is where non-holonomy comes from.

Practical (solved below)

Four questions: the omni triangle matrix (P10.1, = Sample Q10), simulating it in the inertial frame with d = 10 cm (P10.2, done by hand and in the widget), the differential drive’s instantaneous centre of rotation (P10.3), and the bicycle’s kinematics and holonomy (P10.4).

Intuition first

A wheel is a one-way street

A normal wheel rolls forwards and backwards but refuses to slide sideways. That refusal is a constraint on the chassis: it is why a car cannot parallel-park by moving sideways.

An omni wheel is a wheel made of wheels

Small rollers round the rim let it slide freely along one direction while it drives along another. So it constrains nothing: three of them can push the chassis in any direction.

Every point on a turning body circles one point

At each instant a planar rigid body rotates about its instantaneous centre of rotation (ICR). Every wheel axle that cannot slip must point at it, like spokes at a hub.

Holonomic = you can get anywhere, any way

A car can reach any parking spot, but not along any path: its velocity is restricted, not its position. That is a non-holonomic constraint. An omni robot has no such restriction.

Wheeled robots from abovedrawn to scale · grid 0.5 m · exact constant-twist path for the next 6 s
Try: differential drive with φ̇ = (4, 6) rad/s gives the ICR 0.75 m to the left, the same as P10.3. Set the two wheels equal: the ICR runs off to infinity (straight line). Set them opposite: the robot spins about its centre. Omni with φ̇ = (4, −1, −1): a circle of radius 0.5 m. Note that v ≠ 0 is possible only for the omni robot.

1 · Frames and the chassis velocity pp. 11–17

Derivation

Inertial frame {O}; chassis frame {C} at angle θ (anticlockwise from xO). The chassis velocity in its own axes is ζ = (u, v, θ̇): u forwards along xC, v sideways along yC (p.13). In {O} it is ν = (ẋ, ẏ, θ̇):

\[ \boldsymbol\nu=\begin{bmatrix}\dot x\\\dot y\\\dot\theta\end{bmatrix}=\mathbf J(\theta)\,\boldsymbol\zeta=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta&0\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\\\dot\theta\end{bmatrix},\qquad \boldsymbol\zeta=\mathbf J^{-1}(\theta)\boldsymbol\nu=\mathbf J^\top(\theta)\boldsymbol\nu \]

We command wheel speeds, not (u, v, θ̇), so the real relation is \(\boldsymbol\zeta=\mathbf W\dot{\boldsymbol\varphi}\) with W set by the wheel layout (p.17). Forward kinematics (wheels → motion) is for simulation; inverse (motion → wheels) is for control.

2 · Wheel types and pure rolling pp. 18–25

Picture

Five types (p.18): fixed standard (axle fixed to the chassis), steerable standard (axle turns about a vertical axis), castor (offset steering, passive), Swedish/omni (rollers on the rim), spherical (a ball). Only the two standard wheels impose a constraint on the chassis, because they cannot slide sideways. Castor, Swedish and spherical wheels impose none. Assumption throughout: pure rolling, no slip at the contact point (p.20).

Omni wheel in its own frame {W}: xW is the driving direction, yW the wheel-plane normal; the rollers let the contact slide freely along a direction at angle γ from yW (pp. 22–25). The contact velocity splits into a driven part and a free part:

\[ \begin{bmatrix}v_x\\v_y\end{bmatrix}=v_{drive}\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}+v_{free}\begin{bmatrix}-\sin\gamma\\\cos\gamma\end{bmatrix}\;\Rightarrow\;v_{drive}=v_x+v_y\tan\gamma,\qquad \dot\varphi=\frac{v_{drive}}{r}=\begin{bmatrix}\tfrac1r&\tfrac{\tan\gamma}{r}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}v_x\\v_y\end{bmatrix} \]

With rollers perpendicular to the drive direction, γ = 0 and \(\dot\varphi=v_x/r\): the wheel ignores the sideways component.

3 · The generalised wheel model pp. 26–36

Derivation (three steps)

Step 1 (p.28): the wheel frame is turned by βi from the chassis (β = angle from xC to the drive direction), so \({}^C\mathbf v_{W_i}=R(\beta_i)\,{}^{W_i}\mathbf v\).

Step 2 (p.30): the wheel sits at \(({}^Cx_{W_i},{}^Cy_{W_i})\) on a rigid chassis turning at θ̇, so its velocity is the chassis velocity plus \(\dot\theta\hat z\times\mathbf p\):

\[ {}^C\mathbf v_{W_i}=\begin{bmatrix}u-\dot\theta\,{}^Cy_{W_i}\\ v+\dot\theta\,{}^Cx_{W_i}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&-{}^Cy_{W_i}\\0&1&{}^Cx_{W_i}\end{bmatrix}\boldsymbol\zeta \]

Combine and pick out the drive component (p.36), adding R⁻¹(θ) to start from inertial velocities:

\[ \dot\varphi_i=\begin{bmatrix}\tfrac1{r_i}&\tfrac{\tan\gamma_i}{r_i}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\cos\beta_i&\sin\beta_i\\-\sin\beta_i&\cos\beta_i\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&0&-{}^Cy_{W_i}\\0&1&{}^Cx_{W_i}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta&0\\-\sin\theta&\cos\theta&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\dot x\\\dot y\\\dot\theta\end{bmatrix} \]

Read right to left: inertial → chassis; chassis twist → contact-point velocity; chassis axes → wheel axes; keep the driven component, divide by r. equals the contact velocity projected on the drive direction, checked

Standard wheels: two equations (slides 37–42, 68)

Fixed standard wheel: γ = 0, β constant. Steerable standard: γ = 0, β = β(t). Each gives a rolling equation (the model above) and a no-sliding equation (the axle component must vanish):

\[ r_i\dot\varphi_i=\big[\cos\beta_i\;\;\sin\beta_i\;\;-{}^Cy\cos\beta_i+{}^Cx\sin\beta_i\big]R^{-1}(\theta)\boldsymbol\nu,\qquad 0=\big[-\sin\beta_i\;\;\cos\beta_i\;\;{}^Cy\sin\beta_i+{}^Cx\cos\beta_i\big]R^{-1}(\theta)\boldsymbol\nu \]

both rows checked against the model and the rigid-body contact velocity The no-sliding rows are the non-holonomic constraints (p.68).

Exam recipe (any wheeled robot)
  1. Draw {C}. For each wheel write Cx, Cy, β (angle of the drive direction from xC), γ, r. Say which way positive φ̇ drives.
  2. Write one row per wheel: \(r\dot\varphi_i=\cos\beta_i(u-\dot\theta\,{}^Cy)+\sin\beta_i(v+\dot\theta\,{}^Cx)\) (γ = 0).
  3. For standard wheels add the no-slide row. It usually forces v = 0.
  4. Stack the rows: \(\dot{\boldsymbol\varphi}=\mathbf W^{-1}\boldsymbol\zeta\). Invert (or pseudo-invert) for \(\boldsymbol\zeta=\mathbf W\dot{\boldsymbol\varphi}\).
  5. Multiply by J(θ) for inertial velocities. Check a simple motion (straight ahead; spin on the spot).

4 · Differential drive and skid-steer pp. 43–52

Derivation

Two fixed standard wheels at (0, ±a), radius r, β = 0, γ = 0 (p.44). Rolling rows: \(\dot\varphi_1=(u-a\dot\theta)/r\) (left, +a) and \(\dot\varphi_2=(u+a\dot\theta)/r\) (right, −a). No-slide: v = 0. Inverting (p.47):

\[ \begin{bmatrix}u\\v\\\dot\theta\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\tfrac r2&\tfrac r2\\0&0\\-\tfrac{r}{2a}&\tfrac{r}{2a}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\dot\varphi_1\\\dot\varphi_2\end{bmatrix} \]

Skid-steer, 4 standard wheels at (±b, ±a) (pp. 49–52): the rows are (1/r)[1, 0, −a] for the left pair and (1/r)[1, 0, +a] for the right pair. b drops out. The slide’s 3×4 inverse \(u=\tfrac r4\sum\dot\varphi_i\), \(\dot\theta=\tfrac{r}{4a}(-\dot\varphi_1-\dot\varphi_2+\dot\varphi_3+\dot\varphi_4)\) is the least-squares (pseudo-) inverse checked. Note that a real skid-steer must slip to turn at all, which the pure-rolling model ignores.

Worked example

r = 0.05 m, a = 0.15 m, \(\dot\varphi\) = (4, 6) rad/s: u = 0.05(10)/2 = 0.25 m/s, θ̇ = 0.05(2)/0.3 = 0.3333 rad/s. ICR at y = u/θ̇ = 0.75 m to the left. checked

5 · Omnidirectional robots pp. 53–55

Three Swedish wheels at the corners of an equilateral triangle (centre-to-wheel d), drive directions tangential, rollers perpendicular (γ = 0). With the drive directions taken clockwise (β = 0°, −120°, +120°) the rows give

\[ \dot{\boldsymbol\varphi}=\frac1r\begin{bmatrix}1&0&-d\\-\tfrac12&-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2&-d\\-\tfrac12&\tfrac{\sqrt3}2&-d\end{bmatrix}\boldsymbol\zeta,\qquad \boldsymbol\zeta=\frac r3\begin{bmatrix}2&-1&-1\\0&-\sqrt3&\sqrt3\\-\tfrac1d&-\tfrac1d&-\tfrac1d\end{bmatrix}\dot{\boldsymbol\varphi} \]

The matrix is invertible (det = 3√3d/2), so any (u, v, θ̇) is possible: holonomic. Full derivation: Sample Q10. The four-wheel Swedish layout (p.55) works the same way with 45° rollers (tan γ ≠ 0). checked

6 · Tricycle, car, Ackermann, bicycle pp. 56–61, 69

Derivation

Tricycle (pp. 56–58): front wheel W1 at (b, 0), driven and steered (β1(t)); rear wheels fixed and passive. If the rear axle passes through C (the slide assumes this without saying it), the rear no-slide rows force v = 0. Step 2 gives the front contact velocity (u, bθ̇), and step 1 says it equals \(r\dot\varphi_1(\cos\beta_1,\sin\beta_1)\):

\[ \dot\varphi_1=\frac1r\sqrt{u^2+b^2\dot\theta^2},\qquad \beta_1=\operatorname{atan2}(b\dot\theta,\;u) \]

Ackermann steering (p.61): the two front wheels are steered by different amounts so that every axle line passes through one ICR on the rear axle’s line, so no wheel scrubs. Geometry added: \(\cot\beta_{out}-\cot\beta_{in}=\text{track}/\text{wheelbase}\). Example: wheelbase 2.5 m, track 1.5 m, turn radius 6 m about the rear-axle midpoint: inner 25.463°, outer 20.323°. checked

Bicycle (practical Q4, slide 69): rear wheel fixed at C, driven; front wheel at (L, 0), steered by β, not driven. Rear no-slide: v = 0. Front no-slide: \(-u\sin\beta+L\dot\theta\cos\beta=0\), so

\[ \dot\theta=\frac{u\tan\beta}{L},\qquad \text{turning radius } R=\frac{L}{\tan\beta} \]

checked Steering jammed straight (β = 0): θ̇ = 0 and v = 0, so it can only roll forwards or backwards.

7 · Manoeuvrability; holonomic vs non-holonomic pp. 62–68

Definitions

Degree of manoeuvrability δM = δm + δs (p.63). The slide’s informal wording: δm (mobility) ≈ how many directions the chassis can be driven in directly; δs (steerability) ≈ how many independent steering angles. A precise version added: Siegwart et al. ch. 3: stack the no-slide rows of all standard wheels into C1; then \(\delta_m=3-\operatorname{rank}C_1\) and \(\delta_s=\operatorname{rank}C_{1s}\) (the steered wheels’ rows). It reproduces all four slide examples (p.64):

RobotδmδsδM
2 fixed wheels on one axle + castor (differential drive)202
2 fixed + 1 steered standard (tricycle / car-like)112
2 steered standard + 1 Swedish123
3 Swedish (omni triangle)303

rank computation checked for each row

Holonomic constraint (p.66): an equation in positions only, f(x, y, θ, …) = 0. Non-holonomic (p.67): involves velocities and cannot be integrated into a position-only equation. The no-sliding condition of a standard wheel, \(-\dot x\sin\theta+\dot y\cos\theta=0\) for a differential drive, is the classic example. It forbids sideways velocity at every instant but not any final position: parallel parking is possible, just not directly. Holonomic robot: no non-holonomic constraints, so δM = δm = 3 (the omni triangle).

Explain-type marks: “is the bicycle holonomic?” No. Its rear no-slide constraint restricts velocity, not position, and cannot be integrated, yet the bicycle can still reach any (x, y, θ) by manoeuvring. Name the constraint equation, say “velocity, not integrable”, and give the consequence.

Guided problems: solve on paper first

P10.1 · Omni triangle (practical Q1 = Sample Q10)derive

Derive the relation between \(\dot\varphi_1,\dot\varphi_2,\dot\varphi_3\) and (u, v, θ̇) for the three-omni-wheel robot (centre-to-vertex d, rollers ⊥ drive).

Hint 1

Wheels at (0, d), (√3d/2, −d/2), (−√3d/2, −d/2). Pick each drive direction tangential and write its β.

Hint 2

γ = 0, so \(r\dot\varphi_i=\cos\beta_i(u-\dot\theta y_i)+\sin\beta_i(v+\dot\theta x_i)\).

Full solution

See section 5 and Sample Q10 for the full model answer. Row 1 (β = 0): \(r\dot\varphi_1=u-d\dot\theta\). Rows 2 and 3 follow with β = ∓120°. checked

P10.2 · Where does it go? (practical Q2)calculatesketch

d = 0.10 m, r = 0.05 m, constant \(\dot{\boldsymbol\varphi}\) = (4, −1, −1) rad/s, starting at the origin with θ = 0. Find (u, v, θ̇), describe the path, and give the pose after 2 s.

Hint 1

Use the inverse matrix of section 5.

Hint 2

Constant (u, v, θ̇) means a circle about the ICR, which is at \((-v/\dot\theta,\;u/\dot\theta)\) in the chassis frame.

Full solution

u = (0.05/3)(8 + 1 + 1) = 0.1667 m/s; v = (0.05/√3)(−1 + 1) = 0; θ̇ = −(0.05/0.3)(4 − 1 − 1) = −0.3333 rad/s. ICR at (0, u/θ̇) = (0, −0.5) m: a clockwise circle of radius 0.5 m. After 2 s, θ = −0.6667 rad, x = R sin|θ| = 0.5 sin 0.6667 = 0.3092 m, y = −0.5(1 − cos 0.6667) = −0.1071 m. Euler integration with dt = 0.01 s lands within 0.55 mm of this. checked

P10.3 · ICR of a differential drive (practical Q3)derivecalculate

Derive the position of the ICR for wheel speeds \(\dot\varphi_1\) (left, at +a) and \(\dot\varphi_2\) (right, at −a). Evaluate for a = 0.3 m, \(\dot\varphi\) = (2, 5) rad/s.

Hint

The ICR is the chassis point with zero velocity: \(u-\dot\theta y=0\), v = 0 → on the axle at y = u/θ̇.

Full solution

\(y_{ICR}=\dfrac{u}{\dot\theta}=\dfrac{r(\dot\varphi_1+\dot\varphi_2)/2}{r(\dot\varphi_2-\dot\varphi_1)/(2a)}=a\dfrac{\dot\varphi_1+\dot\varphi_2}{\dot\varphi_2-\dot\varphi_1}\), on the axle (x = 0). Equal speeds: at infinity (straight). Opposite speeds: at the centre (spin). Here 0.3 × 7/3 = 0.7 m. r cancels. checked

P10.4 · Bicycle (practical Q4)deriveexplain

Rear wheel fixed and driven, front wheel steered and not driven, wheelbase L. Derive the kinematics. Is it holonomic? Evaluate θ̇ for u = 2 m/s, β = 20°, L = 1.2 m.

Full solution

Rear rolling: \(r\dot\varphi_r=u\). Rear no-slide: v = 0. Front no-slide (β, at (L, 0)): \(-u\sin\beta+L\dot\theta\cos\beta=0\Rightarrow\dot\theta=u\tan\beta/L\). In {O}: \(\dot x=u\cos\theta\), \(\dot y=u\sin\theta\), \(\dot\theta=u\tan\beta/L\). Non-holonomic: \(-\dot x\sin\theta+\dot y\cos\theta=0\) restricts velocity only and cannot be integrated. Numbers: 2 tan 20°/1.2 = 0.6066 rad/s, turning radius 3.297 m. checked

P10.5 · Tricycle wheel commandcalculate

A tricycle with the front wheel at b = 0.6 m (r = 0.1 m) must move at u = 0.4 m/s while turning at θ̇ = 0.5 rad/s. Find \(\dot\varphi_1\) and β1.

Full solution

Contact velocity (0.4, 0.6 × 0.5) = (0.4, 0.3) m/s, magnitude 0.5 m/s, so \(\dot\varphi_1\) = 0.5/0.1 = 5 rad/s and β1 = atan2(0.3, 0.4) = 36.870°. checked

P10.6 · Spot the errorspot the error

“For a differential drive, \(\dot\varphi_1=(u+a\dot\theta)/r\) for the left wheel at y = +a; and since both wheels are standard, v can be any value.”

Answer

The left wheel’s contact velocity is \(u-\dot\theta\,y=u-a\dot\theta\): turning left (θ̇ > 0) slows the inner (left) wheel. And the no-slide constraint of the fixed wheels forces v = 0: a standard wheel cannot slide sideways.

Mini-quiz

Q1concept

Which wheel types constrain the chassis motion?

Answer

Only standard wheels (fixed and steerable), which cannot slide sideways. Castor, Swedish and spherical wheels impose no constraint.

Q2calculate

Differential drive, r = 0.1 m, a = 0.2 m, \(\dot\varphi\) = (−5, 5) rad/s. u and θ̇?

Answer

u = 0; θ̇ = 0.1(10)/0.4 = 2.5 rad/s: a spin on the spot about C.

Q3concept

What does δM = 3 mean for the omni triangle?

Answer

All three chassis velocities (u, v, θ̇) can be set directly and independently: the robot is holonomic and omnidirectional.

Week 11 · Wheeled robot dynamics

What force and torque on the wheels produce which motion of the chassis?

Week 10 told you which chassis velocity a given wheel motion produces. Dynamics asks the reverse of cause and effect: which forces and torques accelerate the chassis. The deck applies Newton–Euler to one rigid planar body, packs the result into \(\mathbf M\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}+c(\boldsymbol\zeta)={}^C\mathbf Q\), and shows how wheel forces build \({}^C\mathbf Q\). This tab rebuilds every line, fixes two slips in the slides (pp. 24–25 and p. 34), and ends with a simulator you drive with wheel torques.

Lecture: Wheeled Robots Dynamics40 slides · Dr KM Digumarti · no practical sheet this week

How this is examined

No W11 question appears among the W13 sample questions. The two nearest are Question 4, “Derive the equations of motion” (W13 p.8, mass, moments of inertia and centre-of-mass positions given), and Question 10, a three-omni-wheel robot (W13 p.20) answered with the W10 wheel model (W13 p.21). W11 is the mobile-robot version of Q4, and its wheel-force step is the transpose of Q10’s kinematic map. Treat a “derive and use \(\mathbf M\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}+c=\mathbf Q\)” question as plausible, not promised.

Where the marks would be (indicative; marks not published): a free-body picture with frames {O}, {C}, {G}; the force and moment balance with the moment-transfer term; the acceleration of G with the \(u\dot\theta\), \(v\dot\theta\) terms; the matrix form with M, c and Q named; the wheel-force matrix \(\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&0\\-a&a\end{bmatrix}\); a one-line check (units, or \(c=0\) at rest).

Where marks are lost: \(v\dot\theta\) written where \(u\dot\theta\) belongs (the slides do it, see section 4); \(\mathbf J\) used where \(\mathbf J^\top\) is needed in \({}^C\mathbf Q=\mathbf J^\top\,{}^O\mathbf Q\); the parallel-axis term \(m(x_G^2+y_G^2)\) forgotten in the third diagonal entry; the sign of the moment-transfer term; mixing chassis-frame and inertial-frame quantities in one equation. The deck has no control content (no look-ahead point, no tracking law); that sits in W8–W9.

Practical (optional, no coding in the exam)

There is no instructor notebook or practical sheet for Week 11 in the course files, so nothing here has saved output. The nearest instructor code is the Week-12 helper diffdrive.py (wheel radius 0.1 m, wheel base 0.5 m). It is kinematic, not dynamic, and it has bugs: it moves along \(\cos/\sin(\omega\,\mathrm{d}t)\) instead of the heading \(\theta\), and it overwrites its angular_velocity argument. Do not copy it as a model answer. The simulator in this tab is the dynamic counterpart.

Intuition first

Dynamics is the cause, kinematics the effect

W10 answered “if the chassis moves like this, how fast must each wheel turn?” W11 answers “how hard must the wheels push to make it move like this?” Like a shopping trolley: speed tells you where it goes, but only a push changes the speed.

One push, one twist

A rigid body obeys two laws: net force \(=m\times\)acceleration of the centre of mass, net torque \(=I\times\)angular acceleration. These are the same Newton and Euler equations as for an arm link in W7 (W7 p.34), now for one body in a plane.

Turning at constant speed still accelerates you

In a car on a bend you are pushed outward even at a steady 60 km/h. Your speed along the car’s nose is constant, but the nose direction keeps rotating, so the velocity vector changes. That is the \(u\dot\theta\) term: a sideways acceleration with no sideways speed.

Add up pushes with lever arms

Each wheel pushes forward at a distance from the axle midpoint. Sum the pushes for the net force. Sum push \(\times\) lever arm for the net twist. That sum is a matrix, and it is the transpose of the W10 wheel-speed matrix, because the power must be the same either way.

Wheels grip sideways like skate blades

A skate glides forward but resists sideways motion. That side grip is what bends the path into a circle. The slide-37 matrix lists only the forward pushes; the sideways force is a reaction that the no-slip rule supplies.
