1 · The dynamics problem: forward and inverse pp. 9–11

Picture

Kinematics (W10) relates motions. Dynamics relates a motion to the forces and torques that cause it. For a planar robot the pose is \(\boldsymbol\xi=(x,y,\theta)^\top\) in the inertial frame, and the net force and torque on it, also in the inertial frame, are \(\mathbf Q=(f_x,f_y,\tau_z)^\top\) (p.9).

Derivation \[ \mathbf Q = f(\boldsymbol\xi,\dot{\boldsymbol\xi},\ddot{\boldsymbol\xi}) \]

Forward dynamics (p.10): given \(\mathbf Q\), find the trajectory \((\boldsymbol\xi,\dot{\boldsymbol\xi},\ddot{\boldsymbol\xi})\). Use: simulation and analysis. Inverse dynamics (p.11): given a desired trajectory, find the \(\mathbf Q\) needed. Use: control.

Both use the same equation. Forward solves for the acceleration and integrates; inverse evaluates the right-hand side along a known path.

Exam recipe
  1. Read which quantities are given. Forces or torques given and motion wanted: forward (integrate).
  2. Motion given and forces wanted: inverse (substitute, no integration).
  3. Name the frame of every vector: \(\mathbf Q\) in {O} is \({}^O\mathbf Q\); in the chassis it is \({}^C\mathbf Q\).
  4. Sanity check with a straight line: \(f=m\ddot x\).
Worked example

A 10 kg robot moves along x. Forward: \(f_x=10\) N gives \(\ddot x=f_x/m=1\) m/s². Inverse: a required path \(x=\tfrac12t^2\) has \(\ddot x=1\) m/s², so \(f_x=m\ddot x=10\) N.

Typical one-line question: “Is simulating the robot from known wheel torques forward or inverse dynamics?” (forward). “Which does a controller use to compute feed-forward torque?” (inverse). Beware the trap “inverse dynamics gives the trajectory”.

2 · Frames, symbols, and the W10 recap pp. 4–6, p. 12

Picture

Three frames (p.12): {O} fixed to the world (inertial); {C} attached to the chassis at a convenient reference point; {G} at the centre of mass, with the same orientation as {C} but a different origin. The chassis has mass \(m\) and a moment of inertia \({}^G I\) about the vertical axis through G. In {C}, G sits at \(({}^Cx_G,{}^Cy_G)\); in {C} the chassis velocity is \(\boldsymbol\zeta=(u,v,\dot\theta)^\top\), with \(u\) along \(\hat x_C\) and \(v\) along \(\hat y_C\).

Derivation: the W10 wheel model, recapped

The generalised wheel model (p.6) gives the angular velocity \(\dot\varphi_i\) of wheel \(i\) from the chassis velocity:

\[ \dot\varphi_i=\begin{bmatrix}\tfrac1{r_i}&\tfrac{\tan\gamma_i}{r_i}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\cos\beta_i&\sin\beta_i\\-\sin\beta_i&\cos\beta_i\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&0&-{}^Cy_{W_i}\\0&1&{}^Cx_{W_i}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta&0\\-\sin\theta&\cos\theta&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\dot x\\\dot y\\\dot\theta\end{bmatrix} \]

\(r_i\): wheel radius (m). \(\gamma_i\): angle between the free-roll velocity and the normal to the wheel plane. \(\beta_i\): angle between the drive velocity and the chassis. \(({}^Cx_{W_i},{}^Cy_{W_i})\): wheel position in {C} (m). \(\theta\): chassis orientation (rad). The last 3×3 matrix is \(\mathbf J^{-1}=\mathbf J^\top\): it turns the global \((\dot x,\dot y,\dot\theta)\) into the chassis-frame \(\boldsymbol\zeta=(u,v,\dot\theta)\). The dynamics below works with \(\boldsymbol\zeta\).

For a standard fixed wheel at \((0,y_W)\) pointing forward (\(\gamma=0,\beta=0\)) this reduces to \(\dot\varphi=(u-y_W\dot\theta)/r\). added

Exam recipe
  1. Sketch {O}, {C}, {G}; mark \(\theta\) from \(\hat x_O\) to \(\hat x_C\), anticlockwise positive.
  2. Write \(\boldsymbol\xi\) (global pose) and \(\boldsymbol\zeta\) (chassis velocity) separately and say which frame each is in.
  3. State the link \(\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}=\mathbf J(\boldsymbol\xi)\boldsymbol\zeta\) with \(\mathbf J\) the rotation about z by \(\theta\) (p.30).
  4. Check \(\mathbf J^{-1}=\mathbf J^\top\) for a rotation.
Worked example

A differential drive: \(r=0.1\) m, wheels at \(y_W=\pm a=\pm0.2\) m (left is \(+y\)). At \(u=1\) m/s, \(\dot\theta=1.6\) rad/s: left \(\dot\varphi_L=(1-0.2\cdot1.6)/0.1=6.8\) rad/s, right \(\dot\varphi_R=(1+0.2\cdot1.6)/0.1=13.2\) rad/s. checked

The recap is the bridge: expect a question that first asks for the wheel speeds (W10 formula) and then for the wheel forces (this week). Keep \(\boldsymbol\xi\) (global) and \(\boldsymbol\zeta\) (chassis) separate: the single most common error is mixing them.

3 · Newton–Euler balance on the chassis pp. 14–17

Picture

Two sets of loads act on the chassis. The applied loads from the wheels, drawn at C: a force \(({}^Cf_x,{}^Cf_y)\) and a torque \({}^Cn_z\). The inertial loads at G: a force \(({}^CF_x,{}^CF_y)=m\,{}^C\ddot{\mathbf P}_G\) and a torque \({}^CN_z\). Newton–Euler says they balance. The twist: the applied force acts at C but the inertial force acts at G, so moving one to the other creates a moment.

Derivation

All terms are in {C} (p.15). Force balance:

\[ {}^C\mathbf F_G-{}^C\mathbf f_C=0\;\Rightarrow\;{}^CF_x={}^Cf_x,\quad {}^CF_y={}^Cf_y \]

Moment balance about G. The applied force acts at C, which is the vector \(-{}^C\mathbf P_{CG}\) from G, so it contributes the moment \((-{}^C\mathbf P_{CG})\times{}^C\mathbf f_C\):

\[ {}^CN_G-{}^Cn_C-(-{}^C\mathbf P_{CG})\times{}^C\mathbf f_C=0\;\Rightarrow\;{}^CN_z={}^Cn_z+\big({}^Cy_{CG}\,{}^Cf_x-{}^Cx_{CG}\,{}^Cf_y\big) \]

The z-component of \((-x,-y,0)\times(f_x,f_y,0)\) is \(-xf_y+yf_x\), which is the bracket. checked The slides write \({}^C\mathbf P_{CG}\) on p.15 and \({}^C\mathbf P_G\) later; they are the same vector (C to G, in {C}).

The inertial loads (p.17) come from Newton and Euler (the same laws as W7 p.34):

\[ {}^C\mathbf F_G=m\,{}^C\dot{\boldsymbol\upsilon}_G\;(F_x=m\,{}^C\ddot x_G,\;F_y=m\,{}^C\ddot y_G),\qquad {}^C\mathbf N_G={}^G\mathbf I\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}+\boldsymbol\omega\times{}^G\mathbf I\boldsymbol\omega\;\Rightarrow\;{}^CN_z={}^GI\,\ddot\theta \]

In planar motion \(\boldsymbol\omega\) is along z and so is \({}^G\mathbf I\boldsymbol\omega\), so the \(\boldsymbol\omega\times{}^G\mathbf I\boldsymbol\omega\) term vanishes. The slide’s handwritten note: \(m\) and \({}^GI\) are known; \(\ddot x_G,\ddot y_G,\ddot\theta\) are the unknowns. The one missing piece is the acceleration of G.

Exam recipe
  1. Draw applied loads at C and inertial loads at G, all in {C}.
  2. Write \(F_x=f_x\), \(F_y=f_y\).
  3. Write the moment about G, remembering the lever arm \(-\mathbf P_{CG}\) for the applied force.
  4. Replace the inertial loads by \(m\,\ddot{\mathbf P}_G\) and \({}^GI\ddot\theta\).
  5. Sanity check: if C = G the lever arm is zero and \({}^Cn_z={}^GI\ddot\theta\).
Worked example

G is 0.05 m ahead of C (\(x_G=0.05\), \(y_G=0\) m). Applied \({}^Cf=(10,4)\) N and \({}^Cn_z=0.4\) N·m. Moment about G: \({}^CN_z=0.4+(0\cdot10-0.05\cdot4)=0.2\) N·m. The sideways push 0.05 m ahead of G produces a clockwise moment about G that reduces the net twist. checked

Calculation or sketch. Marks go to the free-body figure and to the moment-transfer sign. A common slip is to treat the applied torque as acting about G without the \(y f_x-x f_y\) term.

4 · The acceleration of the centre of mass in a rotating frame pp. 19–24

Picture

The chassis frame turns with the robot, so the unit vectors \(\hat x_C,\hat y_C\) rotate at \(\dot\theta\): \(\dot{\hat x}=\dot\theta\,\hat y\) and \(\dot{\hat y}=-\dot\theta\,\hat x\). A velocity written as \(u\hat x+v\hat y\) therefore changes even when \(u\) and \(v\) do not. The \(u\hat x\) part swings towards \(+\hat y\); the \(v\hat y\) part swings towards \(-\hat x\).

Derivation (the slides, then an independent check)

Position of G in {O} (p.19): \({}^O\mathbf P_G={}^O\mathbf P_C+{}^O\mathbf R_C\,{}^C\mathbf P_G\). G is fixed in the chassis, so \({}^C\dot{\mathbf P}_G=0\) and \({}^O\dot{\mathbf R}_C\,\mathbf p={}^O\boldsymbol\omega_C\times{}^O\mathbf R_C\,\mathbf p\). Rotating the result into {C} (p.20):

\[ {}^O\dot{\mathbf P}_G={}^O\mathbf R_C\big[{}^C\dot{\mathbf P}_C+{}^C\boldsymbol\omega_C\times{}^C\mathbf P_G\big] \]

Differentiate once more with the product rule (p.22). The term \({}^C\boldsymbol\omega_C\times{}^C\dot{\mathbf P}_G\) is zero, and the derivative of \({}^O\mathbf R_C\) again produces \(\boldsymbol\omega\times\). Rotating into {C}:

\[ {}^C\ddot{\mathbf P}_G={}^C\ddot{\mathbf P}_C+{}^C\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}_C\times{}^C\mathbf P_{CG}+{}^C\boldsymbol\omega_C\times{}^C\dot{\mathbf P}_C+{}^C\boldsymbol\omega_C\times{}^C\boldsymbol\omega_C\times{}^C\mathbf P_G \]

Here \({}^C\dot{\mathbf P}_C=(u,v,0)\) and \({}^C\ddot{\mathbf P}_C=(\dot u,\dot v,0)\) are just the rates of change of the components. The turning of the frame is carried by the \(\boldsymbol\omega\times\) terms. Insert \(\boldsymbol\omega=(0,0,\dot\theta)\), \(\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}=(0,0,\ddot\theta)\), \({}^C\mathbf P_G=(x_G,y_G,0)\) (p.24), using \((0,0,k)\times(a,b,0)=(-kb,\,ka,\,0)\):

\[ \dot{\boldsymbol\omega}\times\mathbf P_G=\ddot\theta\begin{bmatrix}-y_G\\x_G\\0\end{bmatrix},\quad \boldsymbol\omega\times\dot{\mathbf P}_C=\dot\theta\begin{bmatrix}-v\\u\\0\end{bmatrix},\quad \boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf P_G=\dot\theta^2\begin{bmatrix}-x_G\\-y_G\\0\end{bmatrix} \] \[ {}^C\ddot x_G=\dot u-{}^Cy_G\ddot\theta-v\dot\theta-{}^Cx_G\dot\theta^2,\qquad {}^C\ddot y_G=\dot v+{}^Cx_G\ddot\theta+\boxed{u}\,\dot\theta-{}^Cy_G\dot\theta^2 \]

Cross-check with unit vectors alone: \(\mathbf v_C=u\hat x+v\hat y\), so \(\mathbf a_C=\dot u\hat x+\dot v\hat y+u\dot\theta\hat y-v\dot\theta\hat x=(\dot u-v\dot\theta)\hat x+(\dot v+u\dot\theta)\hat y\). checked symbolically (checks/w11.py derives the full G acceleration from \(\mathbf R(\theta(t))\))

Slides vs derivation

Pages 24 and 25 print \(+v\dot\theta\) in the y-acceleration (\({}^C\ddot y_G=\dot v+{}^Cx_G\ddot\theta+v\dot\theta-{}^Cy_G\dot\theta^2\), and the matching \({}^CF_y\), \({}^Cf_y\)). The correct term is \(+u\dot\theta\). Three independent reasons: (1) the cross product on p.24 itself, \((0,0,\dot\theta)\times(u,v,0)=(-v\dot\theta,\,u\dot\theta,\,0)\), has \(u\dot\theta\) in y; (2) the p.26 matrix already uses \(u\) (row 2 \(m\dot\theta(u-{}^Cy_G\dot\theta)\), row 3 \(m\dot\theta({}^Cx_Gu+{}^Cy_Gv)\)), and the printed p.25 form does not reproduce it (checked symbolically); (3) physics: constant \(u\) on a circle with \(v=0\) needs the centripetal acceleration \(u\dot\theta\) in y, and the printed form gives zero. The x-equation (\(-v\dot\theta\)) is right. Write \(u\dot\theta\) in the exam. checked

Exam recipe
  1. Write \({}^C\ddot{\mathbf P}_G\) as the four-term sum (acceleration of C components, \(\dot\omega\times P\), \(\omega\times\dot P_C\), \(\omega\times\omega\times P\)).
  2. Substitute the vectors; evaluate each cross product with \((0,0,k)\times(a,b,0)=(-kb,ka,0)\).
  3. Collect x and y. Memorise the pattern: x gets \(-v\dot\theta\), y gets \(+u\dot\theta\) (the velocity components swap and the sign flips on the first).
  4. Check: if C = G and \(\ddot\theta=0\), \(\dot u=\dot v=0\), the acceleration is \(\dot\theta\,(-v,u)\), perpendicular to the velocity.
Worked example

C = G, \(u=2\) m/s, \(v=0\), \(\dot\theta=0.5\) rad/s, everything else zero. Then \({}^C\ddot x_G=0\), \({}^C\ddot y_G=u\dot\theta=1.0\) m/s², so a 10 kg chassis needs \({}^Cf_y=10\) N sideways. With G 0.05 m ahead of C the x-equation adds \(-x_G\dot\theta^2=-0.0125\) m/s². checked

A calculation or derivation question, and a spot-the-error one: this is where the printed slide is wrong, so a marker comparing against the slide may expect \(v\dot\theta\). Show the cross-product line so your \(u\dot\theta\) is justified.

5 · Equations of motion in matrix form: \(\mathbf M\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}+c(\boldsymbol\zeta)={}^C\mathbf Q\) pp. 25–27

Picture

Rearranged as “mass times acceleration, plus velocity terms, equals the applied load”: the same shape as an arm’s \(\mathbf M(\mathbf q)\ddot{\mathbf q}+\dots=\boldsymbol\tau\) from W7. \(\mathbf M\) carries mass and geometry. \(c(\boldsymbol\zeta)\) carries the velocity-dependent (centripetal and Coriolis) terms that exist because the frame rotates. \({}^C\mathbf Q\) is what the wheels apply.

Derivation

Equate applied to inertial loads (p.25, with the corrected \(u\dot\theta\)):

\[ {}^Cf_x=m\big(\dot u-{}^Cy_G\ddot\theta-v\dot\theta-{}^Cx_G\dot\theta^2\big),\qquad {}^Cf_y=m\big(\dot v+{}^Cx_G\ddot\theta+u\dot\theta-{}^Cy_G\dot\theta^2\big) \] \[ {}^Cn_z={}^CN_z-\big({}^Cy_G\,{}^Cf_x-{}^Cx_G\,{}^Cf_y\big)={}^GI\ddot\theta-\big({}^Cy_G\,{}^Cf_x-{}^Cx_G\,{}^Cf_y\big) \]

Substitute \(f_x,f_y\) into the moment equation. The coefficient of \(\ddot\theta\) is \({}^GI+m({}^Cx_G^2+{}^Cy_G^2)\). Collect the terms in \(\dot u,\dot v,\ddot\theta\) (p.26):

\[ \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}m&0&-m\,{}^Cy_G\\0&m&m\,{}^Cx_G\\-m\,{}^Cy_G&m\,{}^Cx_G&{}^GI+m({}^Cx_G^2+{}^Cy_G^2)\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf M}\begin{bmatrix}\dot u\\\dot v\\\ddot\theta\end{bmatrix}+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-m\dot\theta\,(v+{}^Cx_G\dot\theta)\\m\dot\theta\,(u-{}^Cy_G\dot\theta)\\m\dot\theta\,({}^Cx_G\,u+{}^Cy_G\,v)\end{bmatrix}}_{c(\boldsymbol\zeta)}=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}{}^Cf_x\\{}^Cf_y\\{}^Cn_z\end{bmatrix}}_{{}^C\mathbf Q} \]

checked symbolically Reading the pieces. \(\mathbf M\) is constant and symmetric; its lower-right entry is the inertia about C by the parallel-axis theorem. \(c\) is zero when \(\boldsymbol\zeta=0\), so at rest \(\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}=\mathbf M^{-1}\,{}^C\mathbf Q\). Everything is written in {C} (the boxed note on p.26). Homework on p.27: derive the same equations with Lagrange’s method. The result must match, since both describe the same body. added (the Lagrange route is not worked in the deck)

Special case C = G (\({}^Cx_G={}^Cy_G=0\)): \(\mathbf M=\mathrm{diag}(m,m,{}^GI)\) and \(c=(-mv\dot\theta,\;mu\dot\theta,\;0)^\top\). The diagonal \(\mathbf M\) means no coupling between force and torque. added

Exam recipe
  1. Start from the two component equations and the moment equation.
  2. Substitute \(f_x,f_y\) into \(n_z\) before collecting terms.
  3. Read \(\mathbf M\) from the coefficients of \(\dot u,\dot v,\ddot\theta\), and \(c\) from everything left (velocity terms).
  4. Check: \(\mathbf M\) symmetric; \(\mathbf M_{33}=I_G+m(x_G^2+y_G^2)\); \(c=0\) at rest.
  5. To find accelerations: \(\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}=\mathbf M^{-1}({}^C\mathbf Q-c)\).
Worked example: off-centre COM

\(m=10\) kg, \({}^GI=0.25\) kg·m², G is 0.05 m ahead of C (\(x_G=0.05\), \(y_G=0\) m). At rest (\(c=0\)) the wheels apply \({}^Cf=(10,0)\) N and \({}^Cn_z=0.4\) N·m. Inertia about C: \(0.25+10(0.05)^2=0.275\) kg·m². The equations:

\[ \begin{bmatrix}10&0&0\\0&10&0.5\\0&0.5&0.275\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\dot u\\\dot v\\\ddot\theta\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}10\\0\\0.4\end{bmatrix} \]

Row 1: \(\dot u=1.0\) m/s². Row 2: \(\dot v=-0.05\,\ddot\theta\). Row 3: \(0.5(-0.05\ddot\theta)+0.275\ddot\theta=0.25\ddot\theta=0.4\), so \(\ddot\theta=1.6\) rad/s² and \(\dot v=-0.08\) m/s². C accelerates sideways because it swings about G (\(a_{C,y}=-x_G\ddot\theta\)). The naive \({}^Cn_z/0.275=1.4545\) rad/s² ignores the coupling and is wrong. checked

Calculation (solve a 3×3 at rest) or explanation (“what does each term mean, and what vanishes when C = G?”). Frequent trap: using \({}^GI\) as the third diagonal entry when C ≠ G.

6 · From the chassis frame to the inertial frame pp. 28–34

Picture

The chassis form is convenient for simulation, but a planner or a world-frame controller works with \((\boldsymbol\xi,\dot{\boldsymbol\xi},\ddot{\boldsymbol\xi})\) and a force \({}^O\mathbf Q\) in world axes. Two ingredients convert it (p.28): a way to write \(\boldsymbol\zeta,\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}\) in terms of \(\boldsymbol\xi\) and its derivatives, and a relation between \({}^C\mathbf Q\) and \({}^O\mathbf Q\).

Derivation

Velocities (p.30): from W10, \(\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}=\mathbf J(\boldsymbol\xi)\boldsymbol\zeta\) with \(\mathbf J\) the rotation about z by \(\theta\) (the slide’s “\(\mathbf J(\eta)\)” is a typo for \(\mathbf J(\boldsymbol\xi)\)). Differentiate:

\[ \ddot{\boldsymbol\xi}=\dot{\mathbf J}\boldsymbol\zeta+\mathbf J\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}\;\Rightarrow\;\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}=\mathbf J^{-1}\big[\ddot{\boldsymbol\xi}-\dot{\mathbf J}\boldsymbol\zeta\big]=\mathbf J^{-1}\big[\ddot{\boldsymbol\xi}-\dot{\mathbf J}\mathbf J^{-1}\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}\big] \]

Loads (p.32): power is the same in any frame, \({}^O\mathbf Q\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}={}^C\mathbf Q\cdot\boldsymbol\zeta\). Insert \(\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}=\mathbf J\boldsymbol\zeta\): \({}^O\mathbf Q^\top\mathbf J\boldsymbol\zeta={}^C\mathbf Q^\top\boldsymbol\zeta\) for every \(\boldsymbol\zeta\), hence

\[ \mathbf J(\boldsymbol\xi)^\top\,{}^O\mathbf Q={}^C\mathbf Q \]

This is the same “transpose of the velocity map maps loads back” rule as \(\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf J^\top\mathbf F\) for arms (statics, W6 p.58). For a rotation \(\mathbf J^\top=\mathbf J^{-1}\), so \({}^O\mathbf Q=\mathbf J\,{}^C\mathbf Q\): rotate the load by \(\theta\). added

Plug in (p.34). Substitute \(\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}\) and \({}^C\mathbf Q\) into \(\mathbf M\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}+c=\,{}^C\mathbf Q\) and multiply by \((\mathbf J^\top)^{-1}\):

\[ {}^O\mathbf M\,\ddot{\boldsymbol\xi}+{}^Oc(\boldsymbol\xi,\dot{\boldsymbol\xi})={}^O\mathbf Q,\qquad {}^O\mathbf M=(\mathbf J^\top)^{-1}\mathbf M\,\mathbf J^{-1},\quad {}^Oc=(\mathbf J^\top)^{-1}\Big[c-\mathbf M\,\mathbf J^{-1}\dot{\mathbf J}\,\mathbf J^{-1}\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}\Big] \]

Entirely in terms of \(\boldsymbol\xi,\dot{\boldsymbol\xi},\ddot{\boldsymbol\xi}\), as the slide says. checked numerically on random poses, velocities and COM offsets

Special case C = G: \((\mathbf J^\top)^{-1}=\mathbf J\), so \({}^O\mathbf M=\mathbf J\,\mathrm{diag}(m,m,{}^GI)\,\mathbf J^\top=\mathrm{diag}(m,m,{}^GI)\), and \({}^Oc=0\). A free rigid body obeys \(m\ddot x=f_x\), \(m\ddot y=f_y\), \({}^GI\ddot\theta=\tau_z\) in world axes, with no velocity terms. The Coriolis-like terms of the chassis form exist only because the chassis axes rotate. checked added

Slides vs derivation

Page 34, third line, drops a \(\mathbf J^{-1}\). The slide prints \({}^Oc=(\mathbf J^\top)^{-1}[c-\mathbf M\,\dot{\mathbf J}\,\mathbf J^{-1}\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}]\). Expanding line 2 of the same slide, \(\mathbf M\mathbf J^{-1}(\ddot{\boldsymbol\xi}-\dot{\mathbf J}\mathbf J^{-1}\dot{\boldsymbol\xi})\), gives the subtracted term \(\mathbf M\,\mathbf J^{-1}\dot{\mathbf J}\,\mathbf J^{-1}\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}\), with an extra \(\mathbf J^{-1}\) in front of \(\dot{\mathbf J}\). The two agree only at \(\theta=0\) (where \(\mathbf J=\mathbf I\)). Test: C = G, \(m=10\), \(\theta=90^\circ\), \(u=1\), \(v=0\), \(\dot\theta=2\): the correct \({}^Oc=0\) (free body), the printed formula gives \((-20,\,20,\,0)\). The p.30 equations are correct. checked

Exam recipe
  1. State \(\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}=\mathbf J\boldsymbol\zeta\) and differentiate to get \(\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}\).
  2. State the power argument and conclude \({}^C\mathbf Q=\mathbf J^\top\,{}^O\mathbf Q\).
  3. Substitute and pre-multiply by \((\mathbf J^\top)^{-1}\) to read \({}^O\mathbf M\) and \({}^Oc\).
  4. For a rotation, use \(\mathbf J^{-1}=\mathbf J^\top\) to simplify.
  5. Check the C = G case: \({}^O\mathbf M\) diagonal and constant.
Worked example

Use the section 8 robot (C = G, \(m=10\), \({}^GI=0.25\)) at rest with \(\theta=30^\circ\) and the wheel wrench \({}^C\mathbf Q=(10,0,0.4)\). Then \({}^O\mathbf Q=\mathbf J\,{}^C\mathbf Q=(10\cos30^\circ,\,10\sin30^\circ,\,0.4)=(8.660,\,5.000,\,0.4)\), and \(\ddot{\boldsymbol\xi}={}^O\mathbf M^{-1}\,{}^O\mathbf Q=(0.866,\,0.5,\,1.6)\) (m/s², m/s², rad/s²). It is the chassis answer \((1,0,1.6)\) with the linear part rotated by \(30^\circ\). checked

A derive question (“show \({}^C\mathbf Q=\mathbf J^\top\,{}^O\mathbf Q\)”, six lines) or a spot-the-error (transpose, inverse, which frame). Say “power is frame-independent” in words; that is the key idea.

7 · Using the model: forward simulation p. 35

Picture

Wheel-ground forces are most natural in the chassis frame, so simulate there (p.35). Start from a known pose and velocity, with the wheel forces given. Each step: compute \(\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}\), integrate to get \(\boldsymbol\zeta\), rotate to \(\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}\), integrate to get \(\boldsymbol\xi\). The simulator above does exactly this.

Derivation \[ \dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}=\mathbf M^{-1}\big[{}^C\mathbf Q-c(\boldsymbol\zeta)\big],\qquad \boldsymbol\zeta\leftarrow\int\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}\,\mathrm dt,\qquad \dot{\boldsymbol\xi}=\mathbf J(\boldsymbol\xi)\boldsymbol\zeta,\qquad \boldsymbol\xi\leftarrow\int\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}\,\mathrm dt \]

The slide says “integrate”; the simulator uses fourth-order Runge–Kutta (RK4) with a 5 ms step, which for this smooth model is far more accurate than explicit Euler. One explicit Euler step is \(\boldsymbol\zeta_{k+1}=\boldsymbol\zeta_k+\Delta t\,\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}_k\). added

Exam recipe
  1. Compute \(c(\boldsymbol\zeta)\) from the current velocity; at rest it is 0.
  2. Solve \(\mathbf M\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}={}^C\mathbf Q-c\) (diagonal \(\mathbf M\): divide).
  3. Update \(\boldsymbol\zeta\), then rotate by \(\mathbf J(\theta)\) for the world velocity.
  4. Update \(\boldsymbol\xi\). Check \(\theta\) is in radians for the rotation.
Worked example

From rest with \(\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}=(1,0,1.6)\) (section 8), one Euler step of 0.1 s gives \(\boldsymbol\zeta_1=(0.1,0,0.16)\). The pose is still the origin after step 1, because \(\boldsymbol\zeta_0=0\) means \(\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}_0=0\). checked

A short “list the steps of forward simulation” or a one-step numerical question. Name the frame of each quantity and the order: acceleration, velocity, then pose.

8 · From wheel forces to chassis loads: the differential drive pp. 36–37

Picture

“Where does the torque on the chassis come from?” (p.36): from the wheel forces at their lever arms. A differential drive has two driven wheels a distance \(2a\) apart, with C and G both at the midpoint of the axle (p.37). \(F_1\) acts on the left wheel (\(+y\)) and \(F_2\) on the right (\(-y\)), both along \(+x\). The figure also shows a small passive wheel at the front (a castor): it carries load but is not driven and does not appear in the equations.

Derivation

Each force along \(+x\) contributes \(f_x\). The moment about the origin is \(n_z=x\,f_y-y\,f_x\): \(F_1\) at \(y=+a\) gives \(-aF_1\), \(F_2\) at \(y=-a\) gives \(+aF_2\). Hence (p.37, the handwritten matrix):

\[ \begin{bmatrix}{}^Cf_x\\{}^Cf_y\\{}^Cn_z\end{bmatrix}=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&0\\-a&a\end{bmatrix}}_{3\times2}\begin{bmatrix}F_1\\F_2\end{bmatrix} \]

The slide stops here. Connect it to the rest. A wheel torque \(\tau_i\) gives a force \(F_i=\tau_i/r\) at the ground (wheel inertia neglected). The W10 wheel-speed map (section 2) for the two wheels is \(\dot{\boldsymbol\varphi}=\mathbf J_w\boldsymbol\zeta\), \(\mathbf J_w=\tfrac1r\begin{bmatrix}1&0&-a\\1&0&a\end{bmatrix}\) (left, right rows). Then \({}^C\mathbf Q=\mathbf J_w^\top\boldsymbol\tau\): the p.37 matrix is \(r\mathbf J_w^\top\) applied to \(F=\tau/r\). This follows because power is conserved: \(\boldsymbol\tau\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol\varphi}=\boldsymbol\tau^\top\mathbf J_w\boldsymbol\zeta={}^C\mathbf Q\cdot\boldsymbol\zeta\). checked added

With C = G the equations of motion (section 5) become

\[ m(\dot u-v\dot\theta)=F_1+F_2,\qquad m(\dot v+u\dot\theta)=f_y,\qquad {}^GI\,\ddot\theta=a(F_2-F_1) \]

The p.37 matrix has \(f_y=0\): the two driven wheels push only forward. The no-slip rule \(v=0\) from W10 (a wheel cannot slide along its axle) then gives \(\dot v=0\) and so requires a sideways reaction \(f_y=mu\dot\theta\) from the tyres. The model reduces to

\[ \dot u=\frac{F_1+F_2}{m},\qquad \ddot\theta=\frac{a\,(F_2-F_1)}{{}^GI},\qquad f_y^{\text{required}}=m\,u\,\dot\theta \]

If you literally set \(f_y=0\) and keep \(v\) free (the simulator’s “lateral grip” unticked), you get \(\dot v=-u\dot\theta\): the body drifts sideways like a puck. Real wheels do not, so the grip version describes a real differential drive.

Slide gap (not an error)

The deck never states the no-slip constraint inside the dynamics. The p.37 matrix lists only the forward drive forces; the lateral force that keeps \(v=0\) is a constraint reaction, absent from \({}^C\mathbf Q\). If a question gives wheel forces and asks for \(\dot u,\dot v,\ddot\theta\), read whether the robot is allowed to slide: with no-slip, \(\dot v=0\); free-body, use \(\mathbf M\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}+c=\mathbf Q\) with \(f_y=0\). For ordinary wheels use no-slip and say so.

Exam recipe
  1. Draw the top view; mark C, G, \(\pm a\), forces \(F_1\) (left, \(+y\)) and \(F_2\) (right, \(-y\)).
  2. Write \(f_x=F_1+F_2\), \(f_y=0\), \(n_z=a(F_2-F_1)\) (the matrix).
  3. If given torques, convert \(F=\tau/r\).
  4. With C = G and no slip: \(\dot u=f_x/m\), \(\ddot\theta=n_z/{}^GI\), \(v=0\).
  5. Check the sign: the right wheel pushing harder turns the robot left (positive \(\dot\theta\)). Check power: \(\boldsymbol\tau\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol\varphi}=f_xu+n_z\dot\theta\).
Worked example: full numbers (no numbers in the deck; mine)

Parameters: \(m=10\) kg, \({}^GI=0.25\) kg·m², \(r=0.1\) m, \(a=0.2\) m (track \(2a=0.4\) m), C = G, no wheel inertia. Wheel torques \(\tau_L=0.4\) and \(\tau_R=0.6\) N·m, from rest.

Forces: \(F_1=\tau_L/r=4\) N, \(F_2=\tau_R/r=6\) N. Wrench: \(f_x=4+6=10\) N, \(f_y=0\), \(n_z=0.2(6-4)=0.4\) N·m.

At rest \(c=0\): \(\dot u=10/10=1.0\) m/s², \(\dot v=0\) (no slip), \(\ddot\theta=0.4/0.25=1.6\) rad/s². checked

Because both accelerations are constant, \(u=t\) and \(\dot\theta=1.6t\), so the path radius \(R=u/\dot\theta=0.625\) m never changes: the robot drives a circle of radius 0.625 m (centre 0.625 m to its left), speeding up. Generally \(R=\dfrac{{}^GI\,f_x}{m\,n_z}\). checked (also against the exact solution \(x=R\sin\theta\), \(y=R(1-\cos\theta)\))

At \(t=1\) s: \(u=1\) m/s, \(\dot\theta=1.6\) rad/s. Wheel speeds \(\dot\varphi_L=(1-0.32)/0.1=6.8\) and \(\dot\varphi_R=(1+0.32)/0.1=13.2\) rad/s. Sideways force to hold \(v=0\): \(mu\dot\theta=16\) N; if free, \(\dot v=-u\dot\theta=-1.6\) m/s². Power: \(0.4(6.8)+0.6(13.2)=10.64\) W \(=f_xu+n_z\dot\theta=10(1)+0.4(1.6)\). checked

At \(t=2\) s the simulator gives \(u=2.0\) m/s, \(\dot\theta=3.2\) rad/s, \(\theta=3.2\) rad, \((x,y)=(-0.036,\,1.249)\) m, matching the exact circle. checked (widget test vectors: checks/w11_vectors.json)

Calculation: “given \(\tau_L,\tau_R\), \(r\), \(a\), \(m\), \(I\), find \(\dot u\) and \(\ddot\theta\)”. Marks for \(F=\tau/r\), the matrix, and the lever arm \(a\). Trap: using \(2a\) as the lever arm (doubles \(\ddot\theta\)) or swapping the sign so a harder right push turns the robot right.

9 · Swedish-wheel robot, castors, and the summary pp. 38–39

Picture

Page 38 is a figure only: a chassis with four Swedish (mecanum-type) wheels, forces \(F_1\)–\(F_4\) drawn along the roller axes at about \(\pm45^\circ\) to the chassis, offsets labelled \(a\) and \(b\), and {C, G} at the centre. No equation is on the slide; the matrix is left as the exercise “write \({}^C\mathbf Q\) as a function of the wheel forces”, like the differential drive. A castor (p.37) is a free-swivelling wheel: it transmits no drive force, so it adds nothing to \({}^C\mathbf Q\).

Method (mine; the slide gives none)

Each wheel \(i\) pushes with force \(F_i\) along a unit vector \(\mathbf d_i=(d_x,d_y)\) at position \((x_i,y_i)\) in {C}. Its column in the 3×4 matrix is

\[ \begin{bmatrix}d_x\\d_y\\x_i d_y-y_i d_x\end{bmatrix} \]

Illustration under my own assumptions (the slide’s \(a,b\) are not dimensioned precisely): wheels at \((\pm b,\pm a)\), drive directions \((1,1)/\sqrt2\) for \(F_1,F_3\) and \((1,-1)/\sqrt2\) for \(F_2,F_4\), as drawn. With \(s=1/\sqrt2\):

\[ \begin{bmatrix}{}^Cf_x\\{}^Cf_y\\{}^Cn_z\end{bmatrix}=s\begin{bmatrix}1&1&1&1\\1&-1&1&-1\\b-a&b-a&a-b&a-b\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}F_1\\F_2\\F_3\\F_4\end{bmatrix} \]

Four wheel forces, three chassis loads: a 3×4 matrix of rank 3 (for \(a\ne b\)) has a one-dimensional null space, so one combination of wheel forces (internal forces that fight each other) produces zero net load. Equal forces on all four give a pure forward force \(4sF\). checked

Summary (p.39): the dynamics equation in the body frame, \(\mathbf M\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}+c=\,{}^C\mathbf Q\); and in the inertial frame, \({}^O\mathbf M\ddot{\boldsymbol\xi}+{}^Oc={}^O\mathbf Q\), linked by \({}^C\mathbf Q=\mathbf J^\top\,{}^O\mathbf Q\).

Exam recipe (any wheeled robot)
  1. For each driven wheel, write position \((x_i,y_i)\) in {C} and the unit direction of its force.
  2. Column \(=(d_x,\,d_y,\,x_id_y-y_id_x)^\top\); stack to get \({}^C\mathbf Q=\mathbf B\mathbf F\).
  3. Count wheels versus the three chassis degrees of freedom: more wheels than 3 means redundancy and a null space.
  4. Check with equal forces (net torque zero for a symmetric layout).
Likely as an explain or sketch question: build \(\mathbf B\) for a given layout, say what its rank and shape mean. The matrix \(\mathbf B\) is the transpose of the W10 wheel-speed matrix (up to the factor \(r\)).

Guided problems: solve on paper first

P11.1 · Differential-drive accelerations from torquescalculate

A differential drive (C = G) has \(m=8\) kg, \({}^GI=0.2\) kg·m², wheel radius \(r=0.08\) m, half-track \(a=0.15\) m. The left and right wheel torques are 0.3 and 0.5 N·m. From rest with no wheel slip, find \(\dot u\) (m/s²) and \(\ddot\theta\) (rad/s²).

Hint 1: forces

\(F=\tau/r\) for each wheel.

Hint 2: the matrix

\(f_x=F_1+F_2\), \(n_z=a(F_2-F_1)\), with \(F_1\) the left wheel.

Hint 3: at rest

\(c=0\) and \(\mathbf M=\mathrm{diag}(m,m,{}^GI)\).

Full solution

\(F_1=0.3/0.08=3.75\) N, \(F_2=0.5/0.08=6.25\) N. \(f_x=10\) N, \(n_z=0.15(6.25-3.75)=0.375\) N·m.

\(\dot u=f_x/m=10/8=1.25\) m/s². \(\ddot\theta=n_z/{}^GI=0.375/0.2=1.875\) rad/s². Path radius \(R=u/\dot\theta=1.25/1.875=0.667\) m. checked

Common wrong answer: dropping the lever arm gives \(\ddot\theta=12.5\) rad/s²; using \(2a\) gives \(3.75\).

Close everything and write the p.37 matrix, with the figure it comes from, in 2 minutes.

P11.2 · Derive the acceleration termsderive

Without the cross-product formula, derive the acceleration of the chassis reference point C, expressed in {C}, for velocity \(u\hat x+v\hat y\) in a frame turning at \(\dot\theta\).

Hint 1

Differentiate \(u\hat x+v\hat y\) as a product: the components change and the unit vectors change.

Hint 2

\(\dot{\hat x}=\dot\theta\,\hat y\) and \(\dot{\hat y}=-\dot\theta\,\hat x\).

Full solution

\(\mathbf a_C=\dot u\hat x+u\dot{\hat x}+\dot v\hat y+v\dot{\hat y}=\dot u\hat x+u\dot\theta\hat y+\dot v\hat y-v\dot\theta\hat x\).

\(\mathbf a_C=(\dot u-v\dot\theta)\,\hat x+(\dot v+u\dot\theta)\,\hat y\). For G offset by \((x_G,y_G)\) add \(\ddot\theta(-y_G,x_G)+\dot\theta^2(-x_G,-y_G)\) to get the p.24 form with \(u\dot\theta\) in y. checked

Common wrong answer: \(\dot u,\dot v\) alone (forgetting that the frame turns), or \(v\dot\theta\) in y (the slide typo).

Derive both terms from the two unit-vector derivatives in 3 minutes.

P11.3 · Spot the error: the slide’s y-accelerationspot the errorcalculate

A chassis (C = G, \(m=10\) kg) drives at constant \(u=2\) m/s, \(v=0\), with constant \(\dot\theta=0.5\) rad/s. Using the slide-p.24/25 form \({}^Cf_y=m(\dot v+v\dot\theta+\dots)\), what sideways force is required? What is the correct sideways force?

Hint 1

All derivatives and \(v\) are zero, so only one term survives in each version.

Full solution

Printed form: \(f_y=m(0+0+v\dot\theta-0)=0\). Correct form: \(f_y=m\,u\dot\theta=10(2)(0.5)=10\) N, the centripetal force on a circle of radius \(u/\dot\theta=4\) m: \(mu^2/R=10\cdot4/4=10\) N. checked

The printed form would say a robot can drive a circle with no sideways force, which is impossible.

P11.4 · Off-centre centre of masscalculateexplain

Same chassis as the worked example in section 5 (\(m=10\) kg, \({}^GI=0.25\) kg·m²), G 0.05 m ahead of C along \(\hat x\). At rest the wheels apply \({}^Cf=(10,0)\) N and \({}^Cn_z=0.4\) N·m about C. Find \(\dot v\) and \(\ddot\theta\), and explain why \(\dot v\ne0\) although \({}^Cf_y=0\).

Hint 1

Build \(\mathbf M\): the \((2,3)\) entry is \(m\,{}^Cx_G=0.5\); the \((3,3)\) entry is \(0.25+10(0.05)^2\).

Hint 2

Rows 2 and 3 form a 2×2 in \(\dot v,\ddot\theta\); solve by substitution.

Full solution

Row 2: \(10\dot v+0.5\ddot\theta=0\Rightarrow\dot v=-0.05\ddot\theta\). Row 3: \(0.5\dot v+0.275\ddot\theta=0.4\Rightarrow(-0.025+0.275)\ddot\theta=0.4\Rightarrow\ddot\theta=1.6\) rad/s², \(\dot v=-0.08\) m/s². checked

Why: the wheels’ force acts through C, not through G, so it spins the body about G. Point C, 0.05 m behind G, swings sideways: \(a_{C,y}=-x_G\ddot\theta=-0.08\) m/s². (The force balance is on G: \(m\,a_{G,y}=f_y=0\).)

Common wrong answer: \(0.4/0.275=1.4545\).

P11.5 · Forward versus inverse, and why the chassis frameexplain

(a) State forward and inverse dynamics and give one use of each. (b) Why does the deck simulate in the chassis frame, and what does it cost? (c) What does \(c(\boldsymbol\zeta)\) represent, and when is it zero?

Model answer

(a) Forward: given forces and torques, find the motion (simulation, analysis). Inverse: given a desired motion, find the forces and torques (control, feed-forward). (b) Wheel–ground forces are naturally expressed in the chassis frame, so \({}^C\mathbf Q\) is easy to write, and \(\mathbf M\) is constant. The cost: velocity terms \(c(\boldsymbol\zeta)\) appear and you must rotate with \(\mathbf J(\theta)\) to get world coordinates. (c) \(c\) holds centripetal/Coriolis effects due to the rotating frame; it is zero when \(\boldsymbol\zeta=0\) (and, for C = G, its third entry is always zero).

P11.6 · Sketch: free-body diagram and ICRsketch

Sketch the top view of a differential drive with \(F_1\) (left) and \(F_2\) (right) forward and \(F_2>F_1\). Mark {C, G}, \(\pm a\), the sideways reaction needed for no slip, the sense of \(\dot\theta\) and the ICR.

Hint 1

The ICR lies on the axle line, on the side of the slower wheel.

Model answer

Draw the axle along \(\hat y\) with F₁ at \(+a\) and F₂ at \(-a\), both along \(+\hat x\). \(F_2>F_1\): net torque \(a(F_2-F_1)>0\), anticlockwise. The ICR is on the \(+\hat y\) (left) side at distance \(R=u/\dot\theta\) from C. The lateral wheel reaction acts along \(\hat y\) at the wheels, towards the ICR, magnitude \(mu\dot\theta\). Use the simulator’s picture for the answer: its dashed line from the chassis to the ICR and the orange force arrows are this sketch.

P11.7 · Frame conversion of a wrenchderivecalculate

Derive \({}^C\mathbf Q=\mathbf J^\top\,{}^O\mathbf Q\) from power invariance. Then, for the wheel wrench \({}^C\mathbf Q=(10,0,0.4)\) with the chassis at \(\theta=90^\circ\), find the inertial-frame force \({}^O\mathbf Q=(f_x,f_y,\tau_z)\).

Hint 1

For a rotation about z, \({}^O\mathbf Q=\mathbf J\,{}^C\mathbf Q\), the same rotation as for velocities.

Full solution

Power: \({}^O\mathbf Q\cdot\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}={}^C\mathbf Q\cdot\boldsymbol\zeta\). With \(\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}=\mathbf J\boldsymbol\zeta\): \({}^O\mathbf Q^\top\mathbf J\boldsymbol\zeta={}^C\mathbf Q^\top\boldsymbol\zeta\) for all \(\boldsymbol\zeta\), so \(\mathbf J^\top\,{}^O\mathbf Q={}^C\mathbf Q\).

\({}^O\mathbf Q=\mathbf J(90^\circ)\,(10,0,0.4)^\top=(0,10,0.4)\): \(f_x=0\), \(f_y=10\) N, \(\tau_z=0.4\) N·m (the torque does not rotate). checked

P11.8 · Spot the error: the inertial-frame bias termspot the error

A student copies p.34 and writes \({}^Oc=(\mathbf J^\top)^{-1}[c-\mathbf M\dot{\mathbf J}\mathbf J^{-1}\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}]\). For C = G, what must \({}^Oc\) be physically, and what is wrong with this expression?

Hint 1

In world axes a free rigid body with C = G has no velocity-dependent force.

Hint 2

Expand \(\mathbf M\,\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}\) with \(\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}=\mathbf J^{-1}[\ddot{\boldsymbol\xi}-\dot{\mathbf J}\mathbf J^{-1}\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}]\).

Full solution

Physically \({}^Oc=0\). The expansion gives \(\mathbf M\mathbf J^{-1}\ddot{\boldsymbol\xi}-\mathbf M\mathbf J^{-1}\dot{\mathbf J}\mathbf J^{-1}\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}\): the subtracted term needs \(\mathbf J^{-1}\) before \(\dot{\mathbf J}\). The printed form omits it. At \(\theta=90^\circ\), \(u=1\), \(v=0\), \(\dot\theta=2\), \(m=10\), the printed form gives \((-20,20,0)\), the corrected form gives 0. checked

P11.9 · Swedish-wheel matrix: redundancyexplain

For the four-Swedish-wheel robot of p.38 the map from wheel forces to chassis loads is 3×4. What does that shape imply, and how would you find a wheel-force set that exerts no net load?

Model answer

Three chassis loads, four wheel forces: there are more actuators than degrees of freedom, so the map \(\mathbf B\) (3×4, rank 3 for a sensible layout) has a one-dimensional null space. Solve \(\mathbf B\mathbf F=0\) for \(\mathbf F\neq0\): forces that cancel and only squeeze the wheels against the floor (internal forces). Any chassis load is reachable with infinitely many force sets, so a controller has a free choice, for example the minimum-norm solution \(\mathbf F=\mathbf B^\top(\mathbf B\mathbf B^\top)^{-1}\,{}^C\mathbf Q\). added (the minimum-norm choice is not in the deck)

Mini-quiz

Q1concept

In \(\mathbf M\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}+c(\boldsymbol\zeta)={}^C\mathbf Q\), what does \(\mathbf M\) depend on, and what does \(c\) depend on?

Answer

\(\mathbf M\) depends only on geometry and mass distribution (\(m\), \({}^GI\), the COM position). \(c\) is a function of the instantaneous velocity \(\boldsymbol\zeta\) (centripetal and Coriolis terms from the rotating frame) (p.26).

Q2calculate

A differential drive (C = G, \(m=10\) kg, \(r=0.1\) m) receives 0.5 N·m on each wheel, from rest. Find \(\dot u\) and \(\ddot\theta\).

Answer

\(F=0.5/0.1=5\) N each, \(f_x=10\) N, \(n_z=a(5-5)=0\). \(\dot u=10/10=1\) m/s² and \(\ddot\theta=0\): a straight line. checked

Q3spot the error

A student writes \({}^C\mathbf Q=\mathbf J\,{}^O\mathbf Q\). Which expression is correct, and how do you remember it?

Answer

\({}^C\mathbf Q=\mathbf J^\top\,{}^O\mathbf Q\), from power invariance \({}^O\mathbf Q^\top\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}={}^C\mathbf Q^\top\boldsymbol\zeta\) with \(\dot{\boldsymbol\xi}=\mathbf J\boldsymbol\zeta\) (p.32). Velocities map with \(\mathbf J\); loads map with \(\mathbf J^\top\). For a rotation \(\mathbf J^\top=\mathbf J^{-1}\), so the student has the rotation backwards.

Week 12 · Planning algorithms

How does a robot find a collision-free route?

Motion planning turns “get from here to there without hitting anything” into a search problem. First squeeze the robot down to a point by working in configuration space. Then either build a graph of the free space and search it (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, A*), or skip the explicit map and sample random points (PRM, RRT). Know what each method guarantees, what it costs, and be able to run Dijkstra and A* by hand.

Lecture: Planning Algorithms83 slides · Dr KM Digumarti · practical sheet is a PDF (no notebook)
Open in new tab ↗
How this is examined

No lecturer-solved archetype. The W13 revision deck (W13) contains no planning question; we searched its text for planning, A*, Dijkstra, RRT and PRM and found none. So the styles below are our inference from the lecture’s own questions (p.22, p.58, p.77) and the practical sheet. Treat them as likely, not certain.

Likely questions (marks not published): (1) run Dijkstra or A* on a small weighted graph and give the expansion order, the path and its cost, with a table of g, h, f; (2) say whether a heuristic is admissible or consistent; (3) pick the right planner for a scenario (high-DoF arm, car with turning limits, clearance, known polygon map); (4) state a completeness property; (5) inflate an obstacle by the robot radius; (6) a short calculation with the practical’s PRM or RRT geometry.

Where marks are lost: not showing the open and closed sets; stopping when a goal is discovered instead of when it is expanded; adding h to the wrong node; saying A* is “always optimal” without “admissible h”; calling BFS optimal on a weighted graph; saying PRM or RRT is “complete”; missing that DFS finds a path, not the best one.

Practical (optional, no coding in the exam)

The sheet ENN581 - Week 12 - Practicals - Planning Algorithms.pdf has three questions and no notebook and no saved results: (1) turn a maze into a graph, run BFS and DFS, compare, and say how to upgrade to A*; (2) implement a PRM on a 10 × 10 map with three polygons; (3, bonus) an RRT on the same map. Its title says “mobile robot kinematics”, a copy error. diffdrive.py in the same folder is differential-drive kinematics left over from W10, not planning; its update uses the angular rate × dt where a heading belongs, so do not learn from it. Every question on the sheet is solved by hand below (P12.5 to P12.7).

Intuition first

Configuration space shrinks the robot to a dot

Walking a sofa through a door is hard because the sofa has size. Pretend instead the sofa is a dot and thicken the walls by the sofa’s reach. Then “can it pass?” is just “can a dot get through?”.

BFS is a ripple, Dijkstra is a ripple that counts distance

Drop a stone in a pond and the ripple reaches every point at the same number of steps. Dijkstra’s ripple instead advances by travelled cost, so it is the right ripple when roads have different lengths.

A* is Dijkstra with a compass

You still add up the distance walked so far (g), but you also add a guess of the distance left (h) and always follow the smallest total. If the guess is never too pessimistic about how short the rest is, you still arrive by the best route.

Sampling is throwing darts at the floor plan

Throw random darts (points), keep those that land on free floor, and join near ones with straight strings that do not cross a wall. PRM builds the whole web first and then searches it. RRT grows one tree outward from the start, like a plant seeking light.In the practical: Q2 asks for the web (PRM), Q3 for the plant (RRT).

Switch to 8-connected: Dijkstra 59 expansions, cost 8.243 (= 7 steps with 3 diagonals). 1 · What planning means, and the framework pp. 4–9, pp. 25–26

Picture

Planning here means motion or path planning: given a map, a start and a goal, find a trajectory the robot can execute (p.5). It sits on top of everything earlier in the unit: kinematics tells you which motions are possible, trajectory generation (W5) smooths the route, control (W8–9) follows it.

Inputs (p.7): geometry of robot and obstacles (the map); kinematics of the robot (degrees of freedom, constraints); start and goal configurations. Output: a continuous sequence of collision-free configurations from start to goal, or a report of failure if none exists. Simplifying assumptions (p.8): the representation is expressive enough, we know where we are and where we want to go, we have a motion model, and the task is usually cast as optimisation (minimum time or distance within constraints).

The field moved from classical (mid-70s: exact models, no sensing), to reactive (mid-80s: no models, heavy sensing), to hybrid (90s: models at high level, reactive at low level), to probabilistic (since mid-90s: models plus sensing, both inaccurate) (p.9).

The framework (p.25): start from the continuous C-space, then discretise, because computers store digital things and standard graph-search algorithms then apply (p.26). Two families:

Combinatorial planningSampling-based planning
IdeaDescribe Cfree explicitly, capture its connectivity in a graph, search the graphUse a collision detector to probe C-space point by point; no explicit Cfree / Cobs split
Slide examplesvisibility graph, Voronoi, cell decomposition, grid + BFS/DFS/Dijkstra/A*PRM (1996), RRT (1998)
Completeness (p.81)visibility graph and Voronoi: complete; BFS: resolution complete; DFS: not complete on infinite treesprobabilistically complete
Completeness (p. 80)
  • Complete: finds a collision-free path whenever one exists and reports failure otherwise.
  • Resolution complete: discretises the space and returns a path wherever one exists at the chosen resolution. A gap narrower than a cell is invisible to it.
  • Probabilistically complete: returns a path with high probability if one exists, and may not terminate if none exists. As samples tend to infinity, the probability of finding a path tends to 1.
Exam recipe
  1. For “which planner?”, first ask: is the map known and polygonal (visibility graph, cells), is clearance wanted (Voronoi), is it a grid with costs (Dijkstra, A*), is the space high-dimensional or the robot non-holonomic (PRM, RRT)?
  2. For a completeness statement, always add the qualifier: “complete”, “resolution complete” or “probabilistically complete”.
  3. Never write “guarantees the shortest path” unless the method is on the list: visibility graph (for the polygon map), Dijkstra, or A* with an admissible heuristic.
  4. Sanity check: does the answer mention what the planner does when no path exists?
Trap: “PRM and RRT are complete” is false; they are probabilistically complete. “BFS is complete” needs “on a finite graph / at the grid resolution”. DFS fails on infinite trees because it can dive forever.

2 · Configuration space, Cfree, Cobs and inflation pp. 11–24

Picture

Task space is the frame where the task is performed, such as the end effector or a mobile robot’s body frame (p.12). Configuration space (C-space) is the set of generalised coordinates that completely describe the robot: joint parameters for an arm, position and orientation for a mobile robot (p.14). One robot configuration is one point in C-space.

The workspace obstacles map to a region Cobs in C-space; everything else is Cfree. Planning means finding a continuous curve inside Cfree from qstart to qgoal (p.15).

Why work there (p.17): nearby configurations are close together, collision checks and joining nearby poses become easy, one algorithm serves many robots (abstraction), and it handles wraparound for rotary joints.

Arm example (p.19): a planar 2-link arm among four rectangles. Each rectangle becomes a curved blob in the (θ1, θ2) plane, and the largest rectangle becomes a large region. The slide shows a vertical line at one θ1: the arm’s second joint can only avoid the blobs along that line.

Mobile robot example, inflation (pp. 20–24): shrink the robot to a point and grow each obstacle by the robot’s size. A circular robot gives a margin of constant width with rounded corners; a polygonal robot gives a polygonal margin. The problem “twist and turn this polygon past that polygon” becomes “find a path for a point past an augmented polygon” (p.24).

Derivation

Free space (p.15), with \(\mathcal C\) the C-space, \(\mathcal C_{obs}\) the obstacle region, \(\phi\) the empty set:

\[ \mathcal C_{free}=\{\,\mathbf q\in\mathcal C \mid \mathbf q\cap\mathcal C_{obs}=\phi\,\} \]
Slides vs textbook

p.15 writes “𝒪 ∈ 𝒲 or 𝒞obs ∈ 𝒞”. The obstacle set is a subset of the workspace or of C-space, so the symbol should be ⊂ (a set, not an element).

Inflation by a disc of radius \(r\) is the Minkowski sum of the obstacle with the disc. Each straight edge moves outward by \(r\), each convex corner becomes a circular arc of radius \(r\). For a convex polygon of area \(A\) and perimeter \(P\) the grown area is (Steiner formula)

\[ A_{grown}=A+P\,r+\pi r^{2} \]

For a square robot of half-side \(r\), aligned with the obstacle, the margin is a square one: a 2 × 2 m square grows to 3 × 3 m when \(r=0.5\) m.

Wraparound: a rotary joint angle \(q\) and \(q+2\pi\) are the same configuration, so C-space for revolute joints is a torus, not a flat rectangle. A path that leaves one edge of the plot re-enters at the opposite edge.

One workspace point can give several C-space points. For a 2-link arm with \(L_1=L_2=1\) m, the tip is at \((1,1)\) m for \(\mathbf q=(0^\circ,\,90^\circ)\) and also for \(\mathbf q=(90^\circ,\,-90^\circ)\) (the two inverse-kinematics branches). A single point obstacle at \((1,1)\) therefore blocks both configurations. A real obstacle has area and the whole arm (not just the tip) can hit it, so the blocked set is a curved region of C-space (the blobs on p.19). checked in checks/w12.py

Exam recipe
  1. State the robot’s configuration variables (joint angles, or x, y, θ).
  2. Replace the robot by a point; grow every obstacle by the robot’s radius (circle) or by its footprint (polygon).
  3. Draw Cobs and Cfree, mark qstart and qgoal.
  4. For a corridor of width \(w\) and robot radius \(r\), the point robot’s free width is \(w-2r\). If it is negative, the robot cannot pass.
  5. Sanity check: the inflated obstacle must contain the original and, for a disc robot, never be thinner than \(r\) on any side.
Worked example

Triangle with vertices (5,3), (6,3), (5,1) m, disc robot \(r=0.5\) m. Area \(A=\tfrac12\cdot1\cdot2=1\) m². Perimeter \(P=1+\sqrt5+2=5.236\) m (edges (5,3)–(6,3) = 1, (6,3)–(5,1) = √5, (5,1)–(5,3) = 2).

\(A_{grown}=1+5.236(0.5)+\pi(0.5)^2=1+2.618+0.785=4.403\ \text{m}^2\). checked

Corridor 1.0 m wide, robot radius 0.4 m: free width \(1.0-2(0.4)=0.2\) m for the point robot, so it fits. A robot of radius 0.55 m gives \(1.0-1.1\lt0\): it cannot enter. checked

Slide questions (pp. 22–23): “Where can the robot move in the vicinity of the obstacle?” (anywhere its centre stays outside the grown obstacle) and the same question for the point. Exam style: draw the inflated obstacle, or decide whether a gap is passable.

3 · Visibility graph and Voronoi diagram pp. 27–40

Picture

Visibility graph (pp. 28–36): “find all non-blocked lines between polygon vertices, start and goal, then search the graph of these lines for the shortest path”. Steps: draw lines from start and goal to every visible vertex (p.30); then lines of sight from every obstacle vertex, including along edges (p.31); repeat; search (p.34). The shortest path touches obstacle corners. The reduced graph (p.36) keeps only lines that go around an object or pass through its extremes; lines through concave corners can sometimes be dropped.

Pros (p.35): the shortest path is easy to find; simple for polygons. Cons: nodes and edges grow with the number of polygons (slow when dense); the path hugs obstacles as closely as possible.

Voronoi diagram (pp. 37–40): ignore optimality and keep as far from obstacles as possible; the path follows curves equidistant from the nearest obstacles and so maximises the closest distance. Pros: a robot with a range sensor (sonar, laser) can follow it with a simple rule, “maximise the sensor readings” (p.40). Cons: a short-range sensor may lose all obstacles and fail. With polygon obstacles the diagram has straight and parabolic segments.

Comparison
Visibility graphVoronoi
Optimisespath lengthclearance (distance to nearest obstacle)
Path shapestraight segments through obstacle cornersstraight and parabolic arcs equidistant from obstacles
Riskno safety margin; needs inflated obstacleslonger than the shortest path; fails with short-range sensors
Complete? (p.81)yesyes
Exam recipe
  1. Inflate obstacles first (visibility paths touch corners).
  2. List vertices: S, G and every polygon corner.
  3. Join every pair whose segment does not enter an obstacle interior (touching and sliding along an edge is allowed).
  4. Weight edges by Euclidean length; run Dijkstra or A*.
  5. Sanity check: the result is no longer than any other route you can sketch, and only bends at obstacle corners.
Worked example

Practical Q2 map, start S = (1.5, 1.5), goal centre G = (9, 9). The straight line S–G is the diagonal \(y=x\), which passes through the rectangle (6,6)–(8,8), so it is blocked. Going round the rectangle’s corner (8,6): \(|S-(8,6)|=\sqrt{6.5^2+4.5^2}=7.906\), \(|(8,6)-G|=\sqrt{1^2+3^2}=3.162\), total 11.068. To the edge of the goal disc (radius 1) subtract 1: 10.068. The corner (6,8) gives the same length by symmetry about \(y=x\). checked

Typical short question: “which method maximises clearance?” (Voronoi) and “which gives the shortest path but hugs obstacles?” (visibility graph). Trap: “Voronoi gives the shortest path”.

4 · Cell decomposition pp. 41–46

Picture

Divide free space into simple connected cells, build an adjacency (connectivity) graph (one node per cell, an edge when two cells touch), find the cells containing start and goal, search the graph, then compute a path inside each cell (p.42). Three flavours (pp. 44–46):

TypeHowTrade-off
Exactvertical trapezoid cells that exactly cover Cfree, plus adjacency graphno information lost; harder to build
Approximateuniform grid; any cell touching an obstacle is blockedsimple; resolution complete only; can lose narrow gaps
Adaptivebig cells in open space, small cells near obstaclesfewer cells than a uniform grid at the same detail

The uniform-grid version is what the rest of the week searches (section 7 onward).

Explain-style: contrast exact and approximate decomposition. Keywords: exact = complete; approximate = resolution complete, resolution is a trade-off between losing narrow passages and search time (p.64).

5 · Graph search, BFS and DFS pp. 47–55

Picture

Graph search solves a least-cost problem between two states on a (directed) graph (p.48). The graph is a discrete picture of the world: nodes are places (cells, vertices), edges are moves with a cost. Two limits: discretising the state space puts completeness at stake, and the feasibility of paths (turning limits and so on) is seldom encoded.

The slide sorts the methods (p.49): deterministic uninformed BFS and DFS, deterministic informed Dijkstra, A*, D*; randomised PRM and RRT. The bracket on the slide is ambiguous about Dijkstra; conventionally Dijkstra is uninformed (it is A* with h = 0), and A* is the informed one.

  • BFS (p.50): keep a first-in-first-out queue. Expand the oldest node, add its unseen neighbours at the back. Nodes are reached in order of number of edges from the start, so BFS returns the path with the fewest edges. That is the cheapest path only when every edge costs the same. Cost \(O(|V|+|E|)\) (p.65); resolution complete.
  • DFS (p.52): keep a last-in-first-out stack (or recurse). Follow one branch as deep as it goes, back up only at a dead end. Uses little memory but finds a path, usually a long one, with no cost guarantee. Not complete on infinite trees. The depth can be limited (p.54).

The grid pictures (p.51, p.53) show the contrast: BFS floods outward as an even front and the path found is short; DFS wanders and the path is long and winding.

Exam recipe
  1. State the tie-break rule (for example alphabetical) before you start; the slides do not give one.
  2. BFS: write the queue after each pop. Mark a node seen when it is added so it is never added twice.
  3. DFS: write the stack (or the recursion) after each step; go to the first unvisited neighbour.
  4. Stop when the goal is popped. Read the path back through parent pointers.
  5. Add up the edge costs yourself. BFS counts edges, not cost.
Worked example (worked by us, verified by script)

The slide’s graph (p.56): start A, goal K, edges A–B 10, B–E 9, A–C 6, C–F 5, F–H 7, H–J 4, J–K 3, A–D 8, D–G 9, F–G 3, G–I 7, I–K 5. The slide (pp. 50, 52) draws the graph unweighted and gives no answer, so the following uses our tie-break: neighbours in alphabetical order.

BFS: visits A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K (K is popped last, 11th). Path A–D–G–I–K has the fewest edges (4) and costs \(8+9+7+5=29\).
DFS (recursive, alphabetical): visits A, B, E, (dead end, back to A), C, F, G, D, (dead end), I, K. Path A–C–F–G–I–K, 5 edges, costs \(6+5+3+7+5=26\).
The best path costs 25 (section 6). Neither BFS (29) nor DFS (26) is cost-optimal. checked

Typical question: “which path does BFS return?” or “which finds the shortest path in a graph with unequal costs?”. Trap: BFS is optimal only with equal costs. A DFS answer depends on neighbour order, so write your order down; a different order gives a different (still valid) path.
Slides vs lecture notes

The BFS and DFS slides for the graph (pp. 50, 52) show the unweighted layout only; no queue, order or answer is printed. The orders above are ours. If a question gives a different tie-break, redo the table with it.

6 · Dijkstra’s algorithm pp. 56–58

Picture

Dijkstra (1959) “searches outwards in order of cost from the start” (p.56). It always expands the node with the smallest past cost \(g\). Because edge costs are not negative, once a node is expanded no cheaper way to it can appear later, so its \(g\) is final. The slide’s table (p.57) is blank; its rows are past cost and parent node.

The weakness (p.58): it “doesn’t really know the goal exists until it reaches it”, so it expands nodes in every direction. The slide asks: can we guide the search toward the goal without breaking the rule that a node is accepted only with its lowest cost of arrival? That is A*.

Algorithm

Keep an open set (discovered, not yet expanded) with tentative costs, and a closed set (expanded, cost final). Start: \(g(\text{start})=0\).

  1. Pop the open node \(n\) with the smallest \(g\) (ties: alphabetical). Move it to closed.
  2. If \(n\) is the goal, stop.
  3. For each neighbour \(m\) of \(n\) not in closed, with edge cost \(w\): if \(g(n)+w\lt g(m)\) (or \(m\) is new), set \(g(m)=g(n)+w\), parent\((m)=n\), and put \(m\) in open (this is relaxation).
  4. Repeat. Trace the parents back from the goal.

Correct only for non-negative edge costs. Dijkstra is A* with \(h=0\).

Worked example (worked by us, verified by script)

The slide’s weighted graph, start A, goal K. Tie-break: alphabetical (no tie actually occurs). Each row lists the open set after expanding the node, as node, tentative \(g\), parent.

StepExpand n (g)Open set after expanding: node g (parent)Closed

The filled-in version of the slide’s empty table (p.57):

Path: K ← J ← H ← F ← C ← A, that is A–C–F–H–J–K, cost 25. Two updates to notice: at step 5, G drops from 17 (via D) to 14 (via F); at step 10, K drops from 26 (via I) to 25 (via J). K is expanded last (11th) because it has the largest \(g\), 25. checked

Exam recipe
  1. Draw the table: columns = nodes; rows = past cost, parent. Set \(g(A)=0\), the rest unknown.
  2. Repeat: pick the smallest \(g\) among unexpanded nodes, fix it, relax each neighbour.
  3. Update a node only if the new \(g\) is strictly smaller.
  4. Stop when the goal is chosen for expansion (not when it is first discovered: K was discovered at step 9 with \(g=26\), but the best is 25).
  5. Sanity check: the goal’s \(g\) equals the sum of edge costs along the traced path.
Trap: stopping when K is first reached gives 26, not 25. Another: relaxing a closed node. Dijkstra is “uninformed”: it uses no knowledge of where the goal is.

7 · A* and heuristics pp. 59–62

Picture

A* is a “focused search that prioritises searching towards the goal, exploiting some knowledge about it” (p.59). Each node carries two numbers: the past cost \(g(n)\) (the slide’s blue arrow, A to D = 8, “cost to arrive at node n”) and an optimistic cost to go \(h(n)\) (the red arrow, D to K = 13, “optimistic cost from node n to goal”). A* expands the open node with the smallest sum.

Derivation \[ f(n)=g(n)+h(n) \qquad (\text{p.59}) \]

\(g(n)\): cost of the best path found so far from the start to \(n\). \(h(n)\): estimated cost from \(n\) to the goal. \(f(n)\): estimated total cost of a path through \(n\). A* = Dijkstra with the priority \(g\) replaced by \(f\); stop when the goal is expanded.

What a good heuristic needs (p.61): fast to compute, reasonably close to the real cost, admissible and consistent. With \(d(n,\text{goal})\) the true cheapest cost from \(n\) to the goal and \(d(n,m)\) the cost of the edge between neighbours \(n\), \(m\):

\[ \text{admissible: } h(n)\le d(n,\text{goal})\ \ \forall n, \qquad \text{consistent: } h(n)\le d(n,m)+h(m)\ \ \forall \text{ neighbours } n,m \]

Admissible means never overestimates (note the non-strict \(\le\): \(h=d\) is allowed). Consistent is the triangle inequality: the estimate may not drop by more than the edge you walked. Consistent \(\Rightarrow\) admissible (given \(h(\text{goal})=0\)), but not the other way round. Typical choices on a grid: Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance, or zero (which turns A* into Dijkstra).

  • Admissible h keeps A* optimal: if \(h\) never overestimates, no better route can hide behind a node whose \(f\) is too high.
  • Consistent h additionally makes the popped \(f\) values non-decreasing and means a closed node never needs re-opening. The lecture asks for both; strictly, admissibility gives optimality with re-opening, and consistency is what lets you use a simple closed set.
  • Overestimating h can send A* the wrong way: it returns a path that may not be optimal.

Comparison (p.62): on one grid with a wall, A* took 277 operations, BFS 1413, Dijkstra 1378 (source on the slide: PathFinding.js visualiser). So A* did about \(1378/277=4.97\) times fewer operations than Dijkstra. checked The figure comes from one demo; do not quote it as a general ratio.

Exam recipe
  1. Write \(h\) beside every node. Check admissibility: compare each \(h(n)\) with the true remaining cost (find it by inspection or a backward Dijkstra).
  2. Check consistency edge by edge, in both directions where \(h\) differs: \(h(n)\le w+h(m)\).
  3. Run the table: pop the smallest \(f=g+h\) (tie: smaller \(h\), then alphabetical; say so). Relax neighbours with \(g(n)+w\).
  4. Stop when the goal is popped. Trace the parents. Report order, path, cost.
  5. Sanity check: \(f(\text{goal})=g(\text{goal})\) = path cost; no open node should have \(f\) below it if \(h\) is admissible; unexpanded nodes (E here) are the saving over Dijkstra.
Worked example (worked by us, verified by script)

The slide’s graph with the red heuristic values (p.59): \(h\) = A 20, B 10, C 17, D 13, E 8, G 8, H 7, I 2, J 2; K = 0 (not printed, the goal). F has no red label (see the box below); we use \(h(F)=9\), the one number printed beside F. Tie-break: lowest \(f\), then lowest \(h\), then alphabetical (no ties occur).

Admissibility. True costs to K: \(d(H)=7\) (H–J–K), \(d(J)=3\), \(d(I)=5\), \(d(G)=12\) (G–I–K), \(d(F)=14\) (F–H–J–K), \(d(C)=19\), \(d(D)=21\), \(d(A)=25\), \(d(B)=35\), \(d(E)=44\). Every \(h(n)\le d(n)\), so \(h\) is admissible, tight at H (7 = 7). checked

Consistency. Two edges break it: H→J: \(h(H)=7\gt d(H,J)+h(J)=4+2=6\); and C→F: \(h(C)=17\gt 5+h(F)=14\) (with \(h(F)=9\)). So \(h\) is admissible but not consistent. In fact no value of \(h(F)\) makes it consistent: C needs \(h(F)\ge 12\) but G needs \(h(F)\le 11\). checked
