\(\mathbf v=u\hat x+v\hat y\), so \(\mathbf a=\dot u\hat x+\dot v\hat y+u\dot{\hat x}+v\dot{\hat y}=(\dot u-v\dot\theta)\hat x+(\dot v+u\dot\theta)\hat y\).

\(a_x=0.3-0.2(0.8)=0.14\) m/s²; \(a_y=-0.1+1.5(0.8)=1.1\) m/s². checked

Physical reading. Driving at 1.5 m/s while turning at 0.8 rad/s needs a sideways acceleration \(u\dot\theta=1.2\) m/s² (centripetal) even though the robot never slides: a 12 kg chassis needs a sideways force of \(12(1.1)=13.2\) N, supplied by the tyres (the no-slip reaction).

A finite difference of the world-frame velocity confirms \((0.14,\,1.1)\).

Common wrong answer. Using the slide’s \(+v\dot\theta\) in the y-equation gives \(a_y=0.06\). Check with the pure-turn case \(v=0\): the acceleration must be \(u\dot\theta\), perpendicular to the velocity.

Q11.5 · Why the dynamics matrix changes when C is not Gexplaincalculate

(a) For a 12 kg chassis with \({}^GI=0.4\) kg·m², explain how \(\mathbf M\) differs between \(C=G\) and \(G\) offset 0.1 m ahead of \(C\); what couples the equations? (b) Give \(M_{33}\) for the 0.1 m offset. (c) For \(C=G\), \(u=2\) m/s, \(v=0\) and \(\dot\theta=0.5\) rad/s, what is the velocity-term \(c_y\) in \(\mathbf M\dot{\boldsymbol\zeta}+c={}^C\mathbf Q\), and what does it mean?

Hint 1

For \(C=G\): \(\mathbf M=\operatorname{diag}(m,m,{}^GI)\). For an offset, parallel axis theorem.

Hint 2

\(c=(-mv\dot\theta,\;mu\dot\theta,\;0)\) for \(C=G\).

Full solution

(a) For \(C=G\) the matrix is diagonal, \(\operatorname{diag}(m,m,{}^GI)\): force and torque are independent. With \(G\) offset by \((x_G,y_G)\) the off-diagonal entries \(-my_G\) and \(mx_G\) appear: a force at \(C\) produces rotation about \(G\) and vice versa (the robot swings about its centre of mass, so \(C\) accelerates sideways when torque is applied). The matrix stays symmetric and constant.

(b) \(M_{33}={}^GI+m(x_G^2+y_G^2)=0.4+12(0.1)^2=0.52\) kg·m² (parallel-axis theorem). checked

(c) \(c_y=mu\dot\theta=12(2)(0.5)=12\) N. checked It is the sideways force the tyres must supply to turn the velocity vector with the body (centripetal force); it exists even at constant \(u\) and \(\dot\theta\) and vanishes at rest.

Common wrong answer. “\(c\) is zero for constant velocity.” Constant speed along a rotating axis is still accelerating.

Q11.6 · Spot the errors: wheel forces and framesspot the error

A student writes: “For a differential drive with \(a=0.2\) m, \(F_1=3\) N (left), \(F_2=7\) N (right), the torque is \(n_z=2a(F_2-F_1)=1.6\) N·m. The robot is simulated with inverse dynamics, and the load in the chassis frame is \({}^C\mathbf Q=\mathbf J\,{}^O\mathbf Q\).” Find the three errors and give the correct \(n_z\).

Hint 1

Each wheel acts at a distance \(a\) from the axle midpoint.

Hint 2

Which dynamics problem takes forces as input?

Full solution

Error 1. Each wheel pushes at lever arm \(a\) about the midpoint: \(n_z=-aF_1+aF_2=a(F_2-F_1)=0.2(4)=0.8\) N·m. checked Using \(2a\) doubles it.

Error 2. Simulating from known forces is forward dynamics (forces in, motion out). Inverse dynamics takes the desired motion and returns the forces.

Error 3. \({}^C\mathbf Q=\mathbf J^\top\,{}^O\mathbf Q\) (equivalently \(\mathbf J^{-1}\,{}^O\mathbf Q\) for a rotation), not \(\mathbf J\,{}^O\mathbf Q\). The latter is the map from chassis to world.

W12 · Planning algorithms

Q12.1 · Growing an obstacle: derive the area formula (W13-style)derivecalculate

A disc robot of radius \(r\) is shrunk to a point and every obstacle is grown by \(r\). (a) For a convex polygon of area \(A\) and perimeter \(P\), derive the area of the grown obstacle. (b) Evaluate for a rectangular obstacle \(3.0\times1.5\) m with \(r=0.4\) m and compare with the (wrong) rectangular margin of \(r\) on every side.

Hint 1

Split the grown region into: the original polygon, one strip of width \(r\) along every edge, and a circular sector at every vertex.

Hint 2

The sectors at the vertices have exterior angles that add up to \(2\pi\) in total.

Full solution

(a) The grown shape is the original polygon, plus a rectangle \(\ell_i\times r\) on each edge of length \(\ell_i\), plus a circular sector at each vertex. The strips add \(\sum\ell_ir=Pr\). The sector at a vertex has radius \(r\) and angle equal to the exterior angle \(\varepsilon_j\), so area \(\tfrac12r^2\varepsilon_j\). For a convex polygon \(\sum\varepsilon_j=2\pi\), so the sectors add \(\tfrac12r^2(2\pi)=\pi r^2\). Hence (Steiner) \[ A_{grown}=A+Pr+\pi r^2 . \] (b) \(A=3.0(1.5)=4.5\) m², \(P=2(3.0+1.5)=9.0\) m. \(Pr=9.0(0.4)=3.6\); \(\pi r^2=\pi(0.16)=0.5027\). \(A_{grown}=4.5+3.6+0.5027=8.6027\) m². checked A Monte-Carlo estimate of the grown region gave 8.603.

A square margin would give \((3.0+0.8)(1.5+0.8)=8.74\) m²: it overstates the blocked area by the four corner pieces, about 0.14 m².

Common wrong answer. Adding \(r\) to each side (the square margin) or forgetting the \(\pi r^2\) corner term.

Q12.2 · How many samples before a PRM or RRT hits the goal?derivecalculate

A planner draws uniform random points in a \(10\times10\) m map. The goal is a disc of radius 0.8 m (fully inside the map). Derive the probability that at least one of \(N\) independent samples lands in the goal, then find the expected number of samples to the first hit and the smallest \(N\) that gives a 95 % chance of at least one hit.

Hint 1

One sample hits with probability \(p=\text{goal area}/\text{map area}\).

Hint 2

None of \(N\) samples hits with probability \((1-p)^N\). Solve \(1-(1-p)^N\ge0.95\) with logarithms.

Full solution

\(p=\pi(0.8)^2/100=0.020106\). The samples are independent, so \(P(\text{no hit in }N)=(1-p)^N\) and \(P(\text{at least one})=1-(1-p)^N\).

The number of draws to the first hit is geometric with mean \(1/p=49.74\). checked At \(N=50\) the chance of a hit is only \(1-(1-p)^{50}=0.638\). checked

For 95 %: \((1-p)^N\le0.05\Rightarrow N\ge\dfrac{\ln0.05}{\ln(1-p)}=\dfrac{-2.9957}{-0.02031}=147.5\), so \(N=148\). checked Check: \(N=147\) gives \(0.9498\lt0.95\); \(N=148\) gives \(\ge0.95\).

Meaning. This is the sense of “probabilistically complete”: as \(N\to\infty\), \(1-(1-p)^N\to1\). It also shows that narrow goals or passages (small \(p\)) need many samples, and that the planner can never prove no path exists.

Common wrong answer. Saying 50 samples suffice for 95 %.

Q12.3 · A* versus Dijkstra on a small graphcalculate

An undirected graph has edges S–A 4, S–B 2, B–A 1, A–C 5, B–D 7, C–G 3, D–G 3. The heuristic is \(h(S)=9\), \(h(A)=7\), \(h(B)=8\), \(h(C)=3\), \(h(D)=3\), \(h(G)=0\). Run A* from S to G with the rule “expand the lowest \(f=g+h\); stop when the goal is expanded”. Give the path cost, the number of nodes A* expands (including G), and the number Dijkstra expands.

Hint 1

Start: S has \(g=0\), \(f=9\). Expand it and list A (g 4) and B (g 2) with their \(f\).

Hint 2

Dijkstra is A* with \(h=0\): expand the lowest \(g\).

Hint 3

Count the goal as expanded when it is popped.

Full solution

A* table (open set after each expansion, \(g+h=f\)):

stepexpandfopen set afterwards
1S0+9=9B 2+8=10; A 4+7=11
2B2+8=10A 3+7=10 (via B); D 9+3=12
3A3+7=10C 8+3=11; D 12
4C8+3=11G 11+0=11; D 12
5G11stop: goal expanded

Path S–B–A–C–G, cost \(2+1+5+3=11\). A* expands 5 nodes; D is discovered (\(f=12\)) but never expanded. checked

Dijkstra expands S (0), B (2), A (3), C (8), D (9), G (11): 6 expansions, the same path and cost. checked D has \(g=9\lt11\), so Dijkstra must expand it; A* skips it because \(f(D)=12\gt11\).

Is \(h\) valid? True costs to G: \(C=3\), \(D=3\), \(A=8\), \(B=9\), \(S=11\). Every \(h\le\) these, so admissible; also \(h(n)\le w+h(m)\) on every edge in both directions, so consistent. checked If \(h(A)\) were overestimated as 30, A* would skip A and return S–B–D–G at cost 12, which is not optimal. checked

Common wrong answer. Counting 6 expansions for A*, or stopping the moment G is first discovered.

Q12.4 · Grid size and heuristicscalculate

(a) A 5-dimensional C-space is gridded with 50 cells per dimension. How many nodes? (b) A 4-connected \(40\times25\) grid has how many edges? (c) On an 8-connected grid (straight cost 1, diagonal cost \(\sqrt2\)) with no obstacles, what is the true cost from cell (0,0) to (7,5)? The Manhattan distance is 12; is it admissible?

Hint 1

Nodes \(N^d\). Neighbours: \(2d\) (axis-aligned) or \(3^d-1\) (with diagonals).

Hint 2

Edges of an \(m\times n\) 4-connected grid: \(m(n-1)+n(m-1)\).

Hint 3

Best path: \(\min(\Delta r,\Delta c)\) diagonal steps, then straight steps for the rest.

Full solution

(a) \(50^5=312\,500\,000\) nodes. checked Each node has 10 axis neighbours or \(3^5-1=242\) with diagonals. The count grows exponentially with the dimension, which is why grid methods fail for arms and why PRM and RRT are used.

(b) Count per direction: \(m(n-1)=40(24)=960\) edges along one axis and \(n(m-1)=25(39)=975\) along the other. Total \(1935\) (of \(1000\) nodes). checked Compare \(2\times1000=2000\), which overcounts the missing border edges.

(c) \(\Delta=(7,5)\): 5 diagonal steps and \(7-5=2\) straight steps: \(5\sqrt2+2=9.0711\). checked A Dijkstra search on the 8-connected grid gives the same. The Manhattan distance 12 exceeds the true cost 9.07, so it is not admissible with diagonal moves. The Euclidean distance \(\sqrt{49+25}=8.602\le9.071\) is admissible. checked

Common wrong answer. Using Manhattan with 8-connected moves and calling A* optimal.

Q12.5 · Can the robot get through, and which planner?explaincalculate

A disc-shaped robot of radius 0.5 m must pass a 0.9 m wide corridor. (a) Show it cannot pass by working in configuration space. (b) What is the largest radius that could pass? (c) The robot is a 7-joint arm with a known map; a colleague proposes a visibility graph. Explain what is wrong and what you would use instead, with the correct completeness wording.

Hint 1

Shrink the robot to a point and grow each wall by \(r\): the corridor shrinks by \(2r\).

Hint 2

Visibility graphs are for 2D polygon maps. What does a 7D C-space look like?

Full solution

(a) Both walls grow by \(r=0.5\) m, so the point robot’s free width is \(0.9-2(0.5)=-0.1\) m. Negative: the inflated walls overlap and there is no free configuration across the corridor. checked

(b) Need \(0.9-2r\ge0\), so \(r\le0.45\) m. (A robot of radius 0.4 m has free width 0.1 m and just fits.) checked

(c) A visibility graph needs explicit polygons in a 2D plane and gives the shortest path there. The arm’s C-space has seven dimensions and curved obstacle regions; building \(\mathcal C_{obs}\) explicitly is impractical, and a grid would have \(N^7\) nodes. Use a sampling-based planner (PRM for repeated queries on a static map, RRT for a single query), which only needs a collision checker. Its guarantee is probabilistically complete, not “complete”: if a path exists, the probability of finding it tends to 1 as the samples tend to infinity; there is no termination guarantee if none exists, and the path is usually not the shortest.

Common wrong answer. “PRM/RRT are complete” or “guarantee the shortest path”.

Q12.6 · Spot the errors: stopping rule and optimalityspot the error

A graph has edges S–A 2, S–B 3, A–G 9, B–C 2, C–G 4. A student runs Dijkstra from S to G and writes: “Expanding S discovers A (2) and B (3). Expanding A discovers G at cost 11, so I stop: the shortest path is S–A–G, cost 11. BFS would also be optimal here, and A* is always optimal.” Find the errors and give the true shortest cost.

Hint 1

A node’s cost is final only when it is expanded, not when it is first discovered.

Hint 2

After A, which node has the lowest cost in the open set?

Full solution

Error 1: stopping at discovery. Dijkstra expands S (0), then A (2), which discovers G at 11. The open set is now B 3, G 11. B (3) is expanded next and discovers C at 5; C (5) is expanded and improves G to \(5+4=9\). Only then is G the lowest-cost open node, so it is expanded last with cost 9. Path S–B–C–G, cost \(3+2+4=9\). checked

Error 2: BFS. BFS returns the path with the fewest edges, here S–A–G (2 edges, cost 11), which is not the cheapest. BFS is optimal only when all edges cost the same.

Error 3: A*. A* is optimal only if \(h\) is admissible (never overestimates; with a simple closed set, also consistent). An overestimating \(h\) can make A* return a worse path.

Common wrong answer. Cost 11, from stopping at discovery.
